memory.abstract: This paper presents a deep learning-assisted framework that uses polymer fingerprints and graph neural networks to predict and screen high-efficiency donor–acceptor combinations for organic photovoltaics, experimentally validating a novel D18:BTP-S11 blend with 19.32% power conversion efficiency and deriving interpretable molecular design rules.

content.background: Organic photovoltaic (OPV) devices have demonstrated significant progress, with certified power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) of single-junction cells now exceeding 19%. This advancement is largely attributed to innovations in donor (D) and acceptor (A) molecular design, particularly through the development of bulk heterojunction (BHJ) active layers composed of optimized D–A combinations. Donors have evolved from homopolymers to donor–acceptor copolymers, while acceptors have transitioned from fullerenes to non-fullerene types, including fused-ring (e.g., Y6) and non-fused-ring structures. According to the Shockley–Queisser theory, reducing energy losses below 0.4 eV could enable PCEs beyond 20%. However, the vast chemical space of possible D and A structures—and their near-infinite combinations—makes traditional trial-and-error experimental screening prohibitively time-consuming and costly. Although machine learning (ML) has emerged as a data-driven strategy for OPV material design, existing models suffer from limited accuracy (R² ≈ 0.5–0.6), insufficient generalizability (often restricted to fixed D or A components), and inadequate structural representation—frequently relying on energy-level descriptors rather than direct chemical structure inputs. These models often neglect critical topological features such as polymer chain connectivity or 3D fused-ring architectures. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a robust, generalizable, and interpretable framework capable of high-throughput screening of novel D–A combinations with high predictive fidelity. This work addresses these bottlenecks by introducing a deep learning (DL)-assisted design paradigm that leverages end-to-end graph neural networks (GNNs) and a novel polymer fingerprint representation to directly link molecular structure to photovoltaic performance, enabling efficient exploration of uncharted chemical space.
content.method:
The core of the proposed framework is a deep learning-assisted pipeline for the rational design of high-efficiency donor–acceptor combinations in OPV materials. The methodology comprises four synergistic components: (1) a novel digital representation scheme called 'polymer fingerprints', (2) a high-quality, comprehensive OPV material database, (3) end-to-end graph neural network (GNN) prediction models, and (4) high-throughput virtual screening coupled with structural gene analysis.

First, to accurately encode the complex topological features of both polymeric donors and small-molecule acceptors, the authors developed a graph-based polymer fingerprint method. Unlike SMILES-based or descriptor-only approaches, this method represents each molecule as a graph where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Atomic features (element type, valence, hybridization, etc.) are embedded into initial atomic fingerprint vectors. An adjacency matrix encodes connectivity, including polymerization sites for donors. These are processed through a message-passing neural network (MPN), which iteratively updates atomic representations by aggregating neighborhood information. The final molecular fingerprint is obtained by summing all updated atomic vectors, thereby preserving both local chemical environments and global topology—including chain periodicity in polymers and fused-ring architectures in acceptors.

Second, a curated database was constructed from literature up to November 2023, containing 2,078 D–A combinations (442 donors, 1,397 acceptors), along with experimental PCE, J_SC, V_OC, FF, and energy levels (HOMO/LUMO). Only the highest reported PCE per combination was retained to reflect intrinsic material potential. t-SNE analysis confirmed that the collected structures span the known chemical space, with donors clustering at the periphery of polymer databases and acceptors (especially fused-ring types like Y6) occupying distinct regions.

Third, end-to-end GNN models were trained to predict photovoltaic properties directly from chemical structures. Inputs include three vector types: (i) polymer fingerprints, (ii) dimensionality-reduced Mordred descriptors (retaining 95% variance via PCA), and (iii) energy-level vectors derived from HOMO/LUMO values. These are concatenated and fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with dropout regularization and early stopping to prevent overfitting. The models predict PCE, J_SC, V_OC, and FF independently, yet remain physically consistent—predicted values satisfy PCE ≈ J_SC × V_OC × FF, as verified by a correlation coefficient of 0.94 between direct and calculated PCEs.

Finally, the framework enables high-throughput virtual screening: all 442 donors and 1,397 acceptors were combinatorially paired to generate ≈617,474 virtual D–A combinations. The trained models predicted their PCEs, identifying 20,247 candidates with PCE > 15%. Structural gene analysis quantified the contribution of each D or A as the fraction of its combinations exceeding 15% PCE. Substructure analysis further dissected BTP-based acceptors into core, side chains, and end groups to derive design rules.
content.experiment:
The experimental validation followed a multi-stage protocol. First, data collection yielded 2,078 D–A combinations with associated photovoltaic metrics. The dataset was split 80:10:10 into training, test, and validation sets. Model performance was evaluated using R² and mean absolute error (MAE), with hyperparameter tuning and regularization (dropout, early stopping) applied to mitigate overfitting.

Baseline comparisons were implicit: the authors noted that prior ML models achieved R² ≈ 0.5–0.6 for PCE prediction, whereas their GNN model reached R² = 0.74 (test) and 0.70 (validation) for overall PCE, with similar performance for fused-ring (R² = 0.74/0.70) and non-fused-ring (R² = 0.74/0.74) acceptors. Models for J_SC, V_OC, and FF also achieved R² ≈ 0.70, demonstrating consistent accuracy across properties.

For high-throughput screening, 617,474 virtual D–A combinations were generated by pairing all 442 donors with all 1,397 acceptors. The DL models predicted PCEs for all, identifying 20,247 combinations (>15% PCE). From these, 34 key donors and 100 key acceptors were selected based on top 10% appearance frequency. A heatmap of their combinations highlighted unexplored high-efficiency pairs.

Experimental verification focused on six D–A combinations: PM6:m-BTP-PhC6, PM6:BTP-Th, PM6:N3, D18:N3, PM6:BTP-S11, and D18:BTP-S11. These were chosen for synthetic accessibility, structural diversity (symmetric/asymmetric acceptors), and predicted PCE range (16–19%). Devices were fabricated using standard BHJ processing, and J–V curves were measured under AM1.5G illumination. Energy levels were characterized via cyclic voltammetry.

Ablation or sensitivity analyses included: (1) t-SNE visualization of chemical space coverage, (2) correlation analysis of photovoltaic parameters (e.g., PCE–J_SC: r = 0.935; PCE–V_OC: r = 0.124), (3) model consistency checks (direct vs. calculated PCE), and (4) substructure frequency analysis for BTP-based acceptors (102 real + 45,084 virtual combinations). Processing condition effects were acknowledged but not modeled due to data heterogeneity.
content.result:
The DL models achieved high prediction accuracy, with R² values of 0.74 (test) and 0.70 (validation) for PCE across diverse D–A combinations. Experimental validation of six screened combinations confirmed exceptional fidelity: measured PCEs (17.58–19.32%) closely matched predictions, with an average accuracy exceeding 96%. Notably, the D18:BTP-S11 combination—previously unreported—achieved 19.32% PCE, among the highest for binary single-junction OPVs. Four of the six tested pairs were absent from the training database, yet were accurately predicted, demonstrating strong extrapolation capability.

Structural gene analysis revealed that top-performing donors include PTzBI-Si, PBZ-2Si, and D18, while effective acceptors are predominantly asymmetric BTP derivatives (e.g., BTP-S12, BTTPC-Br). Substructure analysis of BTP-based acceptors showed that high-efficiency combinations favor: (1) aryl-containing outer side chains paired with branched alkyl inner chains, (2) halogenated thiophene or selenophene side chains, and (3) halogenated aromatic end groups. These findings align with known structure–property relationships and even retrospectively explain the success of the record-efficiency L8-BO acceptor, whose fragments matched top-ranked substructures.

The framework’s main advantage is its ability to navigate vast chemical space efficiently, identifying promising candidates without exhaustive synthesis. Limitations include reliance on existing energy-level data as model inputs—future work will integrate energy-level prediction—and the current omission of explicit morphology descriptors, though solubility/compatibility effects are implicitly captured. The approach is extensible to other OPV material classes and could incorporate processing condition data once standardized. Overall, this work establishes a paradigm for AI-accelerated materials discovery with experimental validation and interpretable design rules.

memory.abstract: This perspective argues that combining accurate black-box deep learning models with chemistry-aware explainable AI methods—such as molecular counterfactuals and descriptor-based natural language explanations—can uncover scientifically meaningful structure–property relationships while maintaining predictive performance.

content.background: Deep learning (DL) models have demonstrated remarkable success in computational chemistry, accurately capturing complex nonlinear structure–property relationships across applications ranging from quantum chemistry to drug discovery and materials design. However, their "black-box" nature—stemming from high parameter counts and opaque internal representations—limits trust, adoption, and scientific utility among chemists. Unlike in domains such as image recognition, where explanations may not yield new scientific insight, in chemistry, understanding *why* a model makes a prediction can directly inform hypotheses about underlying physical or biochemical mechanisms. This interpretability gap is especially critical as AI systems begin to influence high-stakes decisions involving toxicity, environmental impact, or drug efficacy, where regulatory frameworks increasingly demand justifiable predictions. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses this challenge by providing post-hoc or intrinsic methods to interpret model behavior. While XAI is well-established in computer vision and natural language processing, its adaptation to molecular data requires domain-specific considerations: explanations must align with chemical intuition, use chemically meaningful representations, and ideally suggest actionable modifications. Existing approaches often fall short in one or more of these criteria—e.g., feature attribution methods like SHAP yield complete but non-sparse and non-actionable explanations, while many counterfactual generators produce chemically invalid structures or are model-specific. This paper argues that a two-step paradigm—first building a highly accurate black-box model, then applying chemistry-aware XAI techniques—can reconcile the accuracy–interpretability trade-off and recover scientifically meaningful structure–property relationships without sacrificing predictive performance.
content.method: The paper presents a perspective on XAI in molecular property prediction, focusing on two model-agnostic post-hoc explanation methods developed by the authors: Molecular Model Agnostic Counterfactual Explanations (MMACE) and descriptor-based explanations with natural language summaries. MMACE generates counterfactual molecules—minimal structural modifications that alter the model’s prediction—by leveraging the SELFIES molecular representation and the STONED algorithm to explore a local chemical neighborhood around a base molecule. Starting from a given molecule encoded in SELFIES (a robust, surjective string-based representation), MMACE applies random string mutations to generate nearby valid molecules. The black-box model then predicts properties for these variants, and those with contrasting predictions (e.g., switching from non-permeable to permeable for blood–brain barrier tasks) are selected as counterfactuals, ranked by Tanimoto similarity of ECFP4 fingerprints to ensure chemical proximity. This approach guarantees chemically valid outputs and works for both classification and regression. In contrast, the descriptor explanation method fits a local surrogate model—specifically, a weighted least-squares linear regression—using chemically interpretable features (e.g., Mordred descriptors, MACCS keys, or ECFP substructures) instead of raw model inputs. The surrogate approximates the black-box model’s behavior in the vicinity of the instance, and the resulting regression coefficients quantify each descriptor’s contribution to the prediction. Positive coefficients indicate features that increase the predicted property, while negative ones decrease it. Crucially, MACCS descriptors are mapped to human-readable SMARTS patterns, enabling automatic generation of natural language explanations (NLEs) that summarize the rationale in domain-relevant terms (e.g., "carboxylic acid groups enhance solubility due to hydrogen bonding"). Both methods are grounded in the principle that explanations should be faithful to the model, sparse, actionable, and expressed in the language of chemistry. The paper also contextualizes these approaches within broader XAI taxonomy: MMACE falls under counterfactual/contrastive explanations, while descriptor explanations align with surrogate modeling (akin to LIME but chemistry-optimized). The theoretical foundation draws on game theory (for attribution completeness), causal reasoning (for counterfactuals), and human-centered design principles emphasizing domain applicability and correctness relative to known physical mechanisms.
content.experiment: The authors illustrate their XAI methods through three application domains using models and datasets from their prior work. For blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability prediction, they trained two models on the Martins et al. dataset: a random forest (RF) using Mordred descriptors and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) RNN processing molecular strings. MMACE was applied to the RF to generate counterfactuals for a non-permeable molecule, while the GRU was explained via descriptor attributions. In solubility prediction, an RNN was trained on the AqSolDB database to predict log molarity; MMACE produced counterfactuals by minimizing structural distance while ensuring a solubility change exceeding a threshold (Δ), and descriptor explanations used ECFP and MACCS fingerprints. For molecular scent—a multilabel classification task—they trained a graph neural network (GNN) on a dataset where molecules are labeled with multiple odor descriptors (e.g., "fatty", "pineapple"). MMACE was adapted to preserve non-target scents while flipping the target label, and global descriptor explanations aggregated attributions across many "fatty"-scented molecules to derive general structure–odor rules. Baselines are not directly compared in new experiments; instead, the paper references prior benchmarks (e.g., Rao et al. and Sanchez-Lengeling et al.) that evaluated gradient-based and graph explanation methods on molecular tasks, showing integrated gradients and CAM perform well for GNNs. The focus is on qualitative validation: do the explanations align with established chemical knowledge? For instance, counterfactuals for BBB permeability correctly highlight removal of hydrophilic carboxylic acid groups, and solubility explanations emphasize polar functional groups. Natural language outputs are manually assessed for scientific plausibility. Ablation studies are not performed; instead, the paper emphasizes the interpretability and actionability of the outputs as evidence of utility.
content.result: The results demonstrate that both MMACE and descriptor explanations yield chemically intuitive, actionable insights consistent with known structure–property relationships. In BBB permeability, MMACE counterfactuals show that removing or modifying carboxylic acid groups enables permeation—aligning with literature on hydrophobicity and molecular surface area as key determinants. Descriptor explanations for alprazolam correctly identify aromaticity as favorable and hydrogen bond donors as detrimental to BBB penetration. For solubility, counterfactuals reveal that ester modifications and heteroatom changes significantly affect predictions, while descriptor attributions quantitatively link carboxylic acid and heteroaromatic groups to higher solubility, with NLEs providing mechanistic rationales (e.g., hydrogen bonding with water). In scent prediction, the methods recover known rules: "fatty" scents correlate with long alkyl chains (heptanyl fragments) and carbonyl groups, while "pineapple" is associated with esters and absence of aromatic rings—both supported by prior studies on volatile organic compounds. These findings validate the two-step XAI paradigm: accurate black-box models, when paired with chemistry-aware explanation methods, can uncover scientifically meaningful relationships without sacrificing performance. However, limitations remain: MMACE does not guarantee chemical stability of counterfactuals, and both methods depend on the black-box model’s correctness—if the model learns spurious correlations, explanations will reflect those errors. Future directions include developing better molecular distance metrics beyond fingerprint similarity, incorporating synthesis feasibility into counterfactual generation, and establishing standardized benchmarks for XAI evaluation in chemistry, such as using Crippen logP as a ground-truth proxy for attribution correctness.

memory.abstract: Uni-Mol+ significantly improves quantum chemical property prediction accuracy by iteratively refining inexpensive 3D molecular conformations toward DFT-equilibrium structures using a novel two-track Transformer and a pseudo-trajectory training strategy.

content.background: Quantum chemical (QC) property prediction is essential for the computational design of novel materials and molecules, enabling high-throughput screening for desired properties such as free energy or the HOMO-LUMO gap. However, traditional electronic structure methods like density functional theory (DFT) are computationally expensive, often requiring hours per molecule, which limits their scalability. Recent deep learning approaches have sought to accelerate QC property prediction by training neural networks on molecular representations, bypassing costly DFT calculations. Most prior methods rely on 1D SMILES sequences or 2D molecular graphs as input due to their ease of acquisition. Yet, these formats fundamentally mismatch the physical reality that QC properties are derived from 3D equilibrium conformations optimized via DFT—conformations that encode critical spatial and geometric information absent in 1D/2D representations. This discrepancy severely limits the accuracy achievable by existing models. Although some recent works have begun incorporating 3D structural information—either by enhancing 2D representations with latent 3D cues or by using precomputed 3D coordinates—their inference still often depends solely on 2D data or assumes access to high-quality DFT conformations during testing, which is impractical in real-world applications. Moreover, methods that do use 3D inputs typically treat the conformation as static rather than iteratively refining it toward equilibrium. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing Uni-Mol+, a framework that explicitly learns to transform inexpensive, low-fidelity 3D conformations (e.g., generated by RDKit) into accurate DFT-equivalent structures through an iterative neural update process, thereby aligning the model’s internal representation with the true physical basis of QC properties.
content.method:
Uni-Mol+ introduces a two-stage paradigm: first, it generates a raw 3D molecular conformation from 1D/2D data using fast tools like RDKit; second, it iteratively refines this conformation toward the DFT-optimized equilibrium structure using a specialized neural architecture, after which QC properties are predicted from the refined geometry. The core innovation lies in jointly learning conformation refinement and property prediction within a unified end-to-end framework.

The model backbone is a two-track Transformer, inspired by Uni-Mol but significantly enhanced. It maintains separate atom-level (x ∈ ℝ^{n×d_x}) and pair-level (p ∈ ℝ^{n×n×d_p}) representations across L blocks. Atom features (X), edge features (E), and initial 3D coordinates (r) serve as inputs. The pair representation is initialized with rich positional encodings combining three components: (1) 3D spatial encoding via Gaussian kernels applied to interatomic distances, (2) shortest-path graph encoding (ψ^{SP}) capturing topological proximity, and (3) efficient one-hop bond encoding (ψ^{Bond}) replacing the multi-hop scheme in Graphormer. This hybrid encoding ensures both geometric and topological context is preserved.

Within each block, the atom track is updated via a self-attention mechanism biased by the pair representation (SelfAttentionPairBias), allowing pairwise geometric relationships to modulate attention weights. The pair track is updated through three sequential operations: (i) an OuterProduct of atom representations to enable atom-to-pair communication, (ii) a TriangularUpdate operator adapted from AlphaFold’s Evoformer—merging “incoming” and “outgoing” triangular attention into a single step for efficiency—to propagate long-range geometric dependencies, and (iii) a feed-forward network (FFN). These updates enable bidirectional information flow between atom and pair tracks, crucial for modeling complex 3D interactions.

Crucially, Uni-Mol+ performs R iterative updates of the 3D coordinates using a shared-weight backbone. At iteration i, the model takes r^{(i−1)} as input and outputs both a refined conformation r^{(i)} and the final QC property prediction. This mimics physical relaxation processes but requires only 1–2 iterations, far fewer than molecular dynamics or deep potential methods.

Training employs a novel pseudo-trajectory strategy to overcome the lack of intermediate conformations in datasets. Assuming a linear path between RDKit-generated r^{init} and DFT-optimized r^{tgt}, the model samples an intermediate conformation r^{(0)} = q·r^{init} + (1−q)(r^{tgt} + c), where c is Gaussian noise (σ = ν) and q is sampled from a mixture distribution favoring q=0.0 (to learn accurate property mapping from near-equilibrium states) and q=1.0 (to handle raw inputs at inference). This mitigates train-inference distributional shift and enhances robustness. Both QC property prediction and coordinate refinement are trained with L1 loss, enabling end-to-end optimization of the entire pipeline.
content.experiment:
Uni-Mol+ was evaluated on two major benchmarks: PCQM4MV2 and Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) IS2RE. On PCQM4MV2—a dataset of ~4 million organic molecules with HOMO-LUMO gap labels—the goal is to predict the gap from SMILES without DFT conformations at test time. For each molecule, 8 RDKit-generated conformations were produced (~0.01s/molecule). During training, one was randomly selected per epoch; at inference, predictions from all 8 were averaged. The model used 12 layers (with 6- and 18-layer variants tested), AdamW optimizer (lr=2e−4, batch=1024), 1.5M training steps, EMA (decay=0.999), and 8×A100 GPUs over 5 days. The sampling strategy for q assigned 80% probability to q=0.0, 10% to q=1.0, and 10% to uniform sampling in [0.4,0.6].

On OC20 IS2RE—which involves predicting relaxed energy from initial catalyst conformations—the initial 3D structure is provided, so no RDKit generation was needed. The 12-layer Uni-Mol+ was adapted: graph features were removed (as OC20 lacks explicit bonds), pair dimension reduced to 128, and OuterProduct/TriangularUpdate hidden dims set to 16 for efficiency. Periodic boundary conditions were handled via neighbor cell expansion with radius cutoff. Training used batch=64, 1.5M steps, and 16×A100 GPUs over 7 days.

Baselines included state-of-the-art GNNs and Transformers (e.g., Graphormer, GPS++, Transformer-M, EquiFormer). Ablation studies examined the impact of model depth, iterative refinement, and the pseudo-trajectory training strategy. Performance was measured by MAE (lower better) and EwT—percentage of predictions within a threshold (higher better)—on both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) splits.
content.result: Uni-Mol+ achieved state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks. On PCQM4MV2, the 12-layer variant attained a validation MAE of 0.0696, surpassing all prior methods—including GPS++ (0.0778) and Transformer-M (0.0772)—despite using a single model without ensembling or validation-set leakage. Even the 6-layer version (27.7M params) outperformed all previous baselines. On OC20 IS2RE, Uni-Mol+ achieved the lowest MAE across all categories: 0.4088 eV (validation) and 0.4143 eV (test), significantly better than DRFormer (0.4425/0.4509) and EquiFormer+NN (0.4410/0.4660). It also led in EwT metrics (8.61% avg. on validation, 8.23% on test), demonstrating robustness to domain shifts. Ablation studies confirmed that both the iterative refinement and the pseudo-trajectory training strategy were critical: removing either component degraded performance. The method’s success stems from its ability to learn physically meaningful conformation updates, bridging the gap between cheap initial geometries and DFT-quality structures. However, the approach is limited to properties derivable from equilibrium conformations via electronic structure methods; it may not generalize to non-QC properties like toxicity. Future work could extend this framework to dynamic properties or incorporate more sophisticated trajectory modeling beyond linear interpolation.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces SISSO, a compressed-sensing method that identifies optimal low-dimensional descriptors from immense, correlated feature spaces by combining sure independence screening with sparsifying operators, enabling accurate and interpretable models for materials properties even with small training sets.

content.background: The field of materials science has been significantly advanced by high-throughput computational and experimental initiatives under frameworks like the Materials Genome Initiative, generating vast datasets of material properties. However, these datasets remain underutilized due to the lack of reliable methods for identifying descriptors—compact sets of parameters that capture the underlying physical mechanisms governing a material’s property. Traditional data-driven approaches, including various machine learning and statistical methods, often fail when faced with immense and highly correlated feature spaces, especially when prior physical knowledge is limited. Earlier work by Ghiringhelli et al. recast the descriptor discovery problem into a compressed sensing (CS) framework, where the goal is to find a sparse solution to an underdetermined linear system linking candidate features to target properties. While promising, their LASSO-based approach struggled with scalability and correlation among features, breaking down when the feature space exceeded a few thousand elements. This limitation hindered the method’s applicability to complex properties influenced by collective phenomena such as electronic band structures. The core challenge lies in efficiently navigating astronomically large feature spaces (potentially billions of candidates) while maintaining robustness against feature correlations and small training sets—conditions typical in materials science. Addressing this bottleneck is critical for accelerating the discovery of functional materials with targeted properties, such as stable, non-toxic semiconductors with specific band gaps. The present work introduces SISSO (Sure Independence Screening and Sparsifying Operator) as a systematic, scalable solution that overcomes these limitations, enabling the identification of accurate, interpretable, low-dimensional descriptors even in ultra-high-dimensional and correlated feature spaces.
content.method: SISSO is a compressed-sensing-based method designed to identify the optimal low-dimensional descriptor from an immensity of candidate features, potentially exceeding 10^11 elements. The approach operates in two synergistic stages: feature space construction and descriptor identification via a hybrid algorithm combining Sure Independence Screening (SIS) and Sparsifying Operators (SO). The feature space Φₙ is built recursively from a set of primary features Φ₀ (e.g., atomic radii, ionization energies, bond distances) using a predefined set of algebraic and functional operators Ĥ^(m) = {I, +, −, ×, /, exp, log, |·|, √, ⁻¹, ², ³}, with dimensional consistency enforced to exclude unphysical combinations. At each iteration n, Φₙ is formed by applying Ĥ^(m) to all pairs of features from Φₙ₋₁, leading to exponential growth in space size. To handle this combinatorial explosion, SISSO employs SIS as a dimensionality reduction step: for a target property vector P, SIS computes the absolute correlation (inner product) between P and each feature in Φₙ, retaining only the top-ranked features into a subspace S₁D. For higher-dimensional descriptors (nD), SIS is applied iteratively to the residual error Δ₍ₙ₋₁₎D = P − d₍ₙ₋₁₎D c₍ₙ₋₁₎D, generating subspaces S₂D, S₃D, etc. The union of these subspaces (∪SᵢD) forms a manageable candidate set. Within this reduced space, a Sparsifying Operator (SO)—either ℓ₀-norm minimization (exact combinatorial search) or LASSO (ℓ₁ approximation)—selects the optimal n features that minimize the residual error while enforcing sparsity. Crucially, unlike greedy methods like Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), SISSO reselects all features and reoptimizes coefficients at each dimensional increment, avoiding suboptimal paths. The method is grounded in compressed sensing theory: Candès and Romberg’s condition #P ≥ k·n·log(#Φ) guides the selection of subspace sizes to ensure recoverability. For classification tasks (e.g., metal/insulator), SISSO minimizes overlap between convex hulls of categories in descriptor space, using a modified objective that penalizes both overlap count and volume. This design ensures that SISSO remains computationally feasible through parallelization and leverages physical intuition via interpretable analytic descriptors.
content.experiment: The authors conducted two main experiments to validate SISSO: a quantitative regression benchmark and a classification application. In the benchmark, SISSO predicted the ground-state enthalpy difference between rock-salt (RS) and zinc-blende (ZB) structures for 82 octet binary materials using ab initio data from prior work. Primary features (Φ₀, 23 elements) included atomic and structural properties. Three feature spaces were constructed: Φ₁ (~556 features), Φ₂ (~10⁵), and Φ₃ (~10¹¹). Algorithms compared included LASSO, LASSO+ℓ₀, OMP, and SISSO with ℓ₀ or LASSO+ℓ₀ as SO. Performance was evaluated via training root-mean-square error (RMSE) and cross-validation (CV): leave-10%-out (LTO) and leave-one-out (LOO), following a CS-specific CV protocol to detect overfitting. In the classification experiment, SISSO predicted metal/nonmetal behavior for 299 binary compounds using experimental data from SpringerMaterials. Primary features (Φ₀, 7–10 elements) included Pauling electronegativity, ionization energy, covalent radius, atomic composition, and a packing fraction (∑V_atom/V_cell). The feature space Φ₃ contained ~10⁸ elements. The objective minimized overlap between convex hulls of metal and nonmetal domains. The model’s predictive power was tested beyond training: (1) reproducing known pressure-induced insulator-to-metal transitions (HgTe, GaAs, CdTe) by compressing V_cell, and (2) predicting new transition candidates. Ablation studies examined the impact of primary feature selection and prototype diversity (from 1 to 15 crystal structures) on descriptor form and accuracy. Baselines included prior CS work (Ghiringhelli et al.) and the symbolic regression software EUREQA (10¹² function evaluations). All SISSO calculations used trivially parallel implementations (e.g., 64 cores for Φ₃).
content.result: SISSO demonstrated superior performance in both experiments. In the RS/ZB benchmark, SISSO(ℓ₀) with Φ₃ achieved systematically lower training errors than all baselines, including prior work and EUREQA, with 2D–5D descriptors. Cross-validation revealed that a 2D descriptor minimized prediction error, indicating intrinsic model limits given the feature set. LOOCV showed high stability: the same descriptor was selected in 79/82 iterations despite the 10¹¹-feature space. In the metal/insulator classification, SISSO identified a 2D descriptor achieving 99.0% training accuracy. The descriptor combined packing fraction and electronegativity ratios, physically rationalizing metallicity via interstitial charge and electron donation. Crucially, the model correctly reproduced known pressure-induced transitions (HgTe, GaAs, CdTe) and predicted new candidates (e.g., AgBr, GaSb) becoming metallic at 5–15 GPa. LOOCV confirmed robustness (97.6% descriptor reproducibility). Ablation studies showed that descriptor complexity and accuracy depended on primary feature choice and data diversity: simpler descriptors emerged when packing fraction replaced geometric features, and misclassifications (e.g., YP, La₃Te₄) suggested missing physics or experimental errors. SISSO outperformed OMP and LASSO, especially in correlated spaces, and scaled efficiently to huge feature sets where LASSO failed. Limitations include memory demands for storing massive feature matrices and the approximate nature of descriptors, which depend on the completeness of Φ₀. Future work aims at more efficient implementations and expanding primary features to capture additional physics.

memory.abstract: This paper introduces hybrid machine learning frameworks that combine composition-based descriptors with sequence-aware natural language processing techniques and advanced data augmentation (kNNMTD and WGAN-GP) to significantly improve glass transition temperature prediction for styrene-butadiene rubber, achieving R² of 0.85 and 0.95 respectively.

content.background: Polymers are essential materials in diverse applications ranging from electronics to biomedical engineering, owing to their structural diversity and tunable properties. A key thermophysical parameter governing polymer performance is the glass transition temperature (Tg), which marks the transition from a rigid glassy state to a flexible rubbery state and directly influences mechanical strength, thermal stability, and processability. Understanding how polymer composition and sequence structure affect Tg is crucial for rational material design. Traditional experimental and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation approaches, while insightful, struggle to address the vast combinatorial space of polymer chemistries and architectures. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful data-driven alternative for predicting polymer properties, including Tg. However, most existing ML studies rely solely on compositional information—typically represented via monomer SMILES or descriptors—and neglect the sequence arrangement of monomers along the chain, which critically modulates segmental dynamics and intermolecular interactions. This limitation is especially pronounced for synthetic rubbers like solution-polymerized styrene-butadiene rubber (SSBR), which exhibit highly random and diverse chain sequences that are difficult to model with conventional physical or ML methods. Furthermore, data scarcity in polymer science hinders the training of robust ML models. Thus, there is a pressing need for hybrid ML frameworks that integrate both composition and sequence information, coupled with effective data augmentation strategies, to enable accurate and generalizable Tg prediction.
content.method:
The study proposes two complementary hybrid ML frameworks: one based on polymer composition and another on sequence structure. For composition-based prediction, the repeating single-chain structures of SSBR are encoded using SMILES strings, which are then converted into 210-dimensional physicochemical descriptors via RDKit. Feature selection is applied using variance thresholding and Pearson correlation analysis to reduce redundancy, yielding a 22-dimensional descriptor set. To overcome data scarcity (only 40 samples), the k-nearest neighbor megatrend diffusion (kNNMTD) method is employed for data augmentation. kNNMTD identifies k-nearest neighbors for each data point, computes a diffusion coefficient, defines subsample domain bounds (a and b) using skewness-adjusted formulas, and generates synthetic samples via a Gaussian membership function. The pairwise correlation difference (PCD) metric ensures fidelity between real and generated data. Five ensemble ML models—Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and LightGBM—are trained on the augmented dataset, with SHAP used for interpretability.

For sequence-based prediction, the polymer chain is first digitized by encoding styrene, 1,2-butadiene, cis-1,4-butadiene, and trans-1,4-butadiene as '1', '2', '3', and '4', respectively. K-mer encoding (K=4) segments each 60-monomer chain into overlapping 4-monomer subsequences, treated as 'words'. These word sequences are embedded into numerical vectors using the GloVe model, which learns word representations from a global co-occurrence matrix by minimizing a weighted least-squares loss. Given the limited sequence dataset (91 samples), Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) is used for data augmentation. WGAN-GP replaces the standard GAN discriminator with a critic and uses Wasserstein distance as the loss function to stabilize training. A gradient penalty enforces the Lipschitz constraint more effectively than weight clipping, improving sample diversity and quality. The generator and critic networks use LeakyReLU and Tanh activations, trained for 2000 epochs. The augmented word vectors are fed into a CNN-LSTM hybrid model: a 1D convolutional layer extracts local monomer interaction patterns, followed by max-pooling for dimensionality reduction, and three stacked LSTM layers capture long-range sequential dependencies. Dropout and L1/L2 regularization prevent overfitting. Hyperparameters are optimized via Hyperband in Keras Tuner. The framework is also externally validated on diffusion coefficient prediction to assess generalizability.
content.experiment:
The study uses two datasets generated via all-atom MD simulations with the COMPASS II force field. The composition dataset includes 40 SSBR samples, each a 60-monomer chain with varying ratios of four monomer types, represented by SMILES and paired with Tg values. The sequence dataset comprises 91 samples with explicitly defined monomer arrangements along the chain, also labeled with Tg. For composition-based modeling, SMILES strings are converted to descriptors using RDKit; constant and highly correlated (|r| > 0.95) features are removed, and features with low correlation to Tg are discarded, resulting in 22 features. kNNMTD generates 200 synthetic samples; k is optimized via PCD minimization over k=3–9, with k=5 selected. Five ML models are trained on the augmented data and evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation. SHAP analysis interprets feature importance.

For sequence modeling, each chain is digitized and segmented into 57 overlapping 4-mers. GloVe embeddings (window radius=4) produce (57,57)-dimensional word vectors. WGAN-GP generates 200 synthetic sequences; Tg labels for synthetic samples are assigned via KNN regression. UMAP visualizes the distribution of real vs. generated data in 2D. Three neural architectures—CNN, LSTM, and CNN-LSTM—are trained and compared using RMSE, MAE, and R². The CNN-LSTM model is optimized via Hyperband, with architecture details in Table 1. External validation uses a new MD-generated dataset of SSBR sequences labeled with diffusion coefficients; the same WGAN-GP + CNN-LSTM pipeline is applied, and performance is assessed via 5-fold cross-validation. Baseline comparisons include models without data augmentation and composition-only models. Ablation studies compare CNN vs. LSTM vs. CNN-LSTM and assess the impact of kNNMTD and WGAN-GP on predictive performance.
content.result: The composition-based framework achieved significant improvement after kNNMTD augmentation: Random Forest yielded R² = 0.85 and RMSE = 0.38 on the original test set, a 41% increase in R² over the non-augmented baseline (R² ≤ 0.59). SHAP analysis identified BCUT2D_MRHI (positively correlated with Tg) and BalabanJ (negatively correlated) as key descriptors, with their interaction revealing that rigid, polarizable groups combined with simple topology elevate Tg. The sequence-based framework outperformed composition-only models: the WGAN-CNN-LSTM model achieved R² = 0.95 and RMSE = 0.23, surpassing standalone CNN (R² = 0.93) and LSTM (R² = 0.94). UMAP confirmed high similarity between real and WGAN-generated data in both feature and label space. External validation on diffusion coefficients demonstrated strong generalization, with testing R² > 0.74 across all folds. These results confirm that incorporating sequence information via NLP-inspired encoding and augmenting with WGAN-GP captures critical structural nuances missed by composition-only models. Limitations include reliance on simulation-generated data rather than experimental measurements, and applicability currently limited to SSBR. Future work will incorporate experimental datasets and extend the framework to other copolymer systems and properties.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces a deep tensor neural network that unifies quantum-chemical principles with deep learning to achieve uniformly accurate (1 kcal mol⁻¹), size-extensive predictions of molecular energies across compositional and configurational chemical space, while enabling novel quantum-chemical insights such as aromatic ring stability classification and local chemical potential visualization.

content.background: Machine learning has driven transformative advances across diverse scientific domains, including web search, speech recognition, and bioinformatics. In chemistry, the ultimate goal is to accelerate the discovery of molecules and materials with desired properties by leveraging quantum mechanical principles. While electronic structure calculations—particularly density-functional theory (DFT)—provide accurate predictions of molecular properties, they are computationally expensive, limiting high-throughput exploration of chemical space. Recent efforts have combined machine learning with quantum chemistry to build surrogate models trained on large DFT datasets, but most approaches rely on fixed, handcrafted molecular representations (e.g., Coulomb matrices, symmetry functions) and kernel-based regression, which lack adaptability and interpretability. A core challenge in quantum chemistry is the size-extensive and chemically meaningful partitioning of molecular properties into atomic contributions—a problem that remains ambiguous in traditional electronic structure methods due to the non-uniqueness of atomic energy definitions. Moreover, existing machine learning models often fail to generalize uniformly across both compositional (different atom types and stoichiometries) and configurational (conformations and dynamics) chemical spaces, especially for intermediate-sized molecules. This work addresses these limitations by introducing a deep learning framework that unifies quantum-chemical principles with data-driven representation learning, enabling accurate, interpretable, and size-extensive predictions while revealing novel chemical insights beyond the training data.
content.method: The paper introduces the Deep Tensor Neural Network (DTNN), a novel architecture that integrates concepts from many-body quantum Hamiltonians with deep learning to predict quantum-mechanical observables of molecular systems. The DTNN takes as input a molecule’s nuclear charges (Z) and interatomic distance matrix (D), which ensures invariance under translation, rotation, and atom permutation. Each atom i is initially represented by an atom-type-specific descriptor vector c_i^(0) ∈ ℝ^B, inspired by atomic basis set expansions in quantum chemistry. This representation is then refined through T iterative interaction passes that embed each atom into its chemical environment. In each pass t, the coefficient vector is updated via c_i^(t+1) = c_i^(t) + Σ_{j≠i} v_ij, where the interaction term v_ij captures the influence of atom j on atom i at distance D_ij. Critically, v_ij is computed using a low-rank tensor layer that enables non-linear coupling between the atomic representation c_j^(t) and the distance features d̃_ij. The distance D_ij is first expanded into a Gaussian basis to account for varying interaction regimes across distance scales. The full tensor interaction v_ijk = tanh(c_j^(t) V_k d̃_ij + W^c c_j^(t) + W^d d̃_ij + b_k) would be computationally prohibitive due to the large parameter tensor V ∈ ℝ^{B×B×G}. To mitigate this, the authors employ a low-rank factorization: v_ij = tanh[W^{fc}((W^{cf} c_j + b^{f1}) ∘ (W^{df} d̃_ij + b^{f2}))], where ∘ denotes element-wise multiplication. This reduces the number of parameters dramatically while preserving expressive power. After T refinement steps, each atom’s final embedding c_i^(T) is passed through two fully connected layers to predict its atomic energy contribution E_i. The total molecular energy E_M is the sum of all E_i, ensuring size extensivity by construction. The model is trained end-to-end using stochastic gradient descent on DFT-calculated energies, with all weights and descriptors initialized randomly. The recursive, pairwise interaction mechanism implicitly learns an atom-centered basis that adapts to the target property, effectively capturing many-body effects through walks of length T on the molecular graph. This design guarantees physical invariances, enables transferability across molecules, and provides a statistically rigorous partitioning of extensive properties into atomic contributions—addressing a long-standing ambiguity in quantum chemistry.
content.experiment: The authors evaluate DTNN on two main tasks: predicting molecular energies across diverse chemical spaces and extracting quantum-chemical insights. For energy prediction, they use subsets of the GDB database: GDB-7 (7,211 molecules with up to 7 heavy atoms: C, N, O, S, Cl) and GDB-9 (133,885 molecules with up to 9 heavy atoms: C, N, O, F), with DFT-calculated atomization energies (PBE0 for GDB-7, B3LYP for GDB-9). Additionally, they test on molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories of benzene, toluene, malonaldehyde, and salicylic acid at 500 K (627–320k time steps), computed with PBE. The DTNN is trained with up to T=3 interaction passes, 30-dimensional atomic descriptors, 60-factor tensor layers, and distance expansions using Gaussians (σ=Δμ=0.2 Å, μ_min=−1 Å, μ_max=10–20 Å). Models are trained for 3,000 epochs with SGD (momentum=0.9), and early stopping based on validation error. Ablation studies examine the effect of T, training set size, and distance cutoffs (3 Å). For isomer energy prediction, they consider 6,095 C₇O₂H₁₀ isomers from GDB-9, training on equilibrium structures and 50% of short MD trajectories (5,000 steps each for 113 isomers). Baselines include prior machine learning models (e.g., Coulomb matrix + kernel ridge regression), though direct comparisons are contextualized via error metrics rather than side-by-side benchmarking. The local chemical potential Ω_A^M(r) is computed by placing a probe atom (H, C, N, or O) at position r and evaluating its energy contribution without back-propagating influence to the host molecule, visualized on isosurfaces of Σ_i ||r − r_i||⁻². All models are implemented on NVIDIA Tesla K40 GPUs, with training times ranging from 6h (GDB-7, T=1) to 162h (GDB-9, 100k samples, T=3), and prediction times under 1ms per molecule.
content.result: The DTNN achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.0 kcal mol⁻¹ on both GDB-7 and GDB-9 when trained on 5.8k and 25k samples, respectively, demonstrating uniform accuracy across compositional and configurational space. Performance improves with molecule size due to better representation in training data, but extrapolation to larger molecules increases error—mitigated by including a few large molecules in training (e.g., adding small molecules reduces MAE for >20-atom molecules from 2.1 to <1.5 kcal mol⁻¹). MD trajectory predictions show exceptional accuracy (MAE: 0.05–0.39 kcal mol⁻¹), well below thermal energy at room temperature (~0.6 kcal mol⁻¹), enabling reliable thermodynamic sampling. A 3 Å distance cutoff increases error by only 0.1 kcal mol⁻¹, and multiple interaction passes extend the effective range via indirect couplings. Beyond prediction, DTNN reveals chemical insights: it identifies C₆O₃H₆ as the most stable aromatic ring in GDB-9—validated by quantum chemistry—and visualizes local chemical potentials that reflect bond saturation and aromaticity. The model also accurately ranks isomer energies for C₇O₂H₁₀ (MAE=1.7 kcal mol⁻¹) and flags molecules with large prediction errors as having multi-reference character or unconventional bonding, suggesting potential for identifying electronic structure anomalies. Limitations include the need for long-range (van der Waals) interaction modeling in larger systems and the current restriction to extensive properties. Future directions include force prediction, extension to optical properties, and integration with high-level quantum calculations to resolve ambiguous cases.

memory.abstract: MatterSim is a deep learning atomistic model trained via active learning on 17 million first-principles structures across the periodic table and extreme thermodynamic conditions (0–5000 K, 0–1000 GPa), achieving up to ten-fold higher accuracy than prior models in predicting energies, forces, and material properties—including Gibbs free energies within 15 meV/atom of experiment—and enabling efficient phase diagram prediction and customizable simulations with up to 97% less data.

content.background: Accurate and efficient prediction of materials properties across diverse chemical compositions and thermodynamic conditions is central to accelerating in silico materials design. Traditional approaches rely heavily on first-principles methods like density functional theory (DFT), which, while accurate, are computationally prohibitive for large-scale screening or simulations under realistic synthesis and operating conditions (e.g., finite temperatures and pressures). Recent advances in deep learning have enabled machine learning force fields (MLFFs) that predict energies, forces, and stresses with near-DFT accuracy but at a fraction of the cost. However, existing universal MLFFs are typically trained on databases derived from relaxation trajectories of experimentally known crystal structures—data that is chemically biased (e.g., overrepresentation of oxides), structurally redundant (near local energy minima), and lacks coverage of off-equilibrium configurations under extreme temperatures and pressures. This severely limits their generalizability and accuracy for simulating dynamic processes, phase transitions, or materials discovery beyond ground-state stability. The core bottleneck is the lack of a model trained on a sufficiently diverse and physically representative dataset spanning the full periodic table and wide thermodynamic conditions. MatterSim addresses this by actively learning from large-scale first-principles computations across an enriched configurational space, enabling accurate zero-shot prediction of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium material behaviors under realistic conditions—a critical step toward digital transformation in materials science.
content.method:
MatterSim is built on a synergistic integration of deep graph neural networks, active learning, and large-scale first-principles supervision to achieve unprecedented generalizability across chemical elements, temperatures (0–5000 K), and pressures (0–1000 GPa). The core methodology begins with an active learning loop comprising four components: (1) a deep learning model (either M3GNet or Graphormer backbone), (2) a materials explorer, (3) a first-principles supervisor (DFT at PBE+U level), and (4) an ensemble uncertainty monitor. Starting from an initial dataset, the trained model guides the materials explorer to sample new structures in regions of high predictive uncertainty, which are then labeled by DFT and added to the training set. This iterative process ensures minimal data redundancy and maximal coverage of the potential energy surface.

The materials explorer consists of two modules: a ground-state explorer that samples near-equilibrium structures from public and in-house databases, and an off-equilibrium explorer that performs molecular dynamics (MD) simulations across extreme T–P conditions to generate disordered, liquid, and high-stress configurations. This dual strategy yields a dataset of ~17 million structures with significantly improved elemental pair coverage (including noble gases) and 2–3× more distinct atomic environments than prior databases.

Two model architectures are employed: M3GNet, a message-passing GNN with explicit two- and three-body interactions, optimized for fast inference and used for zero-shot MD; and Graphormer, a transformer-based model with enhanced expressivity, used for high-accuracy tasks like MatBench property prediction. Both models operate on materials graphs with periodic boundary conditions, incorporating atomic numbers, coordinates, lattice vectors, and optional state variables (e.g., T, P). Forces and stresses are predicted either via auto-differentiation (M3GNet) or explicit equivariant heads (Graphormer).

Uncertainty quantification is achieved through an ensemble of five models with different random initializations. The standard deviation of energy and force predictions serves as an uncertainty metric, enabling active learning: only high-uncertainty structures from MD trajectories are selected for DFT relabeling, drastically reducing data requirements for fine-tuning. This framework also supports customization to arbitrary levels of theory (e.g., rev-PBE0-D3 for water) by fine-tuning on a small number of high-fidelity data points, leveraging the rich latent representations learned from the large pretraining corpus.
content.experiment:
The experimental evaluation of MatterSim is comprehensive, spanning zero-shot emulation, active learning, theory-level customization, and end-to-end property prediction. The training dataset comprises ~17 million DFT-labeled structures generated via active learning, covering 0–5000 K and 0–1000 GPa, with uniform elemental and pairwise distributions across the first 89 elements.

For zero-shot performance, MatterSim is benchmarked against state-of-the-art universal MLFFs (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE-MP-0) on six tasks using newly created datasets: MPF-TP and Random-TP (sampled from high-T/P AIMD trajectories), MPF-Alkali-TP (ionic conductors), and standard near-equilibrium sets (MPtrj, Alexandria). Metrics include MAE for energy (eV/atom), force (eV/Å), and stress (GPa). In materials discovery, MatterSim is evaluated on MatBench Discovery (WBM dataset) using F1 score and formation energy MAE. For phonons, predictions on the entire PhononDB are compared via max frequency MAE and DOS similarity. Mechanical properties are assessed by computing bulk moduli (0–1000 K) for 59 inorganic crystals using quasi-harmonic approximation (QHA), with MAE against PBE references. Free energy prediction is validated against both PBE-QHA and experimental data (FactSage) for >200 materials. Phase diagrams for MgO and Si are constructed and compared to experiments and prior DFT studies. Robustness in MD is tested on 118 diverse systems (bulk, MOFs, polymers, etc.) heated to 5000 K and compressed to 1000 GPa, with success rate defined as simulation completion ratio.

Active learning is demonstrated on complex systems (molten P, B, Li₂B₁₂H₁₂): models fine-tuned on a small fraction (e.g., 15%) of active-learning-selected AIMD frames match the accuracy of models trained from scratch on full trajectories. For theory customization, MatterSim is fine-tuned on 30 rev-PBE0-D3 water configurations and compared to a scratch-trained model on 900 configurations, evaluating RDFs, ADFs, and diffusion coefficients against experiment. End-to-end property prediction is benchmarked on six MatBench tasks (band gap, shear/bulk modulus, dielectric constant, phonon frequency, exfoliation energy), comparing fine-tuned MatterSim (Graphormer) against specialized models and scratch-trained baselines.
content.result:
MatterSim achieves a ten-fold improvement in accuracy over prior universal MLFFs on off-equilibrium benchmarks (MPF-TP, Random-TP), with energy MAE of 36 meV/atom and force MAE of 0.43 eV/Å. In materials discovery, it attains an F1 score of 0.83 on MatBench Discovery—state-of-the-art—and identified 1,974 new stable binary compounds via large-scale random structure search across 4,005 chemical systems. For phonons, it predicts max frequencies with 0.87 THz MAE, outperforming MACE-MP-0 (1.73 THz). Mechanical properties are predicted with high fidelity: bulk modulus MAE of 2.47 GPa at 0 K and 0.97 GPa over 0–1000 K for AlN. Critically, Gibbs free energies agree with experiments within 15 meV/atom up to 1000 K—surpassing models trained directly on experimental data—and enable accurate phase diagram prediction (e.g., MgO B1–B2 transition at 584 GPa vs. experimental 429–562 GPa). MD simulations show >90% success rate across diverse material classes under extreme conditions.

In customization, fine-tuning MatterSim on only 3% of data (30 vs. 900 configurations) matches scratch-trained model performance for liquid water structure and dynamics (diffusion coefficient error <20%). As a direct property predictor, fine-tuned MatterSim sets new MatBench records on all six tasks, e.g., band gap MAE of 0.129 eV vs. prior best 0.156 eV. Limitations include reliance on semi-local DFT (PBE) for training, poor performance on systems dominated by long-range interactions (e.g., polymers), and lack of explicit surface/interface data. Future work includes multi-task pretraining with higher-level theory data and incorporation of electronic properties (charge, spin).

memory.abstract: The paper introduces the Polymer-unit Graph, a coarse-grained graph representation that treats polymer repeat units as nodes to enhance interpretability and computational efficiency in GNN-based analysis of organic semiconductor polymers, enabling visualization of structure–property relationships and reducing training time by 98%.

content.background: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become powerful tools in materials science for predicting properties and uncovering structure–property relationships, particularly for small organic molecules and periodic crystals. However, their application to organic polymers and macromolecules—especially organic semiconductor (OSC) materials—remains limited due to challenges in graph representation, interpretability, and computational efficiency. Traditional molecular graphs, which treat each atom as a node and each bond as an edge, become excessively complex for large, branched, or repetitive polymer structures, hindering both model performance and human interpretability. Moreover, the physical properties of OSCs are governed not by individual atoms but by the collective behavior of polymer repeat units (polymer-units), such as donor and acceptor moieties like thiophene, benzothiazole (BT), or diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP). Prior attempts to incorporate polymer-unit concepts into machine learning—such as the Polymer-unit Fingerprint (PUFp)—used one-dimensional one-hot vectors that lacked structural and topological information, making them incompatible with GNNs. Although early work by Sumpter and Noid demonstrated the predictive power of polymer-unit-based neural networks, and recent models like POLYMERGNN used paired monomer representations, none have fully integrated polymer-units as graph nodes with rich features and explicit connectivity for GNNs. This gap limits the ability to interpret how specific polymer-units—through mechanisms like fluorination, branched-chain engineering, or donor–acceptor combinations—affect carrier mobility and orbital energy levels. Thus, there is a critical need for a coarse-grained, chemically meaningful graph representation that aligns with the modular nature of polymers while enabling efficient and interpretable GNN modeling.
content.method: The paper introduces the Polymer-unit Graph, a novel coarse-grained graph representation specifically designed for organic polymers and macromolecules in GNN frameworks. The core idea is to treat each polymer repeat unit (polymer-unit)—identified from SMILES strings—as a node in the graph, with edges representing the topological connections between these units. This approach shifts the modeling granularity from atoms to chemically meaningful building blocks, aligning with how polymers are synthesized and how their properties emerge. The generation process involves three steps: (1) polymer-unit identification using the Polymer-unit Recognition Script (PURS), a Python tool that parses SMILES to extract repeat units and their interconnectivity; (2) construction of a polymer-unit database where each unique unit is standardized via RDKit and assigned a fixed-length graph embedding as its node feature; and (3) assembly of the Polymer-unit Graph for each polymer, where nodes correspond to indexed units from the database and edges encode connectivity, atomic details of linkage points, bond lengths, and stereochemical information in an 8-dimensional vector. Two graph embedding methods were evaluated—MACCS (166-bit) and GenWL (280-bit, based on the Weisfeiler-Lehman algorithm)—with MACCS selected for its balance of performance and dimensionality. The Polymer-unit Graph is integrated into two GNN architectures: PU-MPNN, a modified Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) for property prediction, and PU-gn-exp, an interpretable variant based on the gn-exp framework that employs Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to attribute importance to nodes (i.e., polymer-units). In PU-gn-exp, relevance scores from LRP are mapped back to atoms using the atom-to-polymer-unit correspondence from PURS, enabling visualization at both unit and atomic levels. The theoretical foundation lies in the observation that OSC properties arise from interactions among polymer-units rather than individual atoms; thus, coarse-graining preserves essential chemical information while drastically reducing graph complexity. This design synergistically enhances interpretability—by highlighting which units drive property changes—and computational efficiency—by reducing node count and sparsifying message-passing operations.
content.experiment: The experiments were conducted on an organic semiconductor (OSC) dataset comprising 697 polymers (566 p-type, 275 n-type) sourced from literature, with SMILES representations, hole/electron mobilities, and DFT-calculated HOMO/LUMO levels. The dataset was split for classification tasks by binning mobility values into four ranges. Two main models were evaluated: PU-MPNN (for efficiency and accuracy) and PU-gn-exp (for interpretability). Baselines included mol-MPNN (atom-level MPNN) and gn-exp (atom-level interpretable GNN). For PU-gn-exp, the LRP method was used for explainability, with relevance scores weighted by mobility values in statistical analyses (via Equation 1: Rel_i = Σ(μ_j · rel_ji) / num_i). Hyperparameters were tuned based on default gn-exp settings (Tables S1–S2), and both models used three GNN layers with edge/node/graph update-aggregation blocks. Visualization comparisons were made between gn-exp and PU-gn-exp on representative OSC structures, focusing on three design strategies: branched-chain engineering, fluorination, and donor–acceptor (D–A) combinations across four backbone types (DPP, IID, CDT, BTI). Ablation-style comparisons were performed by analyzing pairs of nearly identical polymers differing only in side chains, fluorination, or D–A units. Computational efficiency was measured via training time and memory consumption (batch size = 8). Additionally, statistical analysis identified top-correlated polymer-units for p-type and n-type OSCs, categorized by backbone type, fluorination, and side-chain structure. All models were implemented using PyTorch and RDKit, with DFT calculations performed via Gaussian 09 (B3LYP/6-31G* with gd3bj correction for heavy elements). Code and data were made publicly available on GitHub and in Supporting Information.
content.result: The Polymer-unit Graph significantly enhances both interpretability and computational efficiency in GNN modeling of OSCs. PU-gn-exp successfully identified key structure–property relationships: (1) branched chains like ethylene glycol (OEG) or fluoroalkyl groups showed higher positive correlation with mobility than standard alkyl chains due to improved stability and self-assembly; (2) fluorinated polymer-units enhanced intermolecular interactions and backbone planarity, reducing π–π stacking distance; and (3) optimal D–A combinations (e.g., thiophene with fluorinated IID) aligned frontier orbitals and minimized steric hindrance, boosting mobility. Visualization revealed that polymer-unit-level analysis often contradicted atom-level interpretations (e.g., sulfur atoms positively correlated vs. thiophene units negatively correlated), underscoring the chemical relevance of the coarse-grained approach. Statistically, top-correlated units included benzothiazole (BTz) derivatives, fluorinated main chains, and C8/C10 alkyl side chains with branch points distal to the backbone. PU-MPNN achieved a 98% reduction in training time (2% of mol-MPNN runtime) and halved memory usage while maintaining comparable MSE accuracy. Classification accuracy slightly decreased (p-type: 81.96% vs. 83.2%; n-type: 88.2% vs. 89.6%), but this was attributed to the inherent differences in representation granularity rather than inferior interpretability. Limitations include inapplicability to small molecules (with ≤2 units) and restriction to GNNs. Future directions include extending polymer-units to RNNs/Transformers, applying the concept to biological polymers (e.g., proteins as amino acid sequences), and incorporating 3D conformational data. Overall, the Polymer-unit Graph enables efficient, interpretable, and chemically grounded analysis of organic macromolecules.

memory.abstract: This paper presents a machine learning–accelerated discovery of heat-resistant polysulfates for high-temperature electrostatic energy storage, combining a feed-forward neural network to screen 49,731 candidates for high glass transition temperature and bandgap with rapid synthesis via sulfur fluoride exchange chemistry, yielding a polysulfate that achieves over 90% efficiency and record energy density at 200°C.

content.background: Dielectric polymers are critical components in electrostatic film capacitors due to their light weight, mechanical flexibility, and high-voltage tolerance. However, their application in high-temperature environments—such as inverters in hybrid electric vehicles, underground oil and gas exploration, and aircraft electrification—is severely limited by poor thermal resilience. The industrial standard, biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP), functions well only up to 85°C. While high glass transition temperature (Tg) polymers like polyimide (PI), polyetherimide (PEI), and fluorene polyester (FPE) offer better thermal stability, they typically suffer from narrow electronic bandgaps (Eg), leading to increased leakage currents and degraded performance at elevated temperatures and electric fields. This inverse correlation between thermal stability and electrical insulation presents a fundamental design challenge. Traditional polymer discovery relies on empirical intuition and trial-and-error synthesis, which is slow and inefficient. Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise in accelerating materials discovery—including in dielectric polymers—the scope has been limited by insufficient structural diversity and lack of integration with efficient synthetic methodologies. Hence, there is an urgent need for a high-throughput, ML-guided approach that combines predictive modeling with modular, reliable chemistry to navigate the vast chemical space of potential polymers and rapidly identify candidates with balanced Tg and Eg.
content.method: The authors developed an integrated machine learning–experimental workflow to accelerate the discovery of heat-resistant polysulfate dielectrics. The core idea centers on using a feed-forward neural network (FNN) to predict two key proxy properties—glass transition temperature (Tg) and electronic bandgap (Eg)—for a large library of candidate polymers, followed by experimental validation using sulfur fluoride exchange (SuFEx) click chemistry, which enables rapid, modular, and high-fidelity polymer synthesis. The polymer library was constructed by systematically varying substituents on a 9,9-diarylfluorene repeat unit scaffold, resulting in 49,731 structurally diverse homopolymers. Polymer structures were encoded using polymer-SMILES (p-SMILES) strings, which represent repeat units with asterisks marking chain ends. For ML input representation, Morgan fingerprints with frequency (for Tg prediction) and 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints (for Eg prediction) were generated from p-SMILES using RDKit. The FNN models were trained on datasets from the Polymer Genome (6,906 polymers for Tg; 3,381 for Eg). To improve generalization to polysulfates—a minority class in the original datasets—the authors employed a resampling strategy: known polysulfates were duplicated to increase their representation from 0.20% to 5% (for Tg) and from 0.89% to 9% (for Eg). This biased the models toward better performance on the target chemical family. The trained FNNs achieved high accuracy (R² = 0.99 for training and 0.92–0.90 for validation). Additionally, a synthetic accessibility (SA) score was incorporated to filter candidates by feasibility. Selection criteria combined high Tg (>235–270°C), large Eg (>3.75–3.8 eV), favorable dielectric constant (k > 2.5–3.25), and low SA score (<3.26–3.75), yielding six top candidates. Three—P4, P5, and P6—were selected for synthesis and further analysis. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was used to interpret model predictions, revealing that fused aromatic rings and reduced C–C single bonds contributed to high Tg. The synergy between ML-guided screening and SuFEx chemistry enabled rapid translation from virtual design to validated materials, overcoming the traditional bottleneck of slow, intuition-driven polymer development.
content.experiment: The experimental workflow began with the construction of a virtual library of 49,731 polysulfates based on systematic modifications of the 9,9-diarylfluorene core. ML models were trained using datasets from the Polymer Genome and PolyInfo, with resampling applied to enrich polysulfate representation. The FNNs used ensemble averaging over 12 replicates and were optimized via hyperparameter tuning (e.g., four hidden layers with neuron counts tailored for Tg and Eg prediction). Model performance was validated via parity plots and loss curves (Supplementary Figs. 2–4), showing high R² values. The t-SNE visualization confirmed that the candidate library occupied a distinct chemical space from the training set, justifying the need for resampling. After ML screening, three candidates (P4–P6) were synthesized via SuFEx polymerization using bis-OTBS and bis-fluorosulfate monomers, catalyzed by BEMP in NMP at 130°C. Structural characterization included NMR, FTIR, GPC, and XRD (Supplementary Figs. 9–45). Thermal and electronic properties were measured via DSC (Tg), UV-vis spectroscopy (Eg), and dielectric spectroscopy (k and tan δ). Dielectric performance was evaluated through temperature-dependent measurements (30–275°C), leakage current analysis, and Weibull breakdown statistics at 200°C. Energy storage metrics (Ud and η) were derived from unipolar D–E loops. Baselines included commercial polymers (BOPP, PEI, PI, FPE, etc.) and prior polysulfates (P1–P3). Composite films were also fabricated by incorporating Al₂O₃ nanoparticles or atomic layer deposition (ALD) coatings. Reliability was tested via 100,000 charge–discharge cycles at 200°C and spatial uniformity assessments across a large-area film. All measurements followed standardized protocols detailed in the Methods section, including gold electrode deposition, solvent casting, and environmental controls (e.g., Galden fluid to prevent surface discharge).
content.result: The ML-guided approach successfully identified polysulfate P6—featuring a 9,9-di(naphthalene)-fluorene repeat unit—as a standout candidate. It exhibited a Tg exceeding 300°C and an Eg > 3.7 eV, outperforming commercial high-Tg polymers like PEI and PI, which suffer from Eg < 3.4 eV. P6 demonstrated exceptional dielectric stability: its dielectric constant (k ≈ 3.37–3.39) and loss tangent (tan δ ≤ 0.2%) remained nearly invariant from 30°C to 275°C, with a record-low temperature coefficient (CT = 0.013% °C⁻¹). At 200°C, P6 achieved a Weibull breakdown strength of 695 MV m⁻¹ and the lowest leakage current among P4–P6 (3.72 × 10⁻⁹ A cm⁻² at 200 MV m⁻¹), attributed to its high Tg margin and structural rigidity. In energy storage, P6 delivered Ud = 8.27 J cm⁻³ at 150°C and 6.37 J cm⁻³ at 200°C, both at ≥90% efficiency—far surpassing PEI (~1.8 and ~1.3 J cm⁻³, respectively). Composite variants (P6/Al₂O₃ NPs and P6–Al₂O₃ coatings) further enhanced performance to 9.51 and 7.68 J cm⁻³ at 150°C and 200°C, respectively, exceeding state-of-the-art hybrids. P6 also showed outstanding cycling stability (<0.5% variation over 100,000 cycles at 200°C) and mechanical robustness (Young’s modulus ~1.1 GPa). Large-area film uniformity was confirmed across ten regions. These results validate the efficacy of the ML–SuFEx pipeline. Limitations include reliance on proxy properties (Tg, Eg) rather than direct energy density prediction, and the focus on homopolymers. Future work could expand to copolymers, incorporate multi-objective optimization, and integrate generative models for inverse design.
