memory.abstract: The paper introduces PolyID, a multioutput graph neural network with an interpretable domain-of-validity method that accelerates the discovery of performance-advantaged, sustainable polymers by accurately predicting properties like glass transition temperature and enabling quantitative structure–property analysis across over 1.4 million biobased candidates.

content.background: The transition from fossil-derived plastics to sustainable, biobased polymers is essential for achieving a circular materials economy and mitigating the projected rise in polymer-related greenhouse gas emissions, which could account for 5–15% of the global carbon budget by 2050. Despite this urgency, biobased polymers currently represent less than 1% of the global plastics market, with polylactic acid being the most produced at 282 kilotonnes annually as of 2021. A major barrier to broader adoption is the challenge of balancing multiple performance-critical properties—such as thermal stability, mechanical strength, and barrier characteristics—while maintaining cost-competitiveness. Biobased feedstocks offer unique chemical functionalities that can enhance material performance, but the combinatorial design space is immense: over 10⁵ bioaccessible monomers can be combined into more than 1.4 million potential polymers. Experimentally probing this space is infeasible, necessitating accelerated, data-driven discovery tools. Traditional polymer property prediction methods rely on group contribution theory or static molecular descriptors, which fail to capture the nuanced chemical environments of complex biobased structures. Recent advances in end-to-end machine learning, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), enable simultaneous feature extraction and property prediction, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy for molecular systems. However, existing models often treat polymers as simple repeat units, ignoring structural heterogeneity from regiochemistry, comonomer sequence, and stereochemistry. Moreover, predictive reliability is undermined by poor interpretability and lack of domain-of-validity assessment, making it difficult to know when predictions are trustworthy. This work addresses these gaps by developing PolyID—a multioutput, message-passing neural network specifically designed for high-fidelity polymer property prediction—coupled with a novel, interpretable domain-of-validity method and experimental validation to accelerate the discovery of performance-advantaged, sustainable polymers.
content.method:
PolyID is an end-to-end, multioutput message-passing neural network (MPNN) engineered for accurate and interpretable prediction of polymer properties. Its design integrates three core components: (1) a curated labeled database of 1,791 unique polymers with eight key properties—glass transition temperature (Tg), melt temperature (Tm), density (ρ), modulus (E), and permeabilities to O₂, N₂, CO₂, and H₂O; (2) an in silico polymerization algorithm called "monomers to polymers" (m2p) that generates high-fidelity polymer structures from monomer SMILES strings; and (3) a tailored MPNN architecture that enables both accurate prediction and quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) analysis. 

The m2p algorithm encodes five polymerization chemistries using RDKit’s reaction SMARTS. It probabilistically assembles monomers into polymer chains of user-specified degree of polymerization, incorporating random comonomer order, regio-orientation, and molar ratios. This moves beyond simplistic repeat-unit representations to capture real-world structural heterogeneity, as demonstrated with polypropylene where a 6-mer exhibits regiovariability absent in a 1-mer. For training, a single polymer chain per monomer set is used; for prediction, seven replicate chains are generated to average over structural stochasticity.

The MPNN architecture initializes atom and bond states as one-hot encodings and iteratively updates them through message-passing layers, allowing local chemical environments to differentiate embeddings—as visualized by increasing separation of ester and amide bonds in latent space across layers. Crucially, the network is designed so that each bond’s contribution is pooled into a scalar, and the sum of all bond contributions yields the final property prediction. This enforces interpretability: the relative importance of each bond to a property (e.g., Tg) can be directly analyzed. Hyperparameter optimization identified optimal settings for atom/bond feature vector length, number of message-passing layers (11), and degree of polymerization, balancing bias-variance trade-offs and avoiding oversmoothing or oversquashing.

A novel domain-of-validity (DoV) method complements the model. It uses Morgan fingerprints (radius 2) to count substructures in a predicted polymer that are absent from the training set. Polymers with ≤6 such novel substructures are deemed within the DoV; beyond this threshold, prediction error rises sharply. This method is interpretable—substructures outside the training domain can be visually identified—and guides targeted data augmentation, as shown by improved Tg prediction for cis,cis-muconic acid polymers after adding a single relevant training example.

The model is trained via 10-fold cross-validation on 80% of the data, with the remaining 20% held out for testing. Loss is computed as the mean absolute error across all eight properties, masking missing values. Predictions for new polymers are reported as the mean of the 10 models, with uncertainty as the standard deviation.
content.experiment:
The experimental validation of PolyID involved multiple strategies: internal benchmarking, domain-of-validity analysis, and synthesis of novel polymers. The labeled database of 1,791 polymers was split into 80% training/validation (via 10-fold cross-validation) and 20% held-out test set. Additionally, 22 new polymers—10 polyesters and 12 polyamides—were synthesized that were absent from the database. These included polymers based on biobased monomers like cis,cis-muconic acid and β-ketoadipic acid. 

For the DoV ablation study, two models were trained: one excluding all cis,cis-muconic acid polymers, and another including one such polymer (poly(1,4-butanediol-co-c,c-muconic acid)). Prediction accuracy for three unseen c,c-muconic acid polymers was then compared. Thermal properties were measured via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at 10°C/min after solvent removal verification by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). Molecular weights were estimated via ¹H NMR end-group analysis.

The discovery pipeline screened 1.4 million biobased polymers derived from four metabolite databases (MetaCyc, MINEs, KEGG, BiGG), filtered for bifunctionality, MW < 300 Da, and CHNO composition. From KEGG, 22,447 polyesters were evaluated for PET replacement potential—defined as Tg > 100°C (above water’s boiling point) and O₂ permeability ≤ PET’s. Candidates were filtered by DoV and theoretical yield (≥90% from glucose in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, or P. putida, or from CO₂ in A. thaliana via constraint-based metabolic modeling using cobrapy). One candidate, poly(ethylene 5-carboxyvanillate) (PEC), was synthesized via standard and extended polyester protocols to assess molecular weight effects on Tg.

QSPR interpretability was tested on two nylons: nylon-6,6 and a β-ketoadipate variant. Bond contributions to Tg were extracted from the model and compared to known molecular dynamics insights. Additionally, a heatmap of Tg predictions across diacid–diol combinations (Figure 5B) was generated to guide monomer selection.
content.result:
PolyID achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 19.8°C for Tg on the held-out test set and 26.4°C on the 22 experimentally synthesized polymers, with the higher error attributed to greater substructure novelty (1.6 vs. 0.5 novel Morgan substructures on average). The DoV method proved critical: prediction error decreased significantly as substructure overlap with training data increased, and adding a single c,c-muconic acid polymer to training reduced MAE from 40°C to 23°C for related polymers. Screening of 22,447 KEGG-derived polyesters identified five PET analogues meeting performance and DoV criteria. One, PEC, exhibited a Tg of 85°C (standard synthesis) and 112°C (extended synthesis), the latter falling within PolyID’s predicted range of 106 ± 9°C and exceeding PET’s Tg (~75°C). This confirmed the model’s ability to identify performance-advantaged biobased replacements. 

Interpretability analyses revealed that PolyID correctly assigned higher Tg contribution to the β-ketone bond in β-ketoadipate-based nylon, aligning with known rigidity effects. The monomer-pair heatmap further demonstrated how individual monomers tune Tg, enabling rational design. However, the model could not capture molecular weight dependence of Tg (per the Flory-Fox equation), a limitation for future physics-informed extensions. Key bottlenecks remain: only 5 of 205 predicted PET replacements were within the DoV, and only 8 had calculable metabolic yields for both monomers, highlighting gaps in training data coverage and metabolic model completeness. Future work should expand training sets with diverse biobased motifs, incorporate molecular weight and sequence control, integrate retrosynthesis for chemo-biological routes, and adopt advanced architectures (e.g., variational autoencoders) for enhanced latent-space interpretability.

memory.abstract: UniMatch introduces a dual matching framework that integrates explicit hierarchical molecular matching (across atoms, substructures, and molecules) with implicit task-level matching via meta-learning, significantly improving few-shot molecular property prediction on MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and Meta-MolNet benchmarks.

content.background: Drug discovery is a critical yet highly inefficient process, typically requiring over a decade and exceeding $1 billion in costs, with a success rate below 10%. Artificial Intelligence-Driven Drug Discovery (AIDD) has emerged as a promising avenue to accelerate this process, particularly through Quantitative Structure-Activity/Property Relationship (QSAR/QSPR) models that predict molecular properties from structural data. However, the scarcity of labeled experimental data—due to the high cost and low throughput of wet-lab assays—poses a significant few-shot learning challenge. Existing few-shot molecular property prediction methods predominantly rely on either graph-based or fingerprint-based representations. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) capture molecular topology effectively but suffer from over-smoothing with deeper layers, obscuring substructural details and limiting their ability to model properties governed by local features. Conversely, fingerprint-based methods like CHEF encode only fragmented local patterns (e.g., via ECFP6) and fail to represent global molecular configurations. Crucially, both paradigms overlook the hierarchical nature of molecular structures: atomic composition (e.g., fluorine influencing acidity), substructural motifs (e.g., hydroxyl groups affecting hydrophobicity), and overall molecular geometry (e.g., determining boiling points) each govern distinct properties, as illustrated in Figure 1 of the paper. This multi-scale dependency necessitates a unified framework that can simultaneously capture and align representations across atomic, substructural, and molecular levels while enabling rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal data. The motivation for this research stems from the need to bridge this gap by integrating explicit hierarchical molecular representation with implicit cross-task knowledge transfer, thereby enhancing generalization in data-scarce drug discovery scenarios.
content.method:
The paper proposes Universal Matching Networks (UniMatch), a dual matching framework that synergistically combines explicit hierarchical molecular matching with implicit task-level matching via meta-learning. The architecture comprises two core components: an encoding module and a matching module, followed by a fusion stage. The encoding module adopts Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) as the backbone, leveraging its ability to discriminate graph structures. Critically, instead of using only the final GNN layer output, UniMatch applies mean pooling at every GNN layer to extract multi-level molecular representations: early layers capture atomic and local substructural features, while deeper layers encode increasingly global molecular characteristics. This yields a sequence of representations {z^(l)} for l = 1 to L, where L is the number of GNN layers. The matching module then performs explicit hierarchical alignment between support and query sets at each level l using an attention mechanism. Specifically, for a given task τ, the support set representations z_(τ,s)^(l) serve as keys, query set representations z_(τ,q)^(l) as queries, and support labels y_(τ,s) as values. The attention computes similarity-weighted label predictions per layer: ŷ_(τ,q)^(l) = Softmax((z_(τ,q)^(l)W_q)(z_(τ,s)^(l)W_k)^⊤/√d) y_(τ,s). This layer-wise matching ensures fine-grained comparison across structural scales. The fusion stage concatenates all layer-specific predictions {ŷ_(τ,q)^(l)} and passes them through a linear layer to produce the final prediction ŷ_(τ,q), enabling the model to integrate complementary signals from different structural granularities.

Complementing this explicit mechanism, UniMatch employs a meta-learning strategy for implicit task-level matching. The model f_(θ,w) is trained episodically: θ denotes shared encoder parameters, while w = {W_q, W_k, W_o} are matching/fusion parameters. In the inner loop, for each training task τ, w is adapted to task-specific parameters w_τ via gradient descent on a split support subset. In the outer loop, θ and w are updated to minimize loss on query sets across tasks, promoting cross-task generalization. The paper conceptualizes this meta-learning process as implicit task-level matching, where inter-task relationships are embedded in meta-parameters without explicit modeling. To formalize this, a task relationship matrix M ∈ ℝ^(N_t×N_t) is introduced, with M_(i,j) = g_(θ,w)(T_i, T_j) quantifying similarity between tasks. The inner-loop update is reinterpreted as w_τ = w_τ + Σ_j M_(τ,j)(w_j - w_τ), aligning task parameters via inter-task relationships rather than pure gradients. Similarly, the outer-loop update for θ incorporates M to guide parameter refinement. This dual matching—explicit (hierarchical molecular alignment) and implicit (meta-learned task adaptation)—creates a synergistic framework: hierarchical representations provide rich structural context for task-specific matching, while meta-learning enables efficient knowledge transfer across tasks, collectively enhancing few-shot generalization.
content.experiment: The evaluation of UniMatch spans three benchmarks: MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and Meta-MolNet. On MoleculeNet, experiments use four datasets (Tox21, SIDER, MUV, ToxCast) with a 2-way 10-shot setting (support size=20). Baselines include methods trained from scratch (e.g., CHEF, MixHop, PAR, ADKF-IFT) and pre-trained variants (e.g., Pre-GNN, Pre-PAR). Performance is measured by AUROC, averaged over 10 runs. On FS-Mol—a large-scale benchmark with 5,120 tasks—evaluation uses unbalanced support sets and ΔAUPRC (AUPRC improvement over random baseline) across support sizes (16–256). Baselines span single-task (GP-ST, GNN-ST), multi-task (GNN-MT), self-supervised (MAT), and meta-learning (ProtoNet, GNN-MAML) approaches. An ablation study tests UniMatch’s components on GIN, GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE backbones. Meta-MolNet evaluates cross-domain generalization on seven tasks (GSK3, JNK3, HIV, Tox21, ToxCast, PCBA, MUV) with high molecule/scaffold ratios, using AUROC for balanced tasks and AUPRC for imbalanced ones (support size=2). Baselines include classical ML (SVM, XGBoost), supervised GNNs (GCN, DMPNN), self-supervised models (MolBERT, Pre-GNN), and meta-learning methods (Meta-GAT). All models use Adam/AdamW optimizers; UniMatch’s hyperparameters (e.g., GNN layers=5, hidden dim=300, dropout=0.1) are detailed in Table 3. Visualization experiments on Tox21’s NR-AhR task use PCA to project layer-wise representations of 10 molecules, illustrating hierarchical feature extraction.
content.result: UniMatch achieves state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks. On MoleculeNet, it improves average AUROC by 2.87% over prior methods, with Pre-UniMatch (using Pre-GNN initialization) showing even larger gains (e.g., 86.35% on Tox21 vs. 86.06% for Pre-ADKF-IFT). On FS-Mol, UniMatch outperforms all baselines at every support size, with ΔAUPRC gains of 4.27–8.53%, demonstrating robustness to data scarcity. The ablation study confirms the necessity of both explicit hierarchical matching (via pooling/matching) and implicit task-level matching (via meta-learning), with consistent improvements across GNN backbones. On Meta-MolNet, UniMatch excels on GSK3, JNK3, Tox21, and ToxCast but struggles on HIV, PCBA, and especially MUV—likely due to distributional biases in these datasets. Visualization (Figure 5) validates that deeper GNN layers progressively capture global structures, with PCA projections showing clearer separation of active/inactive molecules at higher layers. Limitations include a simplistic linear fusion module that may underfit regression tasks and computational overhead from multi-layer processing. Future work will explore advanced fusion (e.g., attention-based) and integrate domain knowledge to enhance regression performance and interpretability.

memory.abstract: The paper proposes a hierarchical graph encoder-decoder that generates molecular graphs using large, flexible structural motifs as building blocks, significantly outperforming atom- and substructure-based methods in reconstruction and generation tasks for both polymers and small molecules.

content.background:
Molecular graph generation has emerged as a critical task in drug discovery, with deep learning models increasingly adopted for both property prediction and molecule design. Existing approaches primarily rely on two types of building blocks: atom-by-atom generation (e.g., Li et al., 2018; You et al., 2018a; Liu et al., 2018) or substructure-based strategies limited to simple rings and bonds (e.g., Jin et al., 2018; 2019). While effective for small molecules, these methods suffer significant performance degradation when applied to larger molecules such as polymers. The core limitation stems from the large number of sequential decoding steps required to construct complex molecules, which amplifies error propagation and hinders gradient flow during training. This challenge is evident in reconstruction tasks, where models like CG-VAE fail to accurately reconstruct molecules with more than 80 atoms (Figure 1).

Large molecules often exhibit hierarchical structural organization, built from repeated and chemically meaningful motifs that extend beyond simple rings or bonds. Prior substructure-based methods cannot scale to such larger motifs because their decoding process requires combinatorial enumeration of attachment configurations—an approach whose complexity grows exponentially with motif size. For instance, Jin et al. (2018) restrict substructures to single cycles or bonds (typically ≤6 atoms) and encounter memory errors with rings larger than 10 atoms. This bottleneck prevents leveraging the natural modularity of complex molecules.

The motivation for this work is to explicitly incorporate larger, flexible structural motifs as fundamental building blocks in a generative framework. By doing so, the number of generation steps can be drastically reduced, mitigating error accumulation and enabling accurate reconstruction and generation of large molecules. The authors hypothesize that a hierarchical modeling approach—mirroring the multi-scale nature of molecular structure—can effectively capture dependencies across atomic, attachment, and motif levels, thereby improving both expressiveness and efficiency.
content.method:
The paper introduces a hierarchical variational autoencoder (HierVAE) for molecular graph generation that operates on structural motifs extracted from data. The core innovation lies in a coarse-to-fine autoregressive decoder paired with a fine-to-coarse hierarchical encoder, both operating over a three-layer representation of molecules.

First, motifs are extracted via a preprocessing step applied to the training set. A molecule is decomposed by breaking bridge bonds connecting ring systems, yielding disconnected fragments. Fragments occurring more than 100 times in the training set are retained as motifs; others are further split into rings and bonds. This yields a motif vocabulary V_S and, for each motif S_i, an attachment vocabulary V_A(S_i) encoding possible intersection atom sets with neighboring motifs.

The hierarchical graph representation H_G consists of three layers:
1. **Atom layer**: The original molecular graph G = (V, E), with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges.
2. **Attachment layer**: Nodes represent specific attachment configurations A_i = (S_i, {v_j}), where {v_j} are atoms shared between motif S_i and a neighbor. Edges encode parent-child relationships based on decoding order.
3. **Motif layer**: Nodes correspond to motifs S_i, connected if their atom sets intersect. Due to the decomposition method, this layer forms a tree.

Directed edges connect atoms to their motif’s attachment nodes and attachment nodes to their motif node, enabling cross-layer information flow.

The **hierarchical encoder** uses three message-passing networks (MPNs), one per layer, processing bottom-up:
- The atom-layer MPN computes atom representations h_v using atom and bond embeddings.
- The attachment-layer MPN initializes each node A_i with a concatenation of its embedding e(A_i) and the sum of its constituent atom vectors, then performs message passing using edge embeddings that encode relative decoding order (parent/child indices).
- The motif-layer MPN similarly initializes motif nodes with e(S_i) and the corresponding attachment vector h_{A_i}, followed by message passing.

The latent code z_G is sampled via reparameterization from a Gaussian distribution parameterized by the root motif’s representation h_{S_1}.

The **hierarchical decoder** generates molecules autoregressively in depth-first order, maintaining a stack of frontier motifs. At each step t, given partial graph H_G^{(t)} and latent z_G, it performs three coupled predictions:
1. **Motif prediction**: Classifies the next motif S_t from V_S using MLP(h_{S_k}, z_G), where S_k is the current frontier motif.
2. **Attachment prediction**: Classifies the attachment configuration A_t from V_A(S_t) using the same conditioning, narrowing possible contact points.
3. **Graph prediction**: Determines atom-level connections between S_t and S_k by scoring candidate matchings M = {(u_j, v_j)} via softmax(h_M · z_G), where h_M aggregates pairwise MLP(h_{u_j}, h_{v_j}) scores.

For **graph-to-graph translation**, the architecture is extended as a conditional VAE. Input molecule X is encoded into multi-resolution vectors c_X = c_X^s ∪ c_X^a ∪ c_X^g. During decoding, attention mechanisms (bilinear) over c_X at each resolution guide motif, attachment, and graph predictions. The latent variable z captures translation intent, sampled from an approximate posterior Q(z|X,Y) derived from difference vectors δ_{X,Y}^s and δ_{X,Y}^g computed from motif- and atom-level encodings of X and Y.

This design synergistically reduces combinatorial complexity: motif selection operates over a compact vocabulary; attachment prediction prunes feasible contact sets; and graph prediction is constrained to small, consecutive atom pairs. The hierarchical encoder ensures each decoding decision is informed by multi-scale context.
content.experiment:
Experiments evaluate the model on two tasks: polymer generative modeling and graph-to-graph translation for small-molecule optimization.

**Polymer Generative Modeling**: The dataset comprises 86K polymers from St. John et al. (2019), split into 76K/5K/5K for train/validation/test. Motif extraction yields 436 motifs (avg. 5.24 attachment configs each). Evaluation metrics include reconstruction accuracy (exact reconstruction from z), validity, uniqueness, diversity (Tanimoto distance over Morgan fingerprints), property statistics (Fréchet distance for logP, SA, QED, MW), and structural similarity (SNN, fragment/scaffold cosine similarity). Baselines include SMILES-VAE (Gómez-Bombarelli et al., 2018), CG-VAE (atom-based, Liu et al., 2018), and JT-VAE (substructure-based, Jin et al., 2018). An ablation variant (“small motif”) restricts motifs to single rings/bonds (<10 atoms) while retaining the full architecture.

**Graph-to-Graph Translation**: Four tasks from Jin et al. (2019): logP optimization (δ=0.4/0.6 similarity thresholds), QED (drug-likeness), and DRD2 (bioactivity). Each test molecule is translated 20 times; success requires meeting property and similarity constraints. Metrics include average property improvement (logP) or success rate (QED/DRD2), and output diversity (pairwise Tanimoto distance). Baselines include GCPN (You et al., 2018a), MMPA (Dalke et al., 2018), Seq2Seq (SMILES-based), JTNN (Jin et al., 2019), and a newly developed atom-based translation model (AtomG2G) with comparable architecture but atom-level decoding. Ablations test: (1) replacing the motif decoder with AtomG2G’s decoder (keeping hierarchical encoder), (2) removing the motif layer (“two-layer encoder”), and (3) using only the atom layer (“one-layer encoder”).

**Implementation Details**: HierVAE uses 400-dim hidden layers, |z|=20, λ_KL=0.1. HierG2G uses 270-dim hidden layers, |z|=8, λ_KL=0.3, T=20 MPN iterations. All models have ~5M parameters. Metrics follow Polykovskiy et al. (2018) implementations.
content.result:
On polymer generation, HierVAE achieves 79.9% reconstruction accuracy, significantly outperforming JT-VAE (58.5%) and CG-VAE (42.4%), validating that larger motifs reduce generation steps and error accumulation. It also sets state-of-the-art in distributional fidelity: lowest Fréchet distances for logP (0.525 vs. 1.471 for SMILES) and MW (1928 vs. 4963), and highest structural similarity (SNN: 0.708, Frag: 0.984, Scaf: 0.390). The “small motif” ablation drops reconstruction to 71.0%, confirming the necessity of large motifs. Training is 6.3× faster than JT-VAE due to fewer decoding steps.

In graph translation, HierG2G achieves new state-of-the-art: 76.9% success on QED (+17% over JTNN) and 85.9% on DRD2 (+8.1% over AtomG2G). It also improves diversity (e.g., 0.564 vs. 0.480 for logP at δ=0.4). Ablations reveal that motif-based decoding contributes most to gains—especially on DRD2 (−10.9% with atom decoder)—likely because bioactivity depends on functional groups captured as motifs. Removing hierarchy layers degrades performance (−2.4% with one-layer encoder), underscoring the value of multi-resolution encoding.

The method’s advantages include scalability to large molecules, reduced combinatorial complexity via staged prediction, and multi-resolution context for generation. Limitations include dependency on motif extraction heuristics and potential vocabulary sparsity for rare motifs. Future work could explore end-to-end motif learning or application to other hierarchical graph domains.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces SpinConv, a rotation-invariant graph neural network that captures rich angular information between all neighboring atoms using a per-edge local coordinate frame and a novel spin convolution over the remaining roll degree of freedom, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the OC20, MD17, and QM9 datasets for energy and force prediction.

content.background: Accurate and efficient simulation of atomic systems is critical for accelerating breakthroughs in energy-related applications, such as the discovery of new catalysts to combat climate change. Density Functional Theory (DFT) provides high-fidelity estimates of atomic energies and forces but is computationally prohibitive for large-scale or high-throughput applications. Machine learning (ML) offers a promising path to approximate DFT with dramatically reduced computational cost. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a dominant approach for modeling atomic structures, where atoms are nodes and interatomic relationships are edges. However, a core challenge in designing such models is effectively capturing angular information between neighboring atoms while maintaining rotation invariance—a physical constraint required for meaningful energy predictions. Early GNNs like SchNet used only interatomic distances, ignoring angular dependencies. Later models such as DimeNet introduced triplet-based local coordinate frames to encode angles, improving accuracy but limiting representation to three-atom interactions. Equivariant approaches enforce stricter symmetry constraints but often restrict expressivity or increase complexity. The key bottleneck remains how to incorporate rich, high-order angular information from all neighbors of an atom—not just triplets—while preserving rotation invariance for energy and approximate equivariance for forces. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a novel method that leverages a per-edge local coordinate frame defined by two atoms (source and target) and introduces a 'spin convolution' to handle the remaining rotational degree of freedom (roll about the interatomic axis). This enables the model to encode full spherical neighborhoods of atoms in a rotation-invariant manner, capturing higher-order geometric relationships beyond triplets.
content.method:
The proposed SpinConv model operates on atomic graphs where nodes represent atoms and edges connect neighbors within a cutoff distance (δ = 6 Å). Each edge message is updated over K iterations and consists of a rotation-invariant hidden state, along with geometric information (distance and direction). The core innovation lies in the spin convolution, which processes angular information in a local coordinate frame while ensuring global rotation invariance.

For each directed edge from source atom s to target atom t, a local reference frame is constructed with s at the origin and the z-axis aligned with the vector from s to t. This fixes all rotational degrees of freedom except the roll around the s–t axis. Neighboring atoms of s (i.e., s̃ ∈ Nₛ) are projected onto a unit sphere in this frame, yielding spherical coordinates (φ: inclination, θ: azimuth). Two representations are explored: (1) spherical harmonics up to degree ℓ, producing an ℝᴸ×ℝᴹ feature map (L = (ℓ+1)²), and (2) a discretized grid-based representation ℝ^φ×ℝ^θ×ℝᴹ, where each neighbor’s hidden state is bilinearly interpolated onto its (φ, θ) bin.

A 1D convolution is applied along the θ (azimuthal) dimension—corresponding to the roll degree of freedom—using full-width filters to capture long-range angular dependencies (e.g., opposing atoms at 180°). For spherical harmonics, rotations are implemented via Wigner D-matrices; for the grid, simple cyclic shifts suffice. The convolution outputs a ℝ^θ×ℝᴰ tensor (D filters), which is then globally average-pooled over θ to produce a rotation-invariant ℝᴰ feature vector. This pooling eliminates dependence on the arbitrary roll orientation, ensuring invariance.

This spin convolution output is combined with a distance block and an embedding block to update the edge message. The distance block encodes interatomic distance dₛₜ using learnable Gaussian basis functions, with element-pair-specific gain and offset parameters to account for varying atomic radii. The embedding block integrates atomic numbers aₛ and aₜ via a mixture-of-experts mechanism: a one-hot concatenation of aₛ and aₜ is mapped to a B-dimensional weight vector that linearly combines B expert transformations of the input features.

Two model variants are proposed. The energy-centric model computes total energy E as a sum over atoms of a learned function of aggregated incoming messages (Eq. 1). Forces are derived via f = −∂E/∂x (Eq. 2), enforcing energy conservation. The force-centric model directly predicts per-atom forces using a dedicated force block (Eq. 3). This block applies a similar spin convolution centered on the target atom t, oriented separately along x, y, and z axes to compute each force component. To encourage approximate rotation equivariance—since the force block is not strictly equivariant—the input structure is randomly rotated multiple times during inference; forces are predicted in each rotated frame, rotated back, and averaged. Five rotations are used empirically.

Both variants share the same message-passing backbone but differ in output heads. The energy-centric model uses only the embedding block for energy prediction, while the force-centric adds the force block. The architecture ensures that energy predictions are strictly rotation-invariant, and force predictions are approximately rotation-equivariant through data augmentation and architectural symmetry.
content.experiment:
Experiments were conducted primarily on the Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) dataset, which contains over 130 million DFT-computed atomic structures for catalyst-adsorbate systems, released under CC BY 4.0. Additional evaluations were performed on MD17 (molecular dynamics trajectories for 8 small molecules) and QM9 (quantum properties of 134k small molecules). The main tasks on OC20 include Structure to Energy and Forces (S2EF), Initial Structure to Relaxed Energy (IS2RE), and Initial Structure to Relaxed Structure (IS2RS).

Implementation details: All models used M = 32 message dimensions, K = 3 message-passing layers, D = 256 hidden dimension, and B = 8 embedding experts. Neighbors were limited to the 30 closest atoms within 6 Å. Distance blocks used 256–512 Gaussian bases. L1 loss was applied, with force loss weighted 100× over energy loss (except in force-only training). Models were trained with Adam (amsgrad) on 32× V100 GPUs, using Swish activations and GroupNorm (group size 4). Grid-based spin convolutions used 16×12 (force-centric) or 12×8 (energy-centric) filters due to memory constraints.

Baselines included SchNet, DimeNet++, ForceNet, and their variants. On OC20 S2EF, SpinConv was evaluated using energy MAE, force MAE, force cosine similarity, and EFwT (% of predictions within practical thresholds). For IS2RE, both direct regression and relaxation-based approaches (using predicted forces to relax structure, then predict energy) were tested. IS2RS used ADwT (atom position accuracy) and AFbT (force convergence) metrics.

Ablation studies (Table 3, Figure 4) compared spherical harmonics (ℓ=5) vs. grid representations, model sizes (128 vs. 256 hidden dim), number of layers (2 vs. 3), and the effect of removing spin convolution ('no conv'). The 'no conv' variant aligned the filter to the mean neighbor angle but skipped convolution across θ. Additional ablations tested the number of random rotations in the force block (1 to >5).

On MD17, a smaller 8×8 grid was used due to dataset size (50k training samples). QM9 used an energy-centric 8×8 SpinConv to predict 12 molecular properties. All results were compared against published or re-implemented baselines under consistent evaluation protocols.
content.result:
SpinConv achieved state-of-the-art results on OC20 across all tasks. On S2EF, the force-centric variant outperformed all baselines in energy MAE (0.336 eV) and force MAE (0.0297 eV/Å), while achieving the highest EFwT (0.45%). It also surpassed DimeNet++-large in most domain splits (ID, OOD Ads/Cat/Both), demonstrating robust generalization. The energy-centric variant also exceeded prior energy-conserving models.

For IS2RE, the force-centric SpinConv with relaxation achieved dramatically lower energy MAE (0.42–0.46 eV across splits) compared to DimeNet++ (0.50–0.69 eV) and direct methods (~0.56–0.72 eV), with EwT more than doubling (e.g., 9.37% vs. 6.57% ID). This highlights the advantage of accurate force prediction for structure relaxation.

On IS2RS, SpinConv achieved the best ADwT (53.62% average), indicating superior relaxed structure accuracy, though DimeNet++-large had higher AFbT (21.82% vs. 16.67%) at 3× inference cost (814.6h vs. 263.2h). Ablations confirmed that spin convolution is essential: removing it increased force MAE by ~10%. Grid and spherical harmonic representations yielded similar accuracy, but grids trained faster. Larger models improved performance on OC20 but were unnecessary for smaller datasets like MD17/QM9.

On MD17 (50k), SpinConv matched or exceeded DimeNet on 7/8 molecules, despite not using domain-specific features. On QM9, it performed competitively—though slightly behind DimeNet++ and SphereNet—showing versatility beyond force/energy prediction.

Limitations include residual force/energy errors still too high for direct industrial use, computational cost scaling with filter resolution, and lack of domain knowledge integration (e.g., chemical priors). Future work could incorporate such priors, optimize spin convolution efficiency, and extend to larger molecules or dynamics. Nevertheless, SpinConv demonstrates that full spherical neighbor encoding with spin convolution enables richer angular modeling than triplet-based methods, while maintaining rotation invariance and achieving superior accuracy.

memory.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark of molecular descriptors for machine learning prediction of band gap and hole reorganization energy in 3120 donor-acceptor conjugated polymers, showing that radial/MOLPRINT2D fingerprints excel for band gap while frontier orbital energies are critical for reorganization energy prediction.

content.background: Organic photovoltaics (OPVs), particularly those based on bulk heterojunction (BHJ) architectures, have recently achieved power conversion efficiencies exceeding 20%, driven by the rational design of donor-acceptor (D-A) conjugated polymers (CPs). These materials offer advantages such as lightweight, flexibility, low cost, and solution processability. However, optimizing OPV performance requires balancing critical electronic properties—most notably the band gap (E_g), which governs light absorption range, and the hole reorganization energy (λ_h), which influences charge carrier mobility via Marcus theory. Traditional experimental characterization is labor-intensive and costly, while first-principles methods like density functional theory (DFT) remain computationally expensive despite their accuracy. Machine learning (ML)-based quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) models present a promising alternative, but their reliability hinges on the quality, size, and diversity of training data, as well as the relevance of molecular descriptors. Prior studies often lack large, chemically realistic datasets or fail to systematically benchmark descriptor types for specific electronic properties. This gap limits the generalizability and physical interpretability of ML predictions in organic electronics. To address these challenges, this work constructs a manually curated dataset of 3120 D-A CPs from experimentally validated donor and acceptor units and investigates how different descriptor families—ranging from topological fingerprints to quantum chemical features—affect the predictive performance of ML models for E_g and λ_h. The study emphasizes not just predictive accuracy but also the physical rationale behind descriptor efficacy, aiming to establish best practices for feature selection in materials informatics.
content.method:
The core methodology integrates DFT-computed electronic properties with ML-driven QSPR modeling, using a rigorously constructed dataset of 3120 donor-acceptor conjugated polymers. The dataset was generated by combining 60 common donor and 52 acceptor units via R-group enumeration in Schrödinger’s Materials Science Suite, ensuring a 1:1 D-A stoichiometry and structural consistency (e.g., handling asymmetric cores by selecting one representative isomer). All monomeric D-A structures were geometry-optimized using DFT at the B3LYP/6-311+G(d) level in Jaguar to compute target properties: band gap (E_g = LUMO – HOMO), hole reorganization energy (λ_h), and electron reorganization energy (λ_e). Only λ_h was modeled due to its stronger relevance to hole transport in OPVs and broader distribution in the dataset.

Molecular representations were generated using Schrödinger’s AutoQSAR platform, which supports multiple descriptor types: (1) numerical 2D descriptors (molecular, topological, physicochemical, and functional group counts); (2) polymer-specific descriptors (e.g., backbone atom fraction, sp³ fraction) derived from oligomeric fragments that encode periodicity; (3) cheminformatic descriptors (e.g., polarity, hydrogen bonding); and (4) four binary fingerprint types—dendritic, linear, radial, and MOLPRINT2D—each retaining the top 10,000 informative bits. Feature selection removed descriptors with >90% identical values or pairwise correlations above 0.99 to reduce redundancy.

ML models were built using kernel partial least squares (KPLS) regression and multiple linear regression (MLR), with the dataset randomly split into 80% training (2496 molecules) and 20% test (624 molecules). Over 100 models were automatically generated per descriptor type, and performance was evaluated using R² (training), Q² (test), RMSE, and SD. To assess generalizability, a separate set of 10 unseen D-A monomers—covering a broad E_g range (1.75–3.75 eV) and representative chemical space—was used for external validation. A consensus model averaging predictions from the top 40 models (R² > 0.82) was also constructed. The theoretical foundation lies in the hypothesis that different electronic properties depend on distinct molecular features: E_g is governed by conjugation and topology (captured by fingerprints), while λ_h reflects dynamic geometric relaxation during charge transfer, requiring electronic descriptors like frontier orbital energies. This guided the systematic comparison of descriptor efficacy across prediction tasks.
content.experiment:
The experimental design centers on a large-scale, manually curated dataset of 3120 D-A conjugated polymers, constructed from 60 donors and 52 acceptors selected based on experimental prevalence in organic electronics. Structures were validated and optimized using DFT (B3LYP/6-311+G(d)) to compute E_g, λ_h, and λ_e, with distributions visualized in histograms (Figure 1). The dataset was split into 80% training and 20% test sets via random allocation. Additionally, 10 unseen D-A monomers (not in the 3120) were synthesized in silico and DFT-optimized to serve as an external validation set for assessing model generalizability.

Multiple descriptor families were independently evaluated: (1) numerical descriptors excluding orbital energies (e.g., connectivity indices, dipole moment); (2) polymer descriptors (e.g., ring atom fraction); (3) functional group counts (e.g., carbonyl, electron-withdrawing groups); (4) cheminformatic descriptors (e.g., molecular weight, fluorine count); and (5) four binary fingerprints (radial, MOLPRINT2D, dendritic, linear). Each descriptor set was used to train KPLS or MLR models via AutoQSAR, with hyperparameters (e.g., number of factors) optimized automatically. Baseline comparisons included models using only polymer descriptors (e.g., kpls_desc_11) or combined descriptor-fingerprint sets.

Key ablation studies examined: (i) the impact of including DFT-computed band gap as a descriptor for λ_h prediction; (ii) the effect of integrating frontier orbital energies (HOMO/LUMO) into numerical descriptors; and (iii) the performance of a consensus model averaging top-performing individual models. Evaluation metrics included R², Q², RMSE, and MAD for both internal (test set) and external (unseen molecules) validation. Statistical significance of descriptor contributions was assessed via T-statistics and coefficient analysis in MLR models (Tables S2–S4). All computations leveraged Schrödinger’s Maestro suite, with DFT calculations partially performed on TUBITAK’s TRUBA high-performance computing infrastructure.
content.result:
The study demonstrates that descriptor choice critically determines ML model performance and generalizability. For band gap (E_g) prediction, KPLS models using radial and MOLPRINT2D fingerprints achieved the highest accuracy, with R² = 0.899 and Q² = 0.900 (radial) and R² = 0.895, Q² = 0.914 (MOLPRINT2D). MOLPRINT2D’s superior external performance (R² = 0.919 on unseen molecules) stems from its ability to encode atom-centered topological environments within two-bond distances, capturing local electronic interactions more effectively than linear or dendritic fingerprints. In contrast, models based on polymer descriptors (e.g., kpls_desc_11, R² = 0.073) or functional group counts showed poor performance, underscoring that global polymer metrics are insufficient for E_g prediction.

For hole reorganization energy (λ_h), models relying solely on structural descriptors (e.g., radial fingerprints or polymer features) failed to generalize (R² < 0.25 on unseen data). However, integrating DFT-computed frontier orbital energies (HOMO/LUMO) with numerical descriptors yielded the best-performing model (kpls_desc_35, R² = 0.829, Q² = 0.817), with strong external validation (R² = 0.820). This confirms that λ_h—being sensitive to geometric relaxation upon charging—requires quantum electronic information beyond static topology. Including band gap as a descriptor offered moderate improvement but was less effective than direct orbital energies.

The consensus model enhanced robustness for E_g prediction but could not overcome fundamental descriptor limitations for λ_h. A key limitation is that even the best models show performance drops on unseen molecules when descriptors lack physical relevance (e.g., radial fingerprints for E_g achieved R² = 0.774 externally vs. 0.899 internally). Future work should explore 3D conformational descriptors or graph neural networks to better capture dynamic reorganization effects. Nevertheless, this study establishes that property-specific descriptor selection—topological fingerprints for E_g, quantum descriptors for λ_h—is essential for accurate, interpretable ML in organic electronics.

memory.abstract: The paper proposes SchNet, a deep neural network architecture using continuous-filter convolutional layers to model quantum interactions in molecules, enabling joint prediction of rotationally invariant energies and energy-conserving, rotationally equivariant forces while respecting fundamental physical constraints.

content.background:
The discovery of novel molecules and materials with tailored properties is central to advancements in catalysis, drug design, and energy storage. However, the vastness of chemical compound space and the high computational cost of accurate quantum-chemical calculations—such as those based on density functional theory or coupled-cluster methods—render exhaustive exploration infeasible. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising tool to accelerate this process by learning surrogate models for molecular properties. Existing ML approaches often rely on hand-crafted descriptors or graph-based representations that encode molecular structure via fixed neighborhood relationships and discrete bond types (e.g., one-hot encodings of single, double, or triple bonds). While effective for equilibrium molecules—those at local minima of the potential energy surface (PES)—these methods struggle when applied to non-equilibrium conformations encountered in molecular dynamics (MD), where interatomic forces are non-zero and structural flexibility is significant.

A critical limitation of many prior models is their inability to produce smooth, differentiable potential energy surfaces. Discontinuities arise from discrete input features (e.g., binned distances or categorical bond types), violating fundamental physical principles: the force field must be curl-free (i.e., derivable as the negative gradient of a scalar energy function) to conserve energy, and the PES must be smooth to enable geometry optimization and stable MD simulations. Moreover, most benchmarks like QM9 contain only equilibrium structures with zero forces, offering no test of a model’s ability to generalize across conformational space. This restricts applicability to real-world scenarios involving dynamic molecular behavior.

To address these challenges, the authors propose moving beyond grid-bound convolutional architectures—which assume regularly spaced data like pixels—and instead develop a framework capable of handling atoms at arbitrary 3D positions. The core motivation is to build a joint model for total energy and interatomic forces that inherently respects quantum-mechanical constraints: rotational and translational invariance for energy, rotational equivariance for forces, smoothness of the PES, and energy conservation via a curl-free force field. This necessitates a representation that captures continuous spatial relationships without discretization artifacts, enabling accurate modeling of both chemical (compositional) and conformational (structural) variations.
content.method:
The paper introduces SchNet, a deep neural network architecture built around continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers specifically designed for atomistic systems in ℝ³. Unlike standard convolutions that operate on fixed grids, cfconv layers handle inputs at arbitrary, unevenly spaced locations—such as atomic coordinates—by using a filter-generating function Wˡ: ℝᴰ → ℝᶠ that maps relative positions directly to filter weights. For a set of atoms with feature representations Xˡ = (x₁ˡ, …, xₙˡ) ∈ ℝᶠ and positions R = (r₁, …, rₙ) ∈ ℝᴰ, the cfconv output at position rᵢ is computed as xᵢˡ⁺¹ = Σⱼ xⱼˡ ∘ Wˡ(rᵢ − rⱼ), where ∘ denotes element-wise multiplication. This generalizes discrete convolutions by replacing fixed filter tensors with position-dependent filters generated dynamically by a neural network.

To ensure rotational invariance of the predicted energy—a fundamental requirement in quantum chemistry—the filter-generating network depends only on interatomic distances dᵢⱼ = ‖rᵢ − rⱼ‖, not full vector displacements. However, raw distances lead to highly correlated filters early in training due to near-linear initialization of neural networks. To mitigate this, distances are expanded using radial basis functions (RBFs): eₖ(rᵢ − rⱼ) = exp(−γ‖dᵢⱼ − μₖ‖²), with centers μₖ spaced every 0.1 Å from 0 to 30 Å and γ = 10 Å⁻². This non-linear expansion decorrelates initial filters and accelerates convergence. The RBF-expanded distances are then passed through two dense layers with softplus activations to produce the final filter weights W(rᵢ − rⱼ).

SchNet’s overall architecture processes molecules atom-wise. Each atom i is initialized with an embedding a_{Zᵢ} based on its nuclear charge Zᵢ. The network consists of multiple interaction blocks, each implementing a residual update: xᵢˡ⁺¹ = xᵢˡ + vᵢˡ. The residual vᵢˡ is computed via an atom-wise layer, a cfconv layer, and two additional atom-wise layers with a shifted softplus (ssp(x) = ln(0.5eˣ + 0.5)) non-linearity in between. The ssp activation ensures infinite differentiability, yielding a smooth PES necessary for reliable force predictions and geometry optimization. After several interaction blocks, atom-wise updates produce per-atom features, which are pooled to predict total molecular energy.

Crucially, interatomic forces are not predicted independently but derived as F̂ᵢ = −∂Ê/∂rᵢ, ensuring the force field is energy-conserving by construction. This approach guarantees rotational equivariance of forces (since energy is rotationally invariant) and enforces the physical relationship between energy and forces. The training loss combines mean squared errors for energy and forces: ℓ = ρ‖E − Ê‖² + (1/n)Σᵢ‖Fᵢ + ∂Ê/∂rᵢ‖², with ρ = 0.01 to balance scales. This joint training improves generalization, especially in non-equilibrium settings, by leveraging the physical coupling between the two targets.
content.experiment:
The authors evaluate SchNet on three progressively challenging datasets that span increasing complexity in chemical and conformational space. First, QM9 contains ≈130k equilibrium organic molecules with up to nine heavy atoms (C, O, N, F), where forces are zero by definition. The task is to predict total energy (U₀) across diverse chemical compositions. Models are trained on subsets of 50k, 100k, and 110,462 examples and compared against DTNN and enn-s2s (a message-passing neural network). Second, MD17 comprises eight MD trajectories of individual small organic molecules (e.g., benzene, ethanol, aspirin), each with thousands of non-equilibrium conformations labeled with energies and forces. Here, separate models are trained per molecule to assess conformational generalization. SchNet is compared to GDML (which trains directly on forces) and DTNN. Both energy-only and combined energy-force training are tested with N = 1,000 and N = 50,000 samples. Third, ISO17 is a newly introduced benchmark featuring 645,000 conformations from 5,000-step MD trajectories of 129 isomers of C₇O₂H₁₀. Two test scenarios are defined: (1) known molecules with unseen conformations, and (2) entirely unknown molecules (unseen in training). This tests joint generalization across chemical and conformational space.

All experiments use the same SchNet architecture: three interaction blocks, 64 feature dimensions, RBF expansion over 0–30 Å, and ssp activations. Training employs Adam optimizer (learning rate 10⁻³, decay 0.96 per 100k steps), batch size 32, and exponential moving average of weights. A validation set of 1,000 samples enables early stopping. Baselines include GDML (force-trained kernel method), DTNN (deep tensor network), and enn-s2s (message-passing with bond-type features). Performance is measured via mean absolute error (MAE) in kcal/mol for energy and kcal/mol/Å for forces. Ablation is implicit in comparing energy-only vs. energy+force training, particularly on MD17 and ISO17.
content.result:
SchNet achieves state-of-the-art performance across all benchmarks. On QM9, it attains an MAE of 0.31 kcal/mol with 110k training samples, outperforming DTNN (0.84–0.94) and matching the ensemble enn-s2s-ens5 (0.33). On MD17, SchNet trained with both energy and forces consistently yields accurate predictions: with 50k samples, energy MAEs are ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAEs ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å across all molecules. Notably, SchNet trained on just 1,000 samples with forces surpasses energy-only training on 50,000 samples, demonstrating the value of force information for generalization. It also scales better than GDML, which cannot handle 50k samples due to quadratic memory growth, and outperforms DTNN on most trajectories. On the new ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical accuracy (<1 kcal/mol) for known molecules (0.36 kcal/mol energy MAE with force training) and shows strong generalization to unseen isomers (2.40 kcal/mol). Force inclusion consistently improves performance in both scenarios, confirming that physical consistency enhances transfer across chemical space.

Key advantages include: (1) inherent energy conservation via analytical force derivation, (2) smooth, rotationally invariant PES from continuous filters and ssp activations, (3) scalability to large systems and datasets unlike kernel methods, and (4) joint modeling of chemical and conformational variations. Limitations include fixed filter resolution (via RBF spacing) and lack of explicit angular or many-body terms beyond pairwise interactions mediated through iterative message passing. Future work could explore adaptive filter generation, incorporation of higher-order geometric features, and extension to periodic systems. The introduction of ISO17 establishes a more rigorous benchmark for future ML models in quantum chemistry, emphasizing the need for robustness under both structural and compositional variation.

memory.abstract: This paper demonstrates that graph convolutional networks (GCNs) can reliably predict polymer thermal and mechanical properties—especially glass transition temperature—with performance slightly exceeding that of extended-connectivity fingerprints, and reveals that GCN representations inherently capture backbone rigidity, a key structural determinant of polymer behavior.

content.background: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a transformative tool in materials science and chemistry, enabling rapid property prediction, molecular discovery, and synthesis route optimization. Its application to polymer systems is particularly promising due to the complexity and cost associated with experimental characterization and simulation of polymers, especially in nonequilibrium glassy states spanning multiple time and length scales. However, the success of ML hinges critically on the availability of high-quality databases, which remain limited for polymers. While recent efforts have built polymer databases and explored various learning algorithms, a key challenge lies in molecular representation—how to encode polymer structures into features that effectively capture structure–property relationships. Traditional approaches rely on hand-crafted descriptors or extended-connectivity circular fingerprints (ECFPs), which encode substructural motifs into fixed-length bit vectors. More recently, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have gained traction as a deep learning method capable of generating continuous, data-adaptive molecular representations by leveraging the graph structure of molecules. Although GCNs have shown favorable performance for small molecules, their application to polymers remains underexplored and inconsistent—some studies report poor performance compared to ECFP. Furthermore, the interpretability of complex ML models is crucial for uncovering physical insights and guiding polymer design, yet remains a significant challenge. This work addresses these gaps by systematically evaluating GCN-based models for predicting key thermal and mechanical properties of polyamides—glass transition temperature (Tg), melting temperature (Tm), density (ρ), and elastic modulus (E)—and by investigating how GCN representations capture structural features like backbone rigidity, which is known to strongly influence Tg.
content.method: The authors employ a graph convolutional network (GCN) based on the architecture proposed by Kipf and Welling to generate molecular representations of polyamide monomers. Each polymer is represented as a molecular graph G(ν, ε), where ν denotes atoms (nodes) and ε denotes bonds (edges). The initial atomic features are encoded as a 25-dimensional binary vector combining one-hot encodings of atom type, number of attached hydrogens, atom degree, implicit valence, and aromaticity. The GCN iteratively updates node features through L layers using the propagation rule H^{l+1} = σ(\tilde{D}^{-1/2}\tilde{A}\tilde{D}^{-1/2}H^lW^l), where \tilde{A} = A + I is the adjacency matrix with self-loops, \tilde{D} is the corresponding degree matrix, W^l is a learnable weight matrix, and σ is the ReLU activation function. This operation aggregates neighboring atom features, effectively acting as a low-pass filter that smooths node attributes. After L convolutional layers, a graph-level representation X ∈ ℝ^{m_L} is obtained by summing all node feature vectors (global sum pooling), ensuring permutation invariance. This representation is then fed into either linear regression (LR) or a two-hidden-layer fully connected neural network (NN) for property prediction. For comparison, the extended-connectivity circular fingerprint (ECFP) is also used as a molecular representation, generated via RDKit with optimized radius and bit length. Both GCN and ECFP operate at the monomer level, treating the repeating unit as the input structure. Model hyperparameters—including GCN depth and width, NN architecture, learning rate, weight decay, and training epochs—are optimized via grid search using 5-fold cross-validation (CV) to mitigate overfitting given the modest dataset sizes. Performance is evaluated using root-mean-square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²). To interpret how GCN captures structural information, the authors perform principal component analysis (PCA) on the high-dimensional GCN and latent NN representations, projecting polymers onto the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2). They correlate these embeddings with structural proxies such as the fraction of rotatable bonds—a measure of backbone rigidity—as well as other features like aromatic ring content and sp³ carbon fraction. This analysis is extended to an unlabeled dataset of 100,000 polymers (PI1M) to assess generalization beyond the training domain.
content.experiment: The study uses experimental data for organic polyamides manually curated from the PoLyInfo database, yielding 1388, 942, 390, and 306 homopolymer structures with measured Tg, Tm, ρ, and E, respectively. Multiple measurements per polymer are averaged, and entries with standard deviations exceeding 30 K (for Tg and Tm) are excluded. The E dataset is notably imbalanced, with only six polymers exhibiting E > 6 GPa. Two molecular representations are compared: GCN and ECFP. For GCN, the architecture uses ReLU activation, He initialization, and global sum pooling; for ECFP, RDKit generates fingerprints with optimized radius and bit length. Two regression heads—linear regression (LR) and a two-layer neural network (NN)—are tested with each representation. All models are trained and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation due to limited data size, with hyperparameters optimized via grid search for each property. Baseline comparisons include GCN-LR, GCN-NN, ECFP-LR, and ECFP-NN. Ablation studies examine the effect of training only the NN layers while freezing GCN weights (random initialization), and the impact of including high-modulus outliers in the E dataset. Interpretability experiments involve PCA on GCN and NN latent spaces, mapping distributions of Tg and structural features (e.g., rotatable bond fraction) before and after training. The analysis is extended to the PI1M dataset (100,000 unlabeled polymers) to test generalization. Pearson correlation coefficients between PC1 and structural features quantify how well the representation captures backbone rigidity. Finally, correlations between rotatable bond fraction and each target property are computed to contextualize model performance differences.
content.result: GCN-based models achieve strong prediction performance, particularly for Tg (R² ≈ 0.90 with GCN-NN), followed by Tm (R² ≈ 0.76), ρ (R² ≈ 0.70), and E (R² ≈ 0.54). The GCN-NN consistently outperforms ECFP-based models across all properties, with the largest gain observed for Tm (~10% higher R²). Nonlinear NN regression significantly improves performance over LR for both representations, confirming the need for nonlinear modeling. The poor performance on E is attributed not to dataset size (ρ has similar size but better performance) but to high irreducible error from experimental variability, data imbalance, and the influence of morphological factors (e.g., crystallinity, processing conditions) not captured by monomer-level representations. Interpretability analysis reveals that even untrained GCNs organize polymers in representation space according to backbone rigidity (measured by rotatable bond fraction), with gradients in Tg and rigidity anticorrelated. Training aligns these gradients with the principal axis (PC1), enhancing linearity with the target property. The correlation between PC1 and rotatable bonds increases from R ≈ –0.52 (untrained) to –0.90 (GCN-NN), confirming that GCN learns to emphasize rigidity. This organization generalizes to the PI1M dataset, suggesting transferability to other rigidity-dependent properties. However, the method is limited by its monomer-level featurization, which cannot account for stereochemistry, chain conformation, or mesoscale morphology—critical for properties like E. The authors conclude that GCN is highly effective for properties strongly tied to local backbone structure (e.g., Tg) but insufficient for those dominated by supramolecular or processing-dependent features. Future work should incorporate 3D and morphological information and explore transfer learning for data-scarce properties.

memory.abstract: Using an AI-driven framework (polyVERSE) that integrates reaction-aware polymer generation, multitask graph neural networks for property prediction, and green solvent compatibility screening, the authors discover PONB-2Me5Cl—a polynorbornene dielectric with 8.3 J/cm³ energy density at 200°C, surpassing commercial polymers by 11× and enabling high-temperature electrostatic capacitors without cooling systems.
memory.keyword: AI-assisted discovery polymer dielectrics graph_neural_network ring-opening metathesis polymerization high-temperature energy storage

content.background: Electrostatic capacitors are indispensable in high-power electrical systems across defense, aerospace, energy, and transportation sectors due to their unmatched power density (~10⁷ W/kg). However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the limited energy density (Uₑ) of existing dielectric materials, especially at elevated temperatures (85–200°C), where most commercial polymers fail. The industry standard, biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP), offers high Uₑ at room temperature but suffers from low thermal stability, poor mechanical integrity above 125°C, and rapid performance degradation with rising temperature. Alternatives like polyimide (Kapton®), PEEK, PEI, and FPE provide better thermal stability but compromise on electronic band gap (E_g) and thus Uₑ. This trade-off arises from fundamental chemical constraints: polyolefins lack π-stacking, resulting in low dielectric constant (ε) and poor high-temperature robustness, while aromatic polymers with π-systems often exhibit reduced E_g due to enhanced charge transport. The design of an ideal high-temperature dielectric requires simultaneous optimization of high glass transition temperature (T_g > 100°C), large E_g (>4 eV), and moderate ε (>3)—a multi-objective challenge that traditional trial-and-error approaches cannot efficiently address. The vast chemical space of possible polymers (e.g., 10⁷–10¹⁴ derivatives from a single monomer like styrene) further complicates manual exploration. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising route to navigate this complexity, as demonstrated in recent works that used machine learning (ML) to discover polymers with high Uₑ up to 100°C. However, no existing method integrates reaction-aware chemical generation, accurate multi-property prediction, and practical synthetic feasibility to target the critical 85–200°C operational window—where no commercial solution currently exists. This gap motivates the development of a new AI-driven framework capable of generating synthesizable, high-performance dielectrics tailored for demanding high-temperature applications.
content.method: The authors introduce polyVERSE ("polymers designed by Virtually-Executed Rule-Based Synthesis Experiments"), a four-step AI-assisted paradigm for accelerated polymer discovery: (1) chemical structure generation, (2) property prediction, (3) candidate screening, and (4) experimental validation. The core innovation lies in grounding polymer generation in real, commercially available monomers and established reaction chemistry, ensuring synthetic feasibility—a limitation of prior generative models that often produce hypothetical structures without clear synthetic routes. Starting from ~8 million monomers curated from ZINC15 and ChEMBL databases (filtered by synthetic accessibility score, SAscore), polyVERSE applies handcrafted reaction templates encoding bond-forming/breaking rules and monomer selection criteria. For ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP)—chosen due to its association with state-of-the-art high-temperature dielectrics—the template enforces strict constraints: monomers must be cyclic olefins with ring sizes of 3–5 or 7–11 atoms (to ensure sufficient ring strain for high molecular weight), contain only one reactive site (to avoid branching), and exclude electrophilic groups adjacent to the olefin (which reduce strain). This yields 26,858 ROMP-based polymer repeat units. Property prediction leverages multitask graph neural networks (polyGNN), which convert polymer repeat units into molecular graphs (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges) and learn invariant descriptors through neural message passing. Three key properties—T_g, E_g, and ε at 100 Hz and room temperature (ε₁₀₀ᴿᵀ)—are predicted using models trained on large datasets: T_g with 32°C RMSE, E_g with 0.5 eV RMSE (from DFT-calculated crystal structures), and ε₁₀₀ᴿᵀ with 0.5 RMSE. Multitask learning improves generalization by jointly predicting related properties (e.g., thermal conductivity for T_g; ionization energy for E_g). Screening then applies application-specific filters: T_g > 100°C, ε₁₀₀ᴿᵀ > 3, E_g > 4 eV. Top candidates are rank-ordered by the product T_g × ε₁₀₀ᴿᵀ × E_g and further refined by expert assessment of synthetic cost and feasibility. To address environmental sustainability, a separate solubility prediction model (61-task polyGNN) classifies polymer-solvent pairs into soluble/partially soluble/insoluble, enabling screening for compatibility with green solvents (water, ethanol). This model is applied to a newly generated polyimide library (66,103 structures) created using a polycondensation template that enforces diamine/dianhydride reactivity balance (via Gasteiger charge proxies) and prevents backbiting (by requiring ≥8-atom paths between repeat unit edges).
content.experiment: The experimental workflow begins with in silico generation and screening, followed by synthesis and characterization of top candidates. From the ROMP library, five top-ranked polymers were selected; four—PONB-2Me5Cl, PNB-2,5DM, PNB-2Me5Cl, and PNB-3Cl4Me—were successfully synthesized via a two-step monomer preparation (anhydride + aniline → amic acid → imide) followed by ROMP using Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in dichloromethane. Films were cast and characterized using standardized protocols: T_g via DSC (10°C/min), E_g via UV-Vis spectroscopy, ε and dissipation factor via dielectric spectroscopy (100 Hz–1 MHz, RT–200°C), and breakdown field (E_bd) via Sawyer-Tower D-E loops (100 Hz, half-sinusoidal voltage). Energy density (Uₑ) was calculated from discharged D-E loops. Performance was benchmarked against commercial dielectrics (BOPP, PI, FPE, PEEK) and recent high-temperature polymers (PSBNP-co-PTNI0.02, o-POFNB, PI-oxo-iso). For green solvent compatibility, solubility of PONB-2Me5Cl in water, ethanol, 1-butanol, and ethyl acetate was tested experimentally. The solubility polyGNN model was validated on a test set of 8,961 polymer-solvent pairs (one-third of 26,884 total), achieving 89.7% accuracy and 0.724 F1-score overall, with 100% accuracy for unseen polymers in ethanol and 75.4% in water. The polyimide library was screened using predicted T_g > 200°C, ε₁₀₀ᴿᵀ > 3, E_g > 4 eV, and solubility in water/ethanol (predicted on polyamic acid precursors). Four affordable, synthesizable candidates were identified. All ML predictions used the same lab protocols as experimental validation to ensure comparability (as noted in Fig. 2b,c captions). Ablation is implicit in the comparison of structural variants (e.g., PNB-2Me5Cl vs. PONB-2Me5Cl differing only at R₁) to isolate chemical effects.
content.result: The AI-driven discovery yielded PONB-2Me5Cl, a polynorbornene dielectric with exceptional high-temperature performance: Uₑ = 8.3 J/cm³ at 200°C—11× higher than any commercial polymer at this temperature. This stems from its optimal property combination: high T_g (243°C), large E_g (4.4 eV), and moderate ε (~3.2, stable up to 200°C), enabling E_bd of 750 MV/m at 200°C. Experimental results closely matched ML predictions (mean absolute errors: 12°C for T_g, 0.4 eV for E_g, 0.7 for ε). Structural analysis revealed that backbone rigidity (bicyclic rings, double bonds) and pendant phenyl groups confer thermal stability, while π-systems and polar groups enhance ε without excessive loss. Critically, minor chemical changes significantly impact performance: replacing the backbone carbon (R₁ = –C– in PNB-2Me5Cl) with oxygen (R₁ = –O– in PONB-2Me5Cl) increased Uₑ by >5.5 J/cm³ at 200°C, highlighting design sensitivity. Three other ROMP polymers also outperformed commercial dielectrics across 85–200°C. Environmentally, PONB-2Me5Cl’s three-step synthesis is shorter than competing high-Uₑ polymers (e.g., six steps for PSBNP-co-PTNI0.02), though it requires non-green solvents (DMAc, THF). To address this, the polyimide screen identified four candidates predicted to be soluble in water/ethanol while maintaining T_g > 200°C and E_g > 5.4 eV—attributed to aliphatic rings (for T_g) and absence of aromatic rings (for high E_g). Limitations include the current focus on linear dielectrics (excluding relaxor ferroelectrics), reliance on ε at RT/100 Hz as a proxy for high-temperature behavior, and the need for experimental validation of polyimide candidates. Future work will expand polyVERSE with more reaction templates, incorporate nanofillers/coatings to push performance beyond 200°C, and develop interpretable AI to elucidate structure-property mechanisms.
