memory.abstract: By leveraging natural language processing to extract data from over 3,300 papers, this work demonstrates that active learning strategies could have accelerated the discovery of high-efficiency polymer solar cell donor–acceptor pairs by 75% (15 years) compared to historical trial-and-error approaches.

content.background: Polymer solar cells (PSCs) represent a promising alternative to traditional inorganic photovoltaics due to their low-cost, solution-processable nature and potential for flexible applications. The performance of PSCs hinges critically on the choice of donor and acceptor materials in the bulk heterojunction active layer. Historically, fullerene-based acceptors like PCBM dominated the field, but recent advances have shifted focus to nonfullerene acceptors, which have enabled significant improvements in power conversion efficiency (PCE). However, the vast chemical space of possible donor–acceptor combinations makes exhaustive experimental screening impractical, necessitating more efficient discovery strategies. While machine learning (ML) and active learning have shown promise in accelerating materials discovery across various domains—including dielectric polymers, Heusler alloys, and gas separation membranes—their real-world impact on long-term, decades-spanning discovery processes has not been quantitatively assessed. Prior ML studies in PSCs relied on manually curated datasets limited to ~500 papers, capturing only a fraction of the published literature and thus restricting chemical diversity and model generalizability. This bottleneck stems from the labor-intensive nature of manual data extraction, which fails to scale with the exponential growth of scientific publications. Natural language processing (NLP) offers a scalable solution by automatically extracting structured material property data from unstructured text, enabling the construction of larger, more diverse datasets. This work addresses the critical gap between theoretical ML promise and empirical validation in real-world discovery timelines by leveraging NLP to build a dataset five times larger than previous efforts and using it to simulate how data-driven strategies could have accelerated PSC development over the past two decades.
content.method: The authors developed an end-to-end pipeline that begins with large-scale NLP-based data extraction from scientific literature and culminates in active learning simulations to quantify discovery acceleration. First, they constructed a corpus of 2.4 million materials science papers (2000–2022) from major publishers. Using a domain-specific ontology, they trained a named entity recognition (NER) model on 750 annotated abstracts to identify entities like POLYMER, ORGANIC MATERIAL, and PROPERTY_VALUE. Heuristic rules then linked these entities into structured records, specifically targeting polymer solar cell device characteristics. This yielded PolymerSolarCells_NLP, containing 3,307 papers. To enable ML modeling, they curated a subset—PolymerSolarCells_Curated—by manually verifying NLP extractions and assigning SMILES strings to donors and acceptors (861 papers, 867 unique donor–acceptor pairs). Donors were always polymers; small-molecule donors and ternary systems were excluded to maintain problem simplicity. For ML, they used hand-crafted chemical fingerprints (745-dimensional) for both donors and acceptors, concatenated into a single feature vector. Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with a Matérn kernel (ν=1.5) was chosen over neural networks due to superior generalization in low-data regimes (835 data points vs. 745 features). The model predicted PCE based solely on donor–acceptor structure, assuming abstract-reported PCE values correspond to optimized fabrication conditions—a hypothesis validated on 20 random papers. For active learning simulation, they treated PolymerSolarCells_Curated as the candidate pool and sequentially selected donor–acceptor pairs using seven strategies: GP-UCB (Upper Confidence Bound), GP-PI (Probability of Improvement), GP-EI (Expected Improvement), Greedy (exploiting highest predicted PCE), GP-Thompson Sampling (GP-TS), Linear Contextual Bandits (with Thompson sampling), and Random selection. Each method iteratively trained a GPR model on “measured” data, selected the next candidate, and updated the dataset until the highest-PCE system (16.4% for PBDB-T/BTP-ec9) was found. The discovery time speedup factor (DTSF) was defined as (t_exp_max − t₀)/(t_sim_max − t₀), where t₀ is the timestamp of the earliest system (OC₁C₁₀-PPV/PC₆₁BM) and t_max is when the peak PCE was reached. Timestamps for simulated paths were mapped to experimental publication dates under the assumption that data-driven discovery could proceed at the same rate as historical publication output.
content.experiment: The core dataset, PolymerSolarCells_Curated, comprises 861 curated papers yielding 867 unique donor–acceptor systems with PCE values, extracted from a larger NLP-derived set of 3,307 papers. The curation process involved manual verification of NLP outputs and SMILES assignment using polymergenome.org tools, following the psmiles convention for polymers. The ML model was trained on 85% of the data (709 points) and tested on 15% (126 points), with performance measured by RMSE and R². Two modeling scenarios were compared: (1) donor-only input and (2) donor–acceptor concatenated input, using identical train–test splits to ensure fairness. For active learning simulations, the initial system was fixed as OC₁C₁₀-PPV/PC₆₁BM (the earliest in the dataset), and selection continued until the top-performing system (PBDB-T/BTP-ec9, 16.4% PCE) was identified. Seven acquisition strategies were evaluated: GP-UCB (β=1), GP-PI (ν=0.01), GP-EI, Greedy (β=0 in UCB), GP-TS, Linear Contextual Bandits, and Random. To assess robustness to initial conditions, the first ten historically reported systems were used as alternative starting points for stochastic methods (GP-TS and bandits). Model predictions across the full donor–acceptor space were visualized via UMAP to analyze exploration patterns. Predictive performance evolution was tracked at each active learning iteration by computing test RMSE on the remaining unselected points. Fidelity of the NLP pipeline was quantified using k-tuple metrics (k=2,3,4) against ground-truth annotations, measuring precision, recall, and F1-score for (donor, acceptor, property_name, property_value) tuples. Ablation was implicit in the comparison between donor-only and donor–acceptor models, as well as in the acceptor-type-specific simulations (fullerene-only, nonfullerene-only, and combined).
content.result: The NLP pipeline achieved 42.95% F1-score for full 4-tuples, improving to 69.37% for 2-tuples, demonstrating reasonable but imperfect extraction fidelity. The donor–acceptor ML model achieved a test RMSE of 2.07% PCE, outperforming the donor-only model (2.29% RMSE), confirming that acceptor identity significantly impacts PCE prediction. Active learning simulations revealed that data-driven strategies could have discovered the best-performing system in one-fourth the time of historical trial-and-error—equivalent to a 15-year acceleration (DTSF ≈ 4) when both fullerene and nonfullerene acceptors were considered. Speedup was reduced to ~2× when restricted to only fullerene or nonfullerene systems. Greedy selection achieved the highest average DTSF by rapidly jumping to high-PCE nonfullerene regions, while GP-UCB showed the lowest variance across starting points, indicating robustness. GP-TS, though slower in discovery, uniquely improved model predictive performance over iterations due to its diverse sampling. UMAP visualizations confirmed that Greedy immediately focused on nonfullerene clusters, whereas other methods explored fullerene regions initially. The study identified 10 promising unreported donor–acceptor pairs (e.g., PM6/BTIC-2Br-m, predicted PCE: 14.33%), all involving Y6-derived acceptors. Key limitations include reliance on literature-reported systems (excluding truly novel chemistries), assumption of identical discovery rates between simulated and historical paths, and neglect of fabrication variables. Future work should integrate automated structure-to-SMILES conversion, multi-objective optimization (e.g., PCE vs. stability), and human–machine collaborative loops.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces polyBERT, a Transformer-based chemical language model that treats polymer SMILES strings as a language, enabling an end-to-end, ultrafast polymer informatics pipeline that matches the accuracy of state-of-the-art handcrafted fingerprints while accelerating computation by over two orders of magnitude.

content.background: Polymers are essential to modern life and future technological innovation, yet their vast and diverse chemical space presents both immense opportunities and significant challenges for identifying application-specific candidates. Traditional polymer discovery relies on laborious trial-and-error experimentation, which is infeasible given the astronomical size of the polymer universe. The emerging field of polymer informatics leverages machine learning (ML) to accelerate polymer property prediction and design. A critical bottleneck in existing ML pipelines is the conversion of polymer chemical structures into numerical representations—commonly called fingerprints—used as inputs for predictive models. Historically, these fingerprints have been handcrafted using cheminformatics tools that encode chemical and structural features based on expert knowledge. While effective, such approaches are tedious to develop, computationally expensive (often dominating training and inference time), and lack generalizability across diverse polymer classes, requiring ad hoc feature additions for new chemistries. These limitations hinder the development of fully machine-driven, scalable informatics pipelines suitable for cloud or high-throughput environments. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly Transformer-based models like BERT, offer a promising alternative by treating molecular representations as a 'chemical language.' Prior studies have demonstrated the utility of Transformers for small molecules, and a contemporaneous study applied RoBERTa to polymers but did not benchmark against state-of-the-art handcrafted fingerprinting methods. This work addresses the need for a fast, accurate, generalizable, and fully automated polymer representation method that overcomes the limitations of handcrafted fingerprints while enabling ultrafast, end-to-end polymer informatics at scale.
content.method:
The core innovation of this work is polyBERT, a chemical language model inspired by NLP that treats Polymer Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (PSMILES) strings as the 'chemical language' of polymers. The methodology comprises three key components: (1) generation of a massive hypothetical polymer dataset, (2) unsupervised pretraining of a Transformer-based language model (polyBERT), and (3) supervised multitask learning for property prediction.

First, to enable robust language modeling, the authors generate 100 million chemically valid hypothetical PSMILES strings. This is achieved by decomposing 13,766 known synthesized polymers into 4,424 unique chemical fragments using the BRICS (Breaking Retrosynthetically Interesting Chemical Substructures) algorithm, followed by random and enumerative recombination of these fragments.

Second, polyBERT is built upon the DeBERTa (Decoding-enhanced BERT with disentangled attention) architecture, chosen after empirical comparison with BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT due to its superior performance. The model incorporates a custom three-stage preprocessing pipeline for PSMILES strings: (i) canonicalization using a newly developed Python package to ensure a unique string representation per polymer (addressing translational, multiplicative, and permutational variances inherent in PSMILES syntax); (ii) tokenization via SentencePiece into a vocabulary of 265 tokens covering all periodic table elements, digits, and special characters like [★]; and (iii) masked language modeling, where 15% of tokens are randomly masked, and the model learns to predict them from context. Trained on 80 million PSMILES strings (with 20 million for validation), polyBERT learns the 'grammar' and 'syntax' of polymer chemistry through its 12-layer Transformer encoder with 12 attention heads per layer. The resulting polyBERT fingerprint is derived as the sentence-level embedding—specifically, the average over the token dimension of the final encoder's latent representation.

Third, these unsupervised polyBERT fingerprints are fed into a multitask deep neural network framework to predict 29 diverse polymer properties (thermal, mechanical, electronic, etc.). Multitask learning exploits inherent correlations among properties (e.g., between glass transition and melting temperatures) to enhance prediction accuracy and generalizability. The pipeline is fully end-to-end: from raw PSMILES to property predictions without manual feature engineering. This contrasts with graph neural networks (GNNs), which typically require atom-level feature initialization and learn property-dependent representations, whereas polyBERT’s fingerprints are property-agnostic and reusable. The dense (600-dimensional), low-dimensional nature of polyBERT fingerprints also offers computational advantages over sparse, high-dimensional handcrafted fingerprints (e.g., 945-dimensional Polymer Genome fingerprints with 93.9% sparsity), particularly for models with superlinear time complexity.
content.experiment:
The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering dataset construction, model training, benchmarking, and large-scale prediction.

**Dataset Construction**: The hypothetical training set for polyBERT consists of 100 million PSMILES strings generated via BRICS fragmentation and recombination. For supervised property prediction, a curated dataset of 35,517 data points (28,061 homopolymers, 7,456 random copolymers) spanning 29 properties (including 9 frequency-dependent dielectric constants) is used. This dataset aggregates experimental and DFT-computed values from prior studies and public sources, covering 11,145 monomers and 1,338 copolymer chemistries.

**Model Training**: polyBERT is pretrained on 80 million PSMILES strings using masked language modeling, achieving a validation F1-score >0.99. Copolymer fingerprints are computed as composition-weighted sums of monomer fingerprints. Multitask deep neural networks are trained per property category using five-fold cross-validation and a meta-learner ensemble, with hyperparameters optimized via Hyperband.

**Baseline Comparison**: The primary baseline is the handcrafted Polymer Genome (PG) fingerprint, a state-of-the-art method encoding features at atomic, block, and chain scales. Both fingerprint types are evaluated using identical multitask neural network architectures to isolate the impact of the representation.

**Evaluation Metrics**: Performance is assessed via coefficient of determination (R²) and Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) across cross-validation splits and meta-learner test sets. Computational speed is measured in milliseconds per PSMILES on standardized hardware (Intel Xeon CPU for PG, Quadro GP100 GPU for polyBERT).

**Ablation and Analysis**: The authors analyze polyBERT’s internal mechanisms via attention maps and neuron activation visualizations (using non-negative matrix factorization) to interpret learned chemical motifs. UMAP projections of fingerprints are used to assess chemical relevancy by examining clustering of structurally similar polymers (e.g., poly(but-1-ene) and poly(pent-1-ene)). Carbon emissions are estimated using the ML Impact calculator to quantify environmental cost.
content.result: The results demonstrate that polyBERT achieves near-parity in accuracy with the state-of-the-art handcrafted PG fingerprints while offering dramatic speed improvements. Specifically, polyBERT attains an overall R² of 0.80 across 29 properties, compared to 0.81 for PG, with polyBERT slightly outperforming PG for crystallization tendency and elongation at break. Critically, polyBERT fingerprint computation is 215 times faster than PG (0.76 ms vs. 163.59 ms per PSMILES on GPU vs. CPU), enabling end-to-end property prediction for 29 properties in just 1.06 ms per polymer. This ultrafast pipeline allowed the authors to predict properties for all 100 million hypothetical polymers, establishing potential boundaries of the polymer property space (e.g., extreme values for Tg, band gap, gas permeability). UMAP visualizations confirm that polyBERT fingerprints encode chemically intuitive similarities, clustering structurally related polymers despite being trained solely on PSMILES syntax without explicit chemical knowledge. Attention maps reveal that polyBERT learns meaningful chemical relationships, such as heightened attention to nitrogen-containing motifs in poly(4-vinylpyridine). Beyond speed and accuracy, polyBERT offers advantages in interpretability (via attention analysis), generalizability (applicable to small molecules with minimal modification), and scalability in cloud environments. Limitations include the current inability to decode fingerprints back to PSMILES (due to averaging), which could be addressed in future work with architectural modifications. The method paves the way for high-throughput polymer screening, generative design, and standardized ML benchmarks in polymer informatics.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces a Physics-Enforced Neural Network (PENN) that integrates empirical rheological equations into a neural architecture to predict polymer melt viscosity from chemistry and processing conditions, achieving superior extrapolation and physical consistency compared to physics-unaware machine learning models.

content.background: Additive manufacturing (AM) of polymers requires precise control over rheological properties, particularly melt viscosity (η), which governs flow behavior during extrusion. Melt viscosity is influenced by polymer chemistry, molecular weight (M_w), polydispersity index (PDI), shear rate (γ̇), and temperature (T). While empirical equations capture the functional dependence of η on M_w, γ̇, and T—such as piecewise power laws for M_w, shear-thinning models for γ̇, and the Williams-Landel-Ferry (WLF) equation for T—these require fitting multiple empirical parameters through extensive rheological experiments for each new polymer. This experimental burden severely limits the rapid development of new printable polymer inks, especially given the current reliance on empirical intuition and a narrow palette of known chemistries. Although machine learning (ML) approaches have shown promise in materials informatics for accelerating property prediction, prior efforts to model η using purely data-driven methods often yield unphysical extrapolations, particularly in sparse data regimes where new chemistries or unexplored physical conditions (e.g., extreme M_w, γ̇, or T) are considered. This limitation arises because standard ML models like artificial neural networks (ANNs) or Gaussian process regression (GPR) lack built-in physical constraints, leading to predictions that violate known rheological principles. To address this bottleneck, the authors propose a physics-enforced neural network (PENN) that integrates established empirical rheological equations directly into the model architecture, enabling it to learn only the empirical parameters from data while preserving physical consistency. This approach is motivated by the need for reliable extrapolation in AM material design, where experimental data is scarce but accurate viscosity predictions across wide physical ranges are essential for process optimization.
content.method: The core innovation of the paper is the Physics-Enforced Neural Network (PENN), a hybrid architecture that combines data-driven learning with explicit encoding of known physical relationships governing polymer melt viscosity. The PENN framework begins by representing polymer chemistry using fingerprints derived from the Polymer Genome approach, which encodes atomic-, block-, chain-, and morphology-level features. For copolymers and blends, these fingerprints are aggregated using composition-weighted averages or harmonic means. The input to the model includes this polymer fingerprint along with the polydispersity index (PDI). A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) processes this input to predict a vector of empirical parameters that appear in the established rheological equations: C₁, C₂, and Tᵣ for the WLF temperature dependence; α₁, α₂, M_cr, β_Mw, and k₁ for the molecular weight dependence; and n, γ̇_cr, and β_γ̇ for the shear rate dependence (see Table 1). These predicted parameters are then fed into a computational graph that implements the full physics-based model of η(M_w, T, γ̇). Specifically, the model uses smoothed piecewise functions to capture the transition between unentangled (M_w < M_cr) and entangled (M_w ≥ M_cr) regimes via a smoothed Heaviside function with tunable transition rate β_Mw. Similarly, the shear-thinning behavior is modeled by transitioning from zero-shear viscosity (η₀) to a power-law decay beyond a critical shear rate γ̇_cr, again using a smoothed Heaviside function parameterized by β_γ̇. The temperature dependence is encoded via the WLF equation, which exponentially reduces η₀ as T increases above a reference temperature Tᵣ. The entire architecture is end-to-end differentiable, allowing joint optimization of the MLP and the physics-based computational graph. During training, the loss function includes both a standard mean squared error on log(η) predictions and a regularization term that penalizes deviations of α₁ and α₂ from their theoretically expected values of 1 and 3.4, respectively. This dual loss ensures that the model remains physically plausible even when data is sparse. The PDI is not directly encoded in the viscosity equations due to inconsistent reporting in the dataset, but its influence is implicitly captured through its effect on the transition sharpness parameters β_Mw and β_γ̇, which the MLP learns to adjust based on PDI input. This design enforces known physical trends while allowing chemistry-specific adaptation through learned parameters, creating a synergistic mechanism where data informs parameter values but physics constrains functional form.
content.experiment: The dataset comprises 1,903 melt viscosity measurements collected from the PolyInfo repository and associated literature, covering 93 unique repeat units across homopolymers (1,326 datapoints), copolymers (446), and miscible blends (113). The data spans wide ranges of M_w (10²–10⁷ g/mol), γ̇ (10⁻⁵–10⁶ s⁻¹), T (300–600 K), and PDI (1.0–10.0). Missing PDI values were imputed with the dataset median (2.06). To address underrepresentation of low M_w data, 126 synthetic points were added by extrapolating from high M_w data using the known η₀–M_w relationship. Polymer chemistries were fingerprinted using the Polymer Genome method, with copolymer and blend fingerprints constructed via weighted averaging. The primary evaluation focuses on extrapolation performance under sparse chemical knowledge: monomers were split into 90% train and 10% test sets; within test monomers, data was further split by median values of M_w, γ̇, or T to ensure test points lie in unseen physical regimes relative to training data for that chemistry. This was repeated three times per variable to generate robust statistics. The PENN was benchmarked against two physics-unaware baselines: a standard ANN and a GPR model. All models used identical input features (fingerprint, PDI, log M_w, log γ̇, T) and were trained on the same 9:1 train-test split with 10-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameters were optimized via Hyperband (for ANN/PENN) and Bayesian optimization (for GPR). Model accuracy was assessed using Order of Magnitude Error (OME), defined as the mean absolute error of log₁₀(η) predictions. Additionally, empirical parameters were extracted post-hoc from ANN and GPR by fitting their predictions over wide physical ranges to the physical equations, enabling direct comparison with PENN’s native parameter outputs and with ground-truth parameters fitted from subsets of the original dataset containing ≥5 points per polymer per variable.
content.result: The PENN significantly outperforms both ANN and GPR in extrapolative regimes, demonstrating superior physical consistency and predictive accuracy. In parity plots across unseen M_w, γ̇, and T splits, PENN achieves an average 35.97% reduction in OME and up to 79% higher R² compared to ANN. While GPR performs slightly better than PENN on γ̇ extrapolation in aggregate metrics, detailed analysis of empirical parameters reveals that PENN produces far more physically credible predictions. For instance, PENN predicts α₁ and α₂ with RMSEs of 0.05 and 0.17—close to theoretical values of 1 and 3.4—whereas ANN and GPR exhibit RMSEs >1.3 and often predict non-physical values (e.g., α₁ ≤ 0). Similarly, PENN correctly confines n (shear-thinning exponent) to the expected 0.2–0.8 range and predicts M_cr within the observed 10²·⁵–10⁵ g/mol range, while baselines frequently violate these bounds. The average Kullback-Leibler divergence between predicted and ground-truth parameter distributions is 1.74 for PENN versus 22.24 (ANN) and 14.59 (GPR), confirming its superior physical fidelity. In direct extrapolation tests over wide physical ranges, PENN successfully predicts correct rheological trends in 80.4% of M_w cases, 49.2% of γ̇ cases, and 54.1% of T cases, compared to <20% for baselines. Crucially, ANN and GPR often fit training points accurately but extrapolate unphysically (e.g., missing the M_cr transition or predicting no shear-thinning), highlighting the risk of purely data-driven models in sparse regimes. PENN also offers interpretability: failure cases (e.g., Fig. 5D–F) can be traced to specific mispredicted parameters (e.g., underestimated M_cr or Tᵣ), enabling targeted data collection for improvement. Limitations include sensitivity to chemical diversity—PENN may overfit when training chemistries are too narrow—and imperfect prediction of C₂, which is constrained to lower values than some literature reports. Future work will expand chemical coverage via simulation and literature mining.

memory.abstract: This Review presents an AI-driven, application-specific protocol for designing functional and sustainable polymers by integrating target property criteria, virtual generation of synthetically accessible candidates, machine learning prediction, and experimental validation across energy and sustainability domains.

content.background: Polymeric materials, foundational to modern society since Hermann Staudinger’s pioneering work in the 1920s, exhibit extraordinary versatility due to their tunable chemical structures, processing conditions, and additive formulations. Despite over a century of progress, the traditional polymer development pipeline remains slow—often spanning decades—from conceptualization to commercial deployment. This inefficiency stems from reliance on expert intuition, labor-intensive trial-and-error experimentation, and the staggering size of the chemical and configurational space that polymers occupy. The need for accelerated discovery is especially urgent in critical domains such as energy storage, sustainable materials, and separation technologies, where performance, cost, safety, and environmental impact must be simultaneously optimized. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer a transformative pathway by encoding domain knowledge and historical data into predictive and generative models that can navigate vast polymer spaces efficiently. Early polymer informatics relied on group contribution methods with limited scope, but recent advances in data availability, molecular representation (e.g., graph-based, transformer-based, and chemical language models), and ML algorithms have enabled more robust, scalable, and interpretable property prediction. However, a key bottleneck remains: moving beyond forward prediction to inverse design—recommending polymers that meet specific, multi-objective criteria—while ensuring synthetic feasibility. This Review addresses this challenge by advocating for a practical, application-driven informatics protocol that integrates target property definition, virtual generation of synthetically accessible polymers (e.g., via Virtual Forward Synthesis), ML-based property prediction, and experimental validation.
content.method: The core methodological framework proposed in this Review is an AI-assisted, application-specific polymer design protocol (Box 1) that operates through four synergistic stages. First, application-driven screening criteria are defined in terms of target property values (e.g., high dielectric constant, large bandgap, and elevated glass transition temperature for high-temperature capacitors). These criteria encode the multi-objective optimization problem inherent to real-world applications. Second, a vast but synthetically plausible search space is constructed. A key innovation here is 'Virtual Forward Synthesis' (VFS), which digitally generates polymers by combining commercially available monomers with known polymerization reaction templates (e.g., ring-opening metathesis polymerization), ensuring that candidate materials are likely to be experimentally realizable. Third, reliable ML models are developed to predict the target properties for any candidate polymer. These models rely on advanced numerical representations (fingerprints) that capture features across multiple length scales—from atomic to chain-level—and leverage modern architectures such as graph neural networks (e.g., polyGNN), chemical language models (e.g., polyBERT), and transformer-based systems. Training data may include experimental measurements, high-fidelity computations (e.g., density functional theory for bandgaps), or lower-fidelity simulations (e.g., molecular dynamics for ionic conductivity), often fused via multitask or multifidelity learning to enhance accuracy and coverage. Physics-informed ML is also employed, where known physical laws (e.g., the Arrhenius equation for temperature-dependent conductivity or the solution-diffusion model for membrane transport) are embedded directly into model architectures or loss functions to improve generalizability and physical consistency. Finally, the trained models predict properties for all candidates in the VFS-generated library, and those meeting the screening criteria are recommended for experimental synthesis and validation. The resulting experimental data—whether successful or not—are fed back into the loop for active learning, iteratively refining the models and narrowing the design space. This closed-loop, data-driven strategy is demonstrated across multiple domains: dielectric polymers for capacitors, fuel-cell membranes, solid polymer electrolytes for batteries, gas and liquid separation membranes, conducting polymers, and sustainable (biodegradable or chemically recyclable) polymers.
content.experiment: The Review synthesizes multiple case studies that exemplify the proposed protocol. For high-temperature dielectric polymers, over 50,000 candidates were virtually generated via VFS using ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) templates and commercially available monomers. ML models trained on DFT-computed bandgaps, experimental dielectric constants, and glass transition temperatures identified ~30 candidates meeting criteria (>3 eV bandgap, >3 dielectric constant, >150°C Tg). Five were synthesized; four outperformed biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP), with PONB-2Me5Cl achieving 8.3 J/cm³ at 200°C—over 10× better than commercial alternatives. In fuel-cell applications, ~60,000 reported homopolymers and copolymers were screened using multitask ML models trained on proton conductivity and water uptake data; over 60 candidates were identified for proton exchange membranes (PEMs) and ionomers, though the search was limited to sulfonic acid-containing polymers due to dataset bias. For Li-ion battery electrolytes, databases of solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) were used to train graph neural networks and physics-informed models (e.g., ChemArr, which enforces the Arrhenius relationship). These models screened thousands of candidates, leading to the experimental validation of eight polyphenylene sulfides with conductivities >1.4 mS/cm. In gas separation, ML models trained on experimental and simulated permeability data screened millions of hypothetical polymers, identifying ultrapermeable candidates like P-DNN-C1 and P432092, two of which were synthesized and tested for CO₂/CH₄ separation. For complex liquid mixtures, a multiscale framework combined ML-predicted sorption and diffusivity with Maxwell-Stefan transport modeling to accurately forecast permeation of 9–12 component hydrocarbons and crude oil through five polymer membranes (e.g., Torlon, Matrimid, DUCKY-9). In sustainable polymers, multitask deep neural networks screened 1.4 million PHA-based biopolymers to identify biodegradable replacements for seven commodity plastics. For chemically recyclable polymers, ML models trained on computed and experimental ring-opening enthalpies (ΔH_ROP) accelerated the discovery of depolymerizable systems like polybenzothiocane. Across all cases, experimental validation was the ultimate test, with data from successful and failed syntheses used to refine models iteratively.
content.result: The AI-driven protocol consistently accelerated the discovery of high-performance polymers across diverse applications. In dielectrics, PONB-2Me5Cl demonstrated unprecedented energy density at high temperatures by simultaneously optimizing bandgap, dielectric constant, and Tg—properties rarely balanced in known polymers. In fuel cells, ML identified non-Nafion alternatives meeting conflicting PEM/ionomer requirements, though dataset limitations restricted chemical diversity. For battery electrolytes, ML-guided screening yielded SPEs with conductivities approaching practical targets (>10⁻⁴ S/cm), and physics-informed models improved prediction reliability. Gas separation membranes discovered via ML surpassed historical Robeson upper bounds, though synthetic feasibility remained a hurdle for many candidates. The multiscale model for liquid mixtures achieved <7% error in predicting complex crude oil separations, showcasing generalizability. In sustainability, informatics enabled the design of PHA bioplastics matching petroleum-based properties and identified chemically recyclable polymers with tailored ΔH_ROP. Key advantages include rapid exploration of vast chemical spaces, integration of multi-source data via multitask learning, and enforcement of physical laws for robustness. Limitations persist: dataset scarcity and bias (e.g., sulfonic acid dominance in fuel-cell data), challenges in quantifying biodegradability, and the gap between virtual candidates and scalable synthesis. Future directions include expanding VFS to include ladder and spiro chemistries, automating data extraction from literature via NLP (e.g., Polymer Scholar), fusing computational and experimental data through multifidelity learning, and extending the framework to composites and cross-linked systems. Ultimately, closing the loop between AI prediction and industrial-scale validation remains the definitive test of impact.

memory.abstract: Prompt-MolOpt leverages prompt engineering in a transformer architecture to enable data-efficient, multiproperty molecular optimization—even in zero-shot settings—by using property-specific embeddings to guide fragment modifications while optionally preserving user-specified pharmacophores.

content.background: Molecular optimization in drug and material design is inherently a multiobjective problem, requiring simultaneous balancing of multiple—often conflicting—physicochemical and functional properties such as potency, specificity, ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) profiles, and drug-likeness. Traditional approaches simplify this complexity by focusing on single-property optimization during early-stage hit discovery, followed by lead optimization that refines multiple properties while preserving core bioactivity. However, existing AI-driven methods face significant challenges: (1) scarcity or absence of multiproperty-labeled training data, which limits model generalization; (2) reliance on explicit multiobjective loss functions that oversimplify trade-offs by simple summation of individual objectives; and (3) lack of unified frameworks capable of flexibly optimizing diverse property combinations without retraining separate models. While deep generative models (e.g., VAEs, flow-based models) and specialized tools like Modof have advanced single-site, single-property optimization, they struggle with multiproperty settings and often fail to preserve pharmacophores—the structural motifs essential for biological activity. Prompt engineering in large language models (LLMs) offers a promising paradigm shift, enabling zero- and few-shot learning through task-specific prompts without retraining. This work leverages that insight to address the core bottlenecks in molecular optimization: data scarcity, inflexible objective formulation, and poor generalization across property combinations.
content.method: Prompt-MolOpt is a transformer-based molecular optimization framework that integrates prompt engineering with graph neural networks to enable flexible, data-efficient multiproperty optimization. The method operates in two synergistic stages. First, a multitask molecular property prediction model is built using Multi-Graph Attention networks (MGAs), which generate property-specific atomic embeddings by assigning distinct attention weights to atoms based on the target property (e.g., BBBP, hERG). These embeddings capture how local substructures influence global properties. Second, a sequence-to-sequence transformer is trained on molecular optimization datasets constructed via the Substructure Mask Explanation (SME) method. SME decomposes molecules from DrugBank into Murcko scaffolds, BRICS fragments, and functional groups, then uses attribution scores from the MGA model to identify substructures that negatively impact a target property. By replacing unfavorable substructures with favorable ones from DrugBank, SME generates source-target molecular pairs with improved properties, forming a domain-relevant training set (~160,000 pairs across single- and dual-property tasks). During optimization, Prompt-MolOpt encodes input molecules in SMILES format, prepended with property-specific prompt tokens (e.g., 'BBBP', 'Mutagenicity lipop'). Crucially, atom tokens in the SMILES sequence are enriched with property-specific embeddings from the MGA model, enabling the transformer to condition its fragment modification decisions on the desired optimization objectives. This prompt-augmented embedding allows the same model to handle arbitrary property combinations by simply changing the prompt tokens—enabling zero-shot multiproperty optimization when trained only on single-property data. A specialized variant, Prompt-MolOpt^P, further preserves user-specified pharmacophores by decomposing input molecules into fixed (pharmacophore) and variable (optimizable) components, ensuring modifications occur only outside the core scaffold. This design eliminates the need for explicit multiobjective loss functions and leverages both single- and multiproperty data efficiently.
content.experiment: The authors evaluated Prompt-MolOpt on two main benchmarks. First, they compared against JTNN, hierG2G, and Modof on the DRD2&QED multiproperty optimization task, using the same dataset (55,686 molecular pairs) and evaluation protocol as Modof: 800 test molecules with DRD2 < 0.5 and QED < 0.6 were optimized under Tanimoto similarity constraints (δ = 0.4, 0.5, 0.6). Success required at least one of 20 generated molecules to exceed DRD2 ≥ 0.5 and QED ≥ 0.6 while meeting the similarity threshold. Prompt-MolOpt was tested in standard, zero-shot (trained only on single-property data), and iterative (Prompt-MolOpt^m) modes. Second, they assessed performance on ADMET-related properties (ESOL, Mutag, hERG, BBBP, lipop) using datasets constructed via SME from DrugBank and MoleculeNet. Five molecules were generated per test case, and performance was measured by the Success Rate of All generated molecules (SRA)—the fraction surpassing original molecules in target properties. Ablation studies compared Prompt-MolOpt with and without prompt embeddings. Few-shot experiments added only 184–219 multiproperty pairs to otherwise single-property training sets. Real-world case studies tested Prompt-MolOpt^P’s ability to reproduce historically optimized molecules (e.g., JNJ-42153605 for BBBP) while preserving pharmacophores. All models used 2048D Morgan fingerprints for similarity computation, and property predictions relied on simulated values from consensus GNN models (e.g., SVM for DRD2, nonlinear classifier for QED).
content.result: Prompt-MolOpt achieved state-of-the-art performance in multiproperty optimization. On DRD2&QED, it outperformed Modof by over 15% relative improvement in success rates (29% vs. 24.62% at δ=0.4), and its zero-shot variant surpassed Modof at δ=0.5 and 0.6 despite no multiproperty training data. Iterative Prompt-MolOpt^m further boosted success rates to 66.75% (δ=0.4), exceeding iterative Modof^m. On ADMET tasks, Prompt-MolOpt achieved high SRA across single-property (85.7–93.6%) and multiproperty (79.5–83.7%) optimizations. Ablation confirmed prompt embeddings are critical: removing them reduced SRA by 2–5%. In zero-shot Mutag&ESOL/lipop tasks, combining prompts ('Mutagenicity ESOL') improved SRA from 63.9% to 66.0%, and few-shot learning with minimal multiproperty data (184 pairs) further increased it to 67.5%. Prompt-MolOpt^P successfully reproduced real-world optimizations: it rediscovered JNJ-42153605 using only a 'BBBP' prompt and adjusted lipophilicity when 'lipop' was added, validated by SlogP distributions. Limitations include lack of 3D target information, no explicit chirality handling, and reliance on Murcko/BRICS substructures. However, the authors note these are engineering extensions rather than fundamental flaws. The method’s prompt-based flexibility, zero-shot capability, and pharmacophore preservation demonstrate significant potential for practical drug discovery.

memory.abstract: The authors present SPACIER, an open-source framework that integrates fully automated all-atom classical molecular dynamics (via RadonPy) into Bayesian optimization pipelines for on-demand polymer design, demonstrating its capability by discovering and synthesizing optical polymers that surpass the empirical Pareto frontier between refractive index and Abbe number.

content.background: Machine learning has significantly accelerated materials discovery across diverse systems, including polymers, inorganic compounds, and catalysts, by solving forward (property prediction) and inverse (material design) problems. However, data scarcity remains a critical bottleneck, especially for polymeric materials. The most comprehensive polymer database, PoLyInfo, contains only ~20,000 entries, with most properties having fewer than a few dozen samples—insufficient for robust machine learning. While integrating physics-based simulations like density functional theory (DFT) into machine learning pipelines has mitigated data limitations for small molecules and inorganic solids, automating all-atom classical molecular dynamics (MD) for polymers presents unique challenges. Polymer MD simulations require complex parameterization—force field selection, degree of polymerization, cell construction, and equilibrium protocols—making automation difficult. Moreover, all-atom MD is computationally expensive, leading prior works to rely on coarse-grained models that sacrifice chemical detail and limit applicable properties. Consequently, no open-source, fully automated system existed that integrates high-fidelity all-atom MD with machine learning for on-demand polymer design. This gap impedes the discovery of innovative polymers in unexplored chemical spaces, particularly for multi-objective optimization tasks like balancing refractive index and Abbe number in optical materials, where empirical tradeoffs define a Pareto frontier that new materials must surpass.
content.method: The authors developed SPACIER (materials SPACe frontIER), an open-source framework that integrates RadonPy—a Python library for fully automated all-atom classical MD simulations—into a Bayesian optimization (BO)-driven polymer design pipeline. RadonPy automates the entire simulation workflow: given a polymer repeat unit and degree of polymerization, it performs conformational search, DFT-based atomic charge calculation (using Psi4), force field assignment (GAFF2), polymer chain generation, amorphous cell construction, equilibrium/non-equilibrium MD (via LAMMPS), and property computation. SPACIER leverages this to enable closed-loop BO: a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate model maps a 170-dimensional force-field kernel mean descriptor of the polymer to RadonPy-calculated properties. To address systematic biases between simulation and experiment (e.g., overestimated specific heat due to missing quantum effects), linear calibrators are pre-fitted using experimental data. The BO iteratively selects candidates by maximizing an acquisition function—either multi-objective probability of improvement (PI) for targeting property regions or expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) for Pareto frontier exploration. Candidate polymers are sourced from either a real dataset (1,077 polymers) or a virtual library generated by SMiPoly, which applies 22 polymerization reaction rules to 1,083 monomers to create 101,487 synthesizable polymers. The workflow is fully automated: SPACIER selects top-N candidates per BO cycle, submits RadonPy jobs via a queuing system, and retrains the GP with new data. Key innovations include: (1) end-to-end automation of all-atom MD for polymers, overcoming prior technical barriers; (2) calibration of simulation outputs to align with experimental trends; and (3) integration with rule-based virtual libraries to ensure synthetic feasibility. The refractive index is computed via the Lorentz-Lorenz equation using MD-derived density and DFT-calculated polarizability, while the Abbe number uses wavelength-dependent polarizabilities from truncated TD-DFT (CAM-B3LYP functional) via the sum-over-states approach, balancing accuracy and cost by retaining 0.3% of excited states.
content.experiment: Two case studies validated SPACIER. First, a toy problem targeted specific heat capacity (Cp) and refractive index using 1,077 real polymers. Calibration reduced mean absolute errors from simulation to experiment to 167.53 J/kg·K (Cp) and 0.02 (refractive index). BO with multi-objective PI acquisition searched three Pareto-adjacent regions, outperforming Fix-GP (static model) and Random sampling by identifying all target polymers in 20–30 cycles. Ablation studies confirmed BO’s robustness to initial dataset size and bias. Second, SPACIER designed optical polymers exceeding the empirical refractive index–Abbe number tradeoff. Using 101,487 SMiPoly-generated candidates, multi-objective BO with EHVI ran for 20 cycles, selecting top-10 polymers per cycle. Calibration achieved MAEs of 0.02 (refractive index) and 2.79 (Abbe number). Three sulfur-containing polymers (P1–P3) were synthesized: P1 (polydithiocarbonate) and P3’s analog mpPh-PTU surpassed the Pareto frontier. P1 synthesis used CDI as a carbonyl source for safety, yielding a film-forming polymer (Mn=20,900). P2 precipitated as an insoluble solid, prompting copolymerization to improve solubility (unsuccessfully for film formation). mpPh-PTU’s literature properties served as a proxy for P3. Experimental validation used NMR, SEC, DSC, TGA, and spectroscopic ellipsometry. Baselines included Random and Fix-GP; ablation studies tested initial dataset variations and acquisition functions (EHVI for Pareto search). Candidate filtering excluded polymers with >55 atoms/repeat unit, redundant structures, or non-commercial monomers.
content.result: SPACIER successfully discovered polymers exceeding the empirical Pareto frontier for refractive index and Abbe number: P1 (experimental: n=1.64, ν=32.0) and mpPh-PTU (n=1.81, ν=11.0) aligned closely with RadonPy predictions (n=1.63/1.84, ν=32.0/14.1), validating the calibrated simulation approach. The BO workflow efficiently navigated the property space, with 64% of final-cycle polymers surpassing the empirical limit, and autonomously learned that sulfonyl groups enhance optical performance—a known design principle. In the toy problem, BO exhaustively identified target polymers 2–3× faster than baselines, with selected candidates densely populating target neighborhoods, enabling unbiased expert decisions. Limitations include: (1) candidate diversity constrained to one-step syntheses from commercial monomers, missing multi-step polymers with superior properties; (2) insolubility issues (e.g., P2) not pre-screened; and (3) reliance on linear calibration, though affine transfer models could improve accuracy. Future work will integrate generative models for sequential design, solubility predictors to filter candidates, and expanded force fields for broader elemental coverage. SPACIER’s open-source nature and RadonPy integration establish a foundation for automated, simulation-driven polymer discovery across diverse properties.

memory.abstract: This paper extends Shapley values to explain predictive uncertainty by defining information-theoretic characteristic functions based on conditional entropy and KL divergence, providing feature attributions for local uncertainty with theoretical links to conditional independence and finite-sample error control via conformal inference.

content.background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has predominantly focused on interpreting point predictions of supervised learning models, largely neglecting the explanation of predictive uncertainty—a critical aspect for reliable decision-making, especially in safety-critical or exploratory settings. While methods like SHAP effectively attribute predictions to input features, they fail to capture how features influence higher moments of the predictive distribution, such as variance or entropy. This limitation is significant because predictive uncertainty varies across the feature space and impacts applications like active learning, covariate shift detection, adversarial example identification, and classification with reject options. Existing approaches to explain uncertainty are scarce and often model-specific (e.g., CLUE for Bayesian deep learning), restricting their applicability. Moreover, methods like LossSHAP require ground-truth labels, which are frequently unavailable during test-time uncertainty analysis. The core motivation of this work is to extend the Shapley value framework—renowned for its axiomatic foundation and interpretability—to explain local predictive uncertainty in a model-agnostic manner. By redefining the characteristic function of the cooperative game using information-theoretic quantities like conditional entropy and KL divergence, the authors aim to quantify each feature’s contribution to the uncertainty of individual predictions, thereby broadening XAI’s scope to domains where understanding uncertainty is as important as understanding the prediction itself.
content.method: The paper introduces Information Theoretic Shapley Values (ITSVs) by redefining the characteristic (value) function in the Shapley framework to reflect contributions to predictive uncertainty rather than point predictions. Instead of the standard value function v₀(S, x) = 𝔼[f(x) | X_S = x_S], the authors propose several information-theoretic alternatives. Key among them are v_H(S, x) = H(Y | x_S) (local conditional entropy), v_IG(S, x) = -H(Y | x_S) (information gain), and v_H*(S, x) = 𝔼_𝒟[H(Y | x) | X_S = x_S] (a modified entropy game that conditions on S while marginalizing over out-of-coalition features). They also consider v_KL(S, x) = -D_KL(p_{Y|x} || p_{Y|x_S}) and v_CE(S, x) = -H(p_{Y|x}, p_{Y|x_S}), showing these are equivalent up to an additive constant and yield identical Shapley values. The marginal contribution Δ_v(S, j, x) for these games has clear information-theoretic interpretations: for v_IG and v_H, it equals the local conditional mutual information I(Y; x_j | x_S), representing the reduction in Y’s uncertainty due to x_j given x_S. For v_KL/v_CE, it quantifies the expected additional bits needed to encode Y|x when using a code optimized for Y|x_S instead of Y|x_S∪{j}. Theoretically, the paper establishes deep connections between these Shapley values and conditional independence: global conditional independence Y ⊥ X_j | X_S implies zero marginal contribution across all x, while context-specific independence (CSI) Y ⊥ X_j | x_S implies zero contribution at that specific x. Crucially, the converse holds almost everywhere—the set of distributions where Δ_v = 0 despite dependence has Lebesgue measure zero. To make the method practical, the authors address computational challenges: they use plug-in estimators for entropy (e.g., from model outputs or ensembles to decompose aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty), adopt efficient coalition sampling (e.g., focusing on cardinalities with high Shapley weight), and employ conditional sampling strategies (e.g., DeepSHAP, TreeSHAP) for out-of-coalition features. A key innovation is a split conformal inference procedure for Shapley values: by splitting data into model-fitting and Shapley-computation sets, they construct finite-sample confidence intervals [q̂_lo, q̂_hi] for φ(j, x) with provable coverage P(φ(j, x^{(n+1)}) ∈ [q̂_lo, q̂_hi]) ≥ 1 - α, enabling hypothesis testing (e.g., whether a feature’s attribution is significantly non-zero). This framework is fully model-agnostic and modular, allowing practitioners to choose uncertainty estimators, reference distributions, and samplers suited to their context.
content.experiment: The experiments validate the method across diverse data types and applications. In Section 6.1, proof-of-concept demonstrations are conducted on image (MNIST digit pairs: 1 vs. 7, 3 vs. 8, 4 vs. 9), text (IMDB sentiment reviews), and tabular data. For MNIST, a CNN with MC dropout estimates epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty; ITS using v_H* visualizes pixel contributions to entropy, showing epistemic uncertainty reduced by discriminative features (e.g., 9’s loop) and increased by ambiguous ones (e.g., 8’s angle). For IMDB, a BERT model highlights words contributing to high-entropy predictions (e.g., “not Great Cinema but...”). In tabular simulations, a Gaussian DGP with autocorrelated features (Toeplitz covariance) and heteroskedastic noise allows comparison of conditional sampling methods (KernelSHAP, copula, etc.); results show methods respecting feature dependencies perform better under high autocorrelation. Section 6.2 tests covariate shift explanation: on UCI datasets (BreastCancer, Diabetes, etc.), a perturbed test feature induces high entropy, and ITS correctly attributes excess uncertainty to the perturbed feature. Section 6.3 evaluates feature selection and active acquisition using a modified Friedman benchmark where conditional mean depends on {X₆–X₁₀} and variance on {X₁–X₅}. XGBoost models estimate mean and log-variance; TreeSHAP attributions correctly cluster near zero for irrelevant features in each task. Conformal inference achieves nominal 90% coverage (α=0.1) for all features. In active acquisition, with 0–50% missing data, absolute Shapley values rank features by importance, maintaining AUC > 0.68 even at 50% missingness. Baselines include standard SHAP (for mean) and various imputation strategies; ablations focus on sampling schemes and uncertainty decompositions. All experiments use real/simulated data with details in Appendix C, and code is provided.
content.result: The experiments confirm that ITS effectively explains predictive uncertainty across modalities. Visualizations on MNIST and IMDB intuitively link feature attributions to uncertainty sources (e.g., ambiguous pixels or conflicting words). In tabular settings, ITS accurately identifies features driving heteroskedasticity, outperforming standard SHAP which only explains the mean. The method robustly explains covariate shift by pinpointing perturbed features, even for subtle distributional changes. Feature selection results demonstrate clear separation between mean-relevant and variance-relevant features, validating the disentanglement of predictive information modes. The conformal inference procedure achieves near-nominal coverage (≈90% at α=0.1), enabling reliable feature relevance testing. Active acquisition maintains strong performance under missing data, highlighting practical utility. Advantages include model-agnosticism, theoretical grounding in information theory and conditional independence, and provable error control. Limitations involve computational cost (mitigated by sampling), dependence on quality of uncertainty estimators and conditional samplers, and potential errors from off-manifold imputation. Future work includes extending to reinforcement learning/bandits and deeper integration with distributional regression models.

memory.abstract: The paper proposes KANO, a knowledge graph-enhanced molecular contrastive learning framework that uses an element-oriented knowledge graph to guide both pre-training (via element-guided graph augmentation) and fine-tuning (via functional prompts), achieving state-of-the-art performance and chemically sound interpretability on 14 molecular property prediction benchmarks.

content.background: Molecular property prediction is a cornerstone of drug discovery, traditionally reliant on time-consuming and costly wet-lab experiments. Deep learning models have emerged as powerful tools to accelerate this process by predicting molecular properties from structural data. However, most existing methods are purely data-driven, focusing exclusively on the intrinsic topology of molecular graphs without incorporating fundamental chemical prior knowledge. This heavy reliance on data limits their generalizability across the vast chemical space and results in low interpretability of predictions. Contrastive learning, a popular self-supervised approach, often employs generic graph augmentations like node deletion or edge perturbation, which can violate chemical semantics by altering molecular identity or properties. Furthermore, a significant gap exists between pre-training objectives and downstream tasks, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To address these limitations, this work argues for the integration of structured chemical knowledge—specifically about elements and functional groups—as a guiding prior during both pre-training and fine-tuning. Such knowledge can enforce chemical validity during augmentation and bridge the task gap via prompting, ultimately enabling more robust, generalizable, and interpretable molecular representations.
content.method:
The paper proposes KANO (Knowledge graph-enhanced molecular contrastive learning with functional prompt), a novel framework that integrates a chemical element-oriented knowledge graph (ElementKG) into both pre-training and fine-tuning stages. The core innovation lies in leveraging structured domain knowledge to guide representation learning.

First, ElementKG is constructed by synthesizing information from the Periodic Table and Wikipedia. It encompasses two levels: an instance level containing element and functional group entities, and a class level defining their hierarchical taxonomy (e.g., ReactiveNonmetals ⊂ Nonmetals). Entities are enriched with over 15 data properties (e.g., electron affinity, boiling point) and connected via object properties that capture relationships like shared physical states or period membership. Functional groups are linked to their constituent elements via an 'isPartOf' relation. This KG is embedded using OWL2Vec*, which generates representations by training a word2vec model on a corpus derived from ElementKG’s structure, lexical content, and their combination.

Second, in contrastive pre-training, KANO introduces an element-guided graph augmentation strategy. For a given molecule, its constituent elements are identified, and their corresponding subgraph is retrieved from ElementKG. This subgraph, encoding inter-element relationships, is then linked to the original molecular graph’s atom nodes, creating an augmented graph that preserves molecular topology while adding semantically meaningful connections between atoms of the same element type—even if they are not directly bonded. A contrastive learning framework (using NT-Xent loss) is then applied to maximize agreement between the original and augmented graph views, ensuring the model learns from the injected knowledge without overfitting to the augmented structure.

Third, during fine-tuning, KANO employs functional prompts to bridge the gap between pre-training and downstream tasks. Functional groups are detected in the input molecule using RDKit, and their ElementKG embeddings are retrieved. A learnable mediator vector is introduced, and a self-attention mechanism aggregates the functional group embeddings, weighted by their relevance to the molecule’s global properties. The resulting functional prompt is added to each atom’s initial representation via a learnable scale parameter, creating a prompt-enhanced molecular graph. This prompt stimulates the pre-trained encoder to recall task-relevant knowledge acquired during pre-training, thereby aligning the representation with the specific prediction task.

The graph encoder itself is based on CMPNN, which iteratively updates node and edge representations through a communicative message-passing scheme, enhancing the modeling of atom-bond interactions.
content.experiment:
KANO was evaluated on 14 benchmark datasets from MoleculeNet, spanning four categories: physiology (BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast, SIDER, ClinTox), biophysics (BACE, MUV, HIV), physical chemistry (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity), and quantum mechanics (QM7, QM8, QM9). These include 678 binary classification and 19 regression tasks. The pre-training corpus consisted of 250,000 unlabeled molecules from ZINC15. All experiments used scaffold splitting (8:1:1 train/validation/test) to assess generalization on out-of-distribution scaffolds, except for QM9, which used random splitting for comparability.

KANO was compared against a comprehensive set of baselines: five supervised models (GCN, GIN, MPNN, DMPNN, CMPNN) and eight self-supervised methods (N-GRAM, Hu et al., MGSSL, GEM, GROVER, GraphMVP, MolCLR, MolCLR-CMPNN). For classification, performance was measured by ROC-AUC; for regression, by RMSE (physical chemistry) or MAE (quantum mechanics).

Ablation studies were conducted to validate the necessity of each KANO component. These included: (1) removing the class hierarchy from ElementKG, (2) excluding functional group entities, (3) masking data properties at varying rates, and (4) comparing the functional prompt mechanism against simple addition or concatenation of functional group features. Additional analyses assessed representation quality via alignment (t-SNE clustering by scaffold) and uniformity (kernel density estimation on the unit hypersphere), and interpretability by visualizing attention weights in the functional prompt mechanism across diverse molecular property tasks.
content.result:
KANO consistently outperformed all baselines across all 14 datasets. On classification tasks, it achieved significant improvements, e.g., a 3.39% gain on the challenging ToxCast dataset (617 tasks). On regression tasks, it showed a 15.8% relative improvement on average, with particularly strong gains (21.7% average) on small-data regimes like ESOL and FreeSolv. KANO even surpassed models that use 3D structural information on quantum mechanical tasks, highlighting the power of its knowledge-guided 2D learning.

The ablation studies confirmed that every component of ElementKG is crucial: removing class hierarchy, functional groups, or data properties led to performance degradation, with data properties being especially vital. The functional prompt mechanism was shown to be superior to naive feature integration methods, providing an 8.41% relative improvement over a version without prompts.

Representation analysis revealed that KANO’s embeddings exhibit superior alignment (molecules with the same scaffold cluster tightly) and uniformity (features are more evenly distributed on the hypersphere) compared to baselines. Interpretability analysis demonstrated that the functional prompts assign high attention to chemically relevant groups: e.g., azo and pyridyl groups for toxicity, aromatic heterocycles for BACE inhibition, and fluoro/hydroxyl groups for hydration free energy. These findings validate that KANO’s predictions are grounded in sound chemical principles.

The authors note limitations, including ElementKG’s current scope and the prompts’ potential inability to capture long-range interactions. Future work includes expanding ElementKG, deepening interpretability studies, and combining KANO with other techniques for small-data drug discovery.

memory.abstract: This paper introduces a periodic polymer graph representation that explicitly encodes polymer chain periodicity and combines it with a message-passing neural network to automatically learn chemically relevant descriptors, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on 8 out of 10 polymer property prediction tasks.

content.background: Polymers are essential materials with diverse applications due to their tunable chemical structures, which can be modified through monomer selection, propagation sites, chain length, and additives. However, navigating this vast design space to identify optimal polymers for specific applications remains a significant challenge. Machine learning (ML) offers a promising route to accelerate polymer discovery by learning structure–property relationships, but its success hinges on the quality of polymer representations used as model inputs. Traditional approaches often represent polymers via their monomer repeat units using SMILES strings, molecular descriptors, or monomer graphs—methods originally developed for small molecules. These representations fail to capture the periodic, extended nature of polymers, leading to three critical issues: (i) non-unique representations for distinct polymers sharing the same monomer (e.g., polyvinyl alcohol vs. polyethylene glycol), (ii) incorrect bonding environments due to artificial fragmentation of functional groups (e.g., ether groups broken in monomer representation), and (iii) inconsistency under trivial translations along the polymer backbone. These limitations result in unreliable property predictions and hinder the development of robust ML models. Although message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) have shown success in learning descriptors for small molecules, their application to polymers has not adequately addressed periodicity. Prior graph-based polymer representations—such as dimer or trimer graphs—improve uniqueness but still misrepresent terminal atoms. Crystal graph representations for 3D periodic solids offer inspiration, but a tailored solution for 1D polymeric chains is needed. This work addresses these gaps by introducing a periodic polymer graph representation that explicitly encodes polymer periodicity, enabling accurate and consistent featurization while leveraging MPNNs to automatically learn chemically relevant descriptors without human-designed features.
content.method:
The core innovation of this work is the periodic polymer graph representation, which modifies standard molecular graphs to explicitly incorporate the 1D periodicity inherent in polymer chains. In conventional monomer graphs, atoms are nodes and bonds are edges, but the representation terminates at the monomer boundaries, breaking the true connectivity of the infinite polymer chain. To resolve this, the authors construct a graph from the monomer unit and add an artificial 'periodic edge' connecting the two terminal atoms of the repeat unit (e.g., linking the end carbon to the oxygen in a –C–C–O– backbone). This periodic edge ensures that all atoms experience their correct chemical bonding environment—as they would in an infinitely repeating chain—while maintaining a compact, finite representation. The approach is analogous to crystal graph representations used for 3D periodic materials, where a unit cell interacts with its periodic images; here, the monomer unit transmits chemical information through the added periodic bond.

This graph is then processed by a message-passing neural network (MPNN), specifically the Chemprop architecture, which uses directed bond-level messages rather than atom-level updates. The MPNN begins by initializing learned feature vectors for each atom and bond. Over multiple message-passing steps (T = 3 in this work), information propagates along edges, allowing each atom’s embedding to aggregate chemical context from its extended neighborhood. Critically, the periodic edge enables messages to flow between terminal atoms, ensuring that embeddings reflect the true periodic structure. After message passing, atom embeddings are combined into a single graph-level vector encoding, which is then passed through a two-layer feed-forward neural network (300 neurons per layer, ReLU activation) to predict the target property.

The synergy between the periodic graph and MPNN is key: the graph provides a physically faithful scaffold that preserves periodicity and correct bonding, while the MPNN automatically learns descriptors optimized for the prediction task—eliminating reliance on handcrafted features. The authors note that constructing the periodic graph from a trimer (instead of a monomer) yields negligible performance gains, so the monomer-based periodic graph is used for computational efficiency. This design ensures that polymers with identical monomer SMILES but different connectivities (e.g., head-to-tail vs. head-to-head) produce distinct graph representations, resolving the non-uniqueness problem. Furthermore, because the representation is translation-invariant along the chain, it avoids inconsistencies from arbitrary monomer definitions. The method thus unifies physical accuracy (via periodic graph construction) with data-driven learning (via MPNN), enabling the model to extract chemically meaningful features directly from property data.
content.experiment:
The authors evaluate their approach on a comprehensive dataset of 15,219 data points spanning 10 distinct polymer properties: atomization energy, crystallization tendency, band gap (chain and bulk), electron affinity, ionization energy, refractive index, dielectric constant, glass transition temperature (Tg), and density. These properties cover thermal, structural, optical, and electronic domains and are sourced from both experimental measurements (Tg and density from PoLyInfo) and computational calculations (DFT-based, from Khazana). The dataset includes 9,935 unique homopolymer structures.

Three main representations are compared: (i) molecular descriptors (200 features from RDKit, including chemical characteristics and fragment fingerprints) paired with a Random Forest (RF) model (500 trees); (ii) monomer graphs processed by an MPNN; and (iii) periodic polymer graphs processed by the same MPNN architecture. All models use fivefold cross-validation with an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split and are trained for 50 epochs, with the best model selected based on validation RMSE.

To isolate the impact of graph construction, ablation studies compare monomer, dimer, trimer, and periodic polymer graphs (all using the same MPNN). Additionally, a targeted experiment evaluates performance on a subset of 181 Tg data points where multiple polymers share the same monomer representation (e.g., polyvinyl alcohol vs. polyethylene glycol), testing the ability to distinguish structurally distinct polymers.

Finally, to understand the source of performance gains, the authors extract learned descriptors from the final hidden layer of the MPNN/periodic polymer graph model and train an RF model on these embeddings. They also correlate the top learned features with known RDKit descriptors to interpret chemical relevance.
content.result:
The periodic polymer graph/MPNN model achieves state-of-the-art performance on 8 out of 10 property prediction tasks, with a 20% average reduction in RMSE compared to monomer-based graph models and a 30% reduction compared to RF/molecular descriptors. Notably, it significantly improves predictions for atomization energy (RMSE: 0.039 vs. 0.055 for monomer graph), band gaps (chain: 0.413 vs. 0.509; bulk: 0.498 vs. 0.614), and electron affinity (0.288 vs. 0.326). For Tg, the periodic graph reduces RMSE from 39.83°C to 37.35°C. The only exception is crystallization tendency, where all models perform poorly (R² < 0.3), likely due to low-fidelity data from group contribution methods.

The ablation study confirms that periodicity is critical: removing the periodic edge (yielding a trimer graph) increases error by 6% on average. Dimer and trimer graphs perform similarly, but both outperform monomer graphs, highlighting the value of extended connectivity. The targeted Tg experiment on ambiguous monomers shows dramatic improvement: the monomer graph predicts identical Tg values for distinct polymers (RMSE = 62°C), while the periodic graph achieves RMSE = 19°C by correctly distinguishing their structures.

Analysis of learned descriptors reveals that the MPNN autonomously identifies chemically relevant features—such as polar group presence and ring rigidity—correlating strongly with known Tg determinants. An RF model trained on these learned embeddings matches the full MPNN’s performance, proving that the gains stem from superior representations, not model architecture. Limitations include current applicability only to homopolymers and linear chains; copolymers (block, random) and branched architectures require extensions. Future work could incorporate chain length, branching ratios, or multi-scale structural information to capture additional polymer complexities.
