memory.abstract: This paper demonstrates that BigSMILES achieves polymer property prediction accuracy comparable to SMILES while enabling faster model training and lower computational costs due to its more compact textual representation, establishing it as a practical and efficient alternative for polymer machine learning tasks.

content.background: Polymer machine learning (ML) has been hindered by the inherent structural randomness and complexity of polymers, which conventional molecular representations struggle to capture effectively. The Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES), widely successful for small molecules, lacks the expressiveness needed to represent diverse polymer architectures—particularly random block copolymers and other complex macromolecular topologies. To address this, researchers introduced Polymer-SMILES (pSMILES), which uses '**' symbols to denote polymerization points, and later, BigSMILES—a more comprehensive, structurally grounded line notation capable of encoding any polymer structure, including stochastic and multiblock systems. BigSMILES has gained traction in the polymer community and is now the default representation in emerging polymer databases like CRIPT. However, despite its theoretical advantages, the practical utility of BigSMILES in polymer ML workflows remains underexplored. Specifically, it is unclear whether BigSMILES improves model performance, computational efficiency, or both, compared to SMILES or pSMILES. This gap is critical because as polymer datasets grow exponentially—e.g., with candidate spaces for polyimides estimated at ~2×10¹² compounds—efficient and expressive representations become essential for scalable, sustainable ML. Moreover, current cheminformatics tools do not yet support BigSMILES for descriptor computation, limiting comparisons to text- and image-based ML approaches. Thus, a systematic benchmark of BigSMILES against SMILES in representative polymer ML tasks is urgently needed to validate its practical value and guide future adoption in polymer informatics.
content.method: The study evaluates BigSMILES against SMILES across two primary ML input paradigms: (1) text-induced binary images processed by convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and (2) raw textual strings processed directly by large language models (LLMs). For the CNN approach, polymer representations (SMILES or BigSMILES) are converted into binary images where each character is mapped to a pixel grid. These images serve as inputs to a CNN architecture comprising two convolutional layers (with 256 and 128 kernels, respectively), each followed by pooling, and a fully connected layer with 100 neurons. This setup follows prior work on glass transition temperature (Tg) prediction for homopolymers. For the LLM approach, the authors fine-tune PolyNC—a pre-trained end-to-end polymer language model—using either SMILES or BigSMILES as input strings and corresponding polymer properties as regression targets. PolyNC processes tokenized sequences via a Transformer architecture, enabling direct learning from textual representations. The fine-tuning uses consistent hyperparameters across tasks: batch size 80, 100 epochs, learning rate 1e-5, warmup ratio 0.2, and epsilon 1e-8, implemented on 4 NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. BigSMILES strings are generated from existing SMILES or molecular structures using two recently developed tools: BigSMILES_homopolymer for homopolymers and Olsen et al.’s structure-to-BigSMILES converter for complex architectures. Additionally, the authors adapt the polymer generation model PolyTAO—originally trained on SMILES—to BigSMILES using the PI1M dataset, maintaining identical training protocols except for the representation swap. The core theoretical premise is that BigSMILES’ syntax, which uses delimiters like '{<...>}' to compactly encode polymer connectivity and stochasticity, reduces token count while preserving chemical information. This compactness is hypothesized to lower computational load in sequence models without sacrificing representational fidelity. The methodological design thus isolates representation as the sole variable, enabling a controlled comparison of expressiveness, training efficiency, and predictive accuracy across diverse polymer tasks.
content.experiment: The experimental evaluation spans three main components: (1) CNN-based Tg prediction, (2) LLM-based multi-property regression, and (3) polymer generation. For the CNN task, the authors use a dataset of homopolymer Tg values (polystyrenes and polyacrylates) from prior literature, split 80:20 into train/test sets. Both SMILES and BigSMILES strings are converted to binary images and fed into an identical CNN architecture over 100 epochs, with results averaged over five runs to account for randomness. The loss metric is relative absolute error (RAE). In the LLM experiments, nine polymer property datasets are used: atomization energy (AE), bandgap of chains (BG) and crystals (BGC), charge injection barrier (CIB), crystallization tendency (CT), electron affinity (EA), ionization energy (IE), CO₂ permeability (CO₂), and Tg of polyimides. All datasets exhibit near-normal distributions, ensuring balanced learning conditions. PolyNC is fine-tuned separately for each property using either SMILES or BigSMILES inputs, with performance measured by mean absolute error (MAE) and training time (in seconds). Token lengths are analyzed to explain timing differences. For generation, the SMILES-based PolyTAO model is retrained on PI1M using BigSMILES, with validity of generated structures assessed qualitatively. Baselines are strictly representation-based—SMILES vs. BigSMILES—with all other factors (model architecture, hyperparameters, data splits) held constant. Ablation is implicit in the controlled design: by swapping only the representation, the study isolates its impact. Notably, descriptor-based methods are excluded because BigSMILES is not yet supported by cheminformatics libraries like RDKit, limiting the comparison to text/image pipelines.
content.result: The results demonstrate that BigSMILES achieves performance comparable to SMILES across diverse polymer ML tasks while offering significant computational advantages. In the CNN-based Tg prediction task, BigSMILES-CNN yields a test RAE of 16.57 ± 0.28%, statistically indistinguishable from SMILES-CNN’s 16.46 ± 0.12%, confirming equivalent predictive accuracy for homopolymers. In LLM fine-tuning across nine properties, BigSMILES-based models show slightly higher MAEs than SMILES-based ones—likely because PolyNC was pretrained on SMILES—but the difference is marginal, indicating that BigSMILES retains sufficient chemical information for accurate property prediction. Crucially, BigSMILES consistently reduces fine-tuning time: for example, a representative polymer requires 24 tokens in BigSMILES versus 27 in SMILES due to more efficient encoding of polymerization sites (e.g., '{<...>}' vs. '[*]...[*]'). This token reduction translates to faster training and lower energy consumption, a critical advantage as polymer datasets scale. However, in polymer generation, the BigSMILES-adapted PolyTAO model produces fewer valid structures than its SMILES counterpart, suggesting that BigSMILES’ syntax may convey weaker chemical constraints or that current tokenizers are suboptimal for its grammar. The authors attribute this to insufficient syntactic richness or lack of BigSMILES-specific tokenization. Overall, BigSMILES proves to be a viable, often superior alternative to SMILES in polymer ML—matching accuracy while improving efficiency. Future work should focus on refining BigSMILES syntax, developing dedicated tokenizers, and integrating it into cheminformatics tools to unlock descriptor-based modeling. As polymer data volumes grow, these efficiencies could accelerate both forward prediction and inverse design pipelines.

memory.abstract: This paper proposes Chem-DAGNN, a chemical-knowledge-based interpretable graph neural network that leverages small data by augmenting polyimide-specific datasets with diverse polymer glass transition temperature data, enabling the rapid discovery and experimental validation of 89 novel polyimides with exceptional heat resistance (Tg > 405°C, up to 450°C).

content.background: Polymers with exceptional heat resistance, particularly polyimides (PIs), are critical for next-generation flexible organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), where processing temperatures for low-temperature polycrystalline silicon thin-film transistors (LTPS-TFTs) exceed 350°C and can reach 400°C. This necessitates PIs with high glass transition temperatures (Tg) to maintain shape stability under such thermal stress. However, the pool of known PIs capable of withstanding such extreme temperatures is extremely limited. Traditional Edisonian approaches to polymer discovery are inefficient due to the vast chemical space of possible PI structures, making exhaustive experimental screening impractical. Machine learning (ML) offers a promising alternative for accelerating materials discovery, but its application to polymer design is hindered by the 'small data' problem: available datasets for specific polymer properties like Tg are typically sparse (ranging from 40 to 500 entries) and nonuniform in chemical structure coverage. This scarcity and imbalance—particularly the overrepresentation of rigid structures and underrepresentation of flexible motifs in PI datasets—lead to models that overfit and generalize poorly. While pretraining and transfer learning have been explored, they often require substantial computational resources and can suffer from performance degradation due to distribution shifts. Thus, a fundamental challenge remains: how to develop high-performance, generalizable ML models for polymer property prediction using limited, biased data in a data-efficient manner. This work addresses this bottleneck by proposing a chemical-knowledge-based strategy that leverages existing Tg data from diverse polymers—not just PIs—to enrich the training chemical space, thereby enabling more accurate and robust predictions without extensive data mining or computationally expensive pretraining.
content.method:
The authors propose Chem-DAGNN (Chemical-knowledge-based Data Augmentation Graph Neural Network), a strategy that enhances ML model performance for polymer Tg prediction under small-data constraints by strategically expanding the chemical space of the training data. The core idea is inspired by chemical intuition: rather than relying solely on scarce PI-specific data (Dataset 1, n=373), the model incorporates readily available Tg data from a broader set of diverse polymers (Dataset 0, n=314), which collectively provide a more comprehensive and balanced representation of functional groups and chain flexibilities. This chemical-knowledge-based data augmentation merges Dataset 0 and Dataset 1 into an Enhanced-Dataset (n=687), creating a more uniform chemical space for model training.

The ML architecture is an atom-wise Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). Polymer structures are represented using Polymer SMILES (P-SMILES), where polymerization points are marked with asterisks (*). Each polymer is converted into a molecular graph where nodes represent atoms and edges represent bonds. The GCN uses 75 atomic features (including atomic number, degree, formal charge, hybridization, and bond types) and learns latent representations through iterative message passing. At each graph convolution layer k, each atom i aggregates messages from its neighbors N(i) via a message aggregation function φₘᵏ (eq. 1), then updates its own feature vector hᵢᵏ using a message combination function φᵤᵏ (eq. 2). This allows atoms to 'perceive' their local chemical environment. After multiple convolution layers, a readout function R (eq. 3)—specifically, a sum operation via GraphGather from DeepChem—aggregates all atom-level features into a single molecular feature vector, which is then fed into a feed-forward neural network to predict Tg.

To ensure interpretability and validate that the model learns correct chemical knowledge, the authors employ an Atomic Contribution Map (ACM), derived from RDKit’s SimilarityMaps method. ACM visualizes the contribution of each atom to the predicted Tg: green indicates positive contribution, red negative, with color intensity reflecting magnitude. Additionally, to quantitatively assess the uniformity of the chemical space, they use t-SNE to project molecular fingerprints (2048D from RDKit) into 2D, then compute the Radial Distribution Function (RDF) on this space. RDF peak positions indicate characteristic inter-data-point distances, while peak intensities reflect data density; fewer, broader peaks suggest a more uniform chemical space, which is hypothesized to improve model generalization. This combination of data augmentation, interpretable GCN, and chemical space analysis forms a synergistic framework for data-efficient, knowledge-driven polymer discovery.
content.experiment:
The experimental setup begins with dataset curation. Dataset 1 (PIs, n=373) was manually collected from literature and a specialized handbook. Dataset 0 (diverse polymers, n=314) was selected from published sources for its accessibility, structural diversity, and balance with Dataset 1. Both datasets contain P-SMILES and experimental Tg values (°C). The Enhanced-Dataset (n=687) was formed by merging them. A large Candidate Dataset (>8.2 million PIs) was generated via virtual synthesis from commercially available monomers.

The Chem-DAGNN model (GNN_enhanced) was trained on the Enhanced-Dataset using an 80:20 train-test split, with hyperparameters (1–4 GCN layers, batch size 10/20, 1–2 hidden layers of 64–256 units, 10% dropout, ReLU activation, L2 loss) tuned for optimal performance. Model performance was evaluated using R², RMSE, and MAE. Ablation studies systematically varied the augmentation ratio (10–100% of Dataset 0) to assess the impact of chemical space enrichment.

Baseline comparisons were comprehensive. GNN_original, trained only on Dataset 1, served as the primary control. Performance was also benchmarked against 11 prior works (Kim38 to Chen45) covering a range of data sizes (42–7372 entries) and models (GPR, MLR, SVR, FFNN, RNN, GCN, Transformer), including pretraining-based transfer learning (Pretrain_split and Pretrain_cv). Substructure analysis used the BRICS algorithm to decompose polymers in Dataset 0, Dataset 1, and top candidates (Candidate 1: 1 million highest-predicted-Tg PIs) to identify key motifs.

For experimental validation, a top-down screening pipeline was applied: first selecting PIs with predicted Tg > 350°C or in the top 100,000, then filtering by synthetic accessibility (SAscore < 3.2) to yield 89 candidates (Candidate 2). From these, four ML-screened PIs and four ML-inspired 3,4′-isomer PIs were synthesized via a two-step process (polyamide acid formation followed by thermal imidization). Their structures were confirmed by FTIR and GC/MS. Tg was measured by DSC (thermodynamic) and DMA (kinetic, using tan δ peak as the criterion). Interpretability was assessed via ACM on all eight synthesized PIs, and novelty was confirmed using TMAP to ensure they were absent from the training/test sets.
content.result:
Chem-DAGNN achieved state-of-the-art performance, with GNN_enhanced attaining R² = 0.95 ± 0.004, significantly outperforming GNN_original (R² = 0.86) and all prior baselines (R² < 0.90), representing up to a 46% improvement. This demonstrates that chemical-knowledge-based augmentation is more effective than simply increasing data volume or using complex architectures like Transformers (which required 7 days of training vs. <1 hour for Chem-DAGNN). Ablation studies revealed that model performance improved as augmentation enriched the chemical space, plateauing at ~60% supplementation. RDF analysis confirmed that performance gains correlated with increased chemical space uniformity (fewer RDF peaks), validating the hypothesis that uniformity—not just quantity—drives generalization.

Interpretability analysis via ACM showed that GNN_enhanced correctly identified key Tg-enhancing substructures (e.g., phenyl rings in PI-0), whereas GNN_original misattributed their effects. Substructure analysis revealed that high-Tg candidates were enriched in aromatic rings and secondary amines (enabling hydrogen bonding), and that 3,4′-isomeric PIs—less common in literature—were predicted to have superior heat resistance. Experimental validation confirmed this: all eight synthesized PIs exhibited exceptional heat resistance, with DMA-measured tan δ peaks exceeding 405°C and two (PI-2b, PI-3b) surpassing 450°C. Notably, GNN_original failed to identify half of the top candidates, underscoring Chem-DAGNN’s superior discovery capability. The method’s main limitation is its reliance on P-SMILES, which omits critical polymer characteristics like molecular weight and crystallinity; future work could integrate more expressive representations like BigSMILES. Nonetheless, Chem-DAGNN provides a highly efficient, interpretable, and experimentally validated framework for small-data polymer discovery.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces a Strongly Correlated Neural Network (SCN) that represents molecular units as adaptive neural networks and uses a self-consistent feedback loop to model strong correlations, enabling accurate forward structural prediction and one-to-many inverse design in the HP lattice protein model.

content.background: Structural prediction and inverse design in polymer and protein physics involve mapping between molecular sequences (e.g., amino acid chains or block copolymers) and their resulting three-dimensional structures. Traditional approaches rely on physics-based simulations such as Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, or self-consistent field theory, which are computationally intensive and often require detailed knowledge of interaction potentials and thermodynamic ensembles. While machine learning, particularly neural networks (NNs), has been increasingly applied to physical problems—such as phase classification, partition function estimation, and solving differential equations—most existing NN methods focus on dimensionality reduction or simplified representations of molecular units (e.g., one-hot encoding or static vectors). These approaches lack the flexibility to model how each molecular unit dynamically responds to its local environment and collectively influences the global structure. This limitation becomes especially critical in inverse design, where multiple sequences may fold into the same structure (degeneracy), requiring a model capable of one-to-many mappings. The paper addresses these bottlenecks by proposing a novel framework that treats molecular units not as fixed symbols but as adaptive neural networks, enabling strong correlations through a self-consistent feedback mechanism. This approach aims to capture the emergent structural complexity arising from molecular interactions without explicit physical modeling, thereby bridging the gap between sequence information and spatial organization in both forward and inverse problems.
content.method:
The core innovation of the paper is the Strongly Correlated Neural Network (SCN), a framework that reimagines molecular units as individual neural networks rather than static encodings. In the SCN architecture, each molecular entity (e.g., H or P in the HP model) is represented by a feed-forward neural network in an 'identity layer.' All instances of the same entity share identical network parameters but receive distinct inputs based on their local context, allowing each unit to produce environment-dependent outputs. This design grants maximal adaptability, contrasting sharply with conventional one-hot or vector-based representations that lack dynamic responsiveness.

The outputs from the identity layer are fed into a deep convolutional neural network (CNN), which performs nonlinear mixing to establish correlations among all units. Critically, the CNN produces two output channels: a Result Channel (RC) that predicts the physical feature of interest (e.g., folded coordinates), and a Self-Consistent Channel (SCC) that feeds back into the identity layer’s input. This feedback loop enforces a self-consistency condition: the input vector **v** to the identity layer must satisfy **v = F(v)**, where **F** encapsulates the combined transformation through the identity layer and CNN. Convergence to this fixed point ensures that all molecular units are strongly correlated in a high-dimensional network space, mimicking the physical self-assembly process.

The SCN is trained via supervised learning. In the forward problem (structural prediction), the input is a sequence (feature 1), and the RC outputs probabilities for folding directions on a lattice, which are compared to known native structures using a cross-entropy loss. In the inverse problem (inverse design), roles are reversed: the input becomes the target structure (now feature 1), and the RC predicts the sequence (now feature 2). The self-consistent loop’s sensitivity to initial conditions enables one-to-many predictions—multiple sequences can be generated for a single structure by initializing the loop with different random environmental inputs, naturally accommodating degeneracy.

This architecture synergistically combines local adaptability (via identity networks), global correlation (via CNN), and iterative self-consistency to emulate physical folding without explicit energy functions. The method thus embeds the physics of self-assembly implicitly through learned network parameters, offering a data-driven alternative to traditional simulation-based approaches.
content.experiment:
The authors evaluate the SCN using the 19-mer HP lattice model, a well-established benchmark in protein folding where sequences of hydrophobic (H) and hydrophilic (P) monomers fold on a 2D square lattice to minimize H-H contact energy. The dataset comprises 13,454 sequences with unique native structures, split into 11,454 for training and 2,000 for testing in the forward problem. For the inverse problem, the 1,345 unique structures (from 13,454 sequences) are divided into 1,145 (from 12,482 sequences) for training and 200 (from 972 sequences) for testing.

In the forward setup, the identity layer consists of 19 feed-forward networks (one per monomer), each with one hidden layer of 50 neurons and 8-dimensional input/output vectors. The CNN includes two convolutional layers and fully connected layers, outputting an SCC (19×8) and an RC of size (17×3), representing directional probabilities for monomers 3 to 19 (monomers 1 and 2 are fixed to break symmetry). Training minimizes cross-entropy loss over 10 self-consistency loops per epoch.

The SCN is compared against three baselines of similar capacity: (1) Vector (VEC), where each entity is a trainable 8D vector; (2) Scalar (SCL), using fixed scalars (e.g., 0/1); and (3) Fully Connected NN (FNN), a standard deep network without identity-layer structure or feedback. All models use identical datasets and training protocols.

For inverse design, the identity layer represents structural turns ('left', 'forward', 'right') as three entity types, each with its own network. The RC outputs a 19×2 matrix predicting H/P probabilities. To handle degeneracy, the authors perform M prediction trials per structure using different random initializations of the SCC input, measuring Designability (D: % of structures with ≥1 correct sequence) and Recoverability (R: % of all correct sequences recovered).

Ablation is implicit in the comparison with VEC/SCL/FNN, which lack the self-consistent feedback loop and adaptive identity networks, isolating the contribution of strong correlation and dynamic representation.
content.result:
In structural prediction, the SCN achieves ~80% accuracy on the test set—defined as exact reproduction of native coordinates—significantly outperforming VEC (~60%), SCL (~40%), and FNN (~50%) (Fig. 2). Training accuracy also rises steadily, confirming effective learning. Although SCN is computationally slower due to self-consistency loops, the trade-off is justified by superior performance.

For inverse design, SCN demonstrates robust one-to-many capability. As the number of prediction trials (M) increases, both Designability (D) and Recoverability (R) improve, with R reaching ~60% at M=2000 (Fig. 3a). Performance varies with degeneracy (g): structures with higher g (more sequences per fold) show greater recoverability, as expected (Fig. 3b). This confirms SCN’s ability to sample degenerate solutions by leveraging initial-condition sensitivity in the self-consistent loop—a feature absent in conventional models.

The key advantage of SCN lies in its biologically inspired design: by treating molecular units as responsive agents and enforcing global consistency, it captures emergent structural correlations without explicit physics. Limitations include computational overhead from iterative loops and reliance on exhaustive datasets for training. Future work could extend SCN to 3D off-lattice models, incorporate solvent effects, or integrate with generative models for de novo design. The framework’s success in both forward and inverse tasks highlights its potential for broader applications in soft matter and biomolecular engineering.

memory.abstract: This Account presents a machine learning-assisted design framework for advanced polymeric materials, addressing data scarcity and multiscale structure–property complexity through novel representations (e.g., polymer fingerprints), multifidelity modeling, and high-throughput virtual screening, thereby accelerating the discovery of high-performance polymers.

content.background: Polymeric material research is undergoing a paradigm shift driven by machine learning (ML) and big data, moving beyond traditional labor-intensive trial-and-error approaches. Historically, material innovation relied on empirical experimentation (first paradigm), theoretical modeling (second), and computer simulations (third). The emergence of the fourth paradigm—data-intensive science—has enabled ML-assisted design as a powerful strategy for accelerating the discovery of high-performance polymeric materials. However, this approach faces significant challenges: the relative scarcity of high-quality polymer data and the inherent complexity of multiscale structure–property relationships in polymers, which span from molecular repeating units to chain architectures and aggregation morphologies (e.g., cross-linking, crystallization). Unlike small molecules or inorganic materials, polymers exhibit vast structural diversity and hierarchical organization, making their digital representation and property prediction particularly difficult. Existing cheminformatics methods—such as SMILES, molecular fingerprints, and graph representations—often fail to capture critical polymeric features like chain periodicity, branching, or cross-link density. Moreover, experimental polymer databases are limited in size and scope, especially for thermosets, and often lack consistency due to multisource, isomerous data (experimental vs. computational, numerical vs. spectral). These data and modeling bottlenecks hinder the development of accurate, generalizable ML models. This Account addresses these challenges by advocating for an integrated ML-assisted design framework that advances structure representation, leverages multifidelity data, and employs cutting-edge algorithms to enable virtual screening and rational design of advanced polymeric materials.
content.method:
The paper outlines a comprehensive ML-assisted design framework for polymeric materials structured around three core stages: (1) structure representation and database construction, (2) establishment of ML-based property prediction models, and (3) virtual design and high-throughput screening. 

In structure representation, the authors emphasize the need to move beyond conventional small-molecule descriptors to capture polymer-specific multiscale features. They review standard methods like SMILES (text-based), molecular fingerprints (binary feature vectors), and molecular graphs (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges), but highlight their limitations for polymers—e.g., SMILES cannot represent 3D conformation or chain topology unambiguously. To address this, they introduce advanced representations: BigSMILES, which extends SMILES with stochastic grammar to describe branching and connectivity; and a novel polymer fingerprint method that combines repeating-unit fingerprints with periodic graph embeddings to encode chain-scale information. Additionally, they propose cross-linking descriptors based on gelation theory to quantify network density in thermosets. Feature engineering further refines inputs via dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA, LASSO) and descriptor extraction (e.g., molecular weight, polarity via RDKit).

For database construction, the authors stress rigorous data curation from heterogeneous sources (literature, public databases like PolyInfo and Khazana, simulations). They note the scarcity of thermoset data and highlight their own 'AI plus Polymers' platform containing ~150,000 property entries for 34,000 structures. Data cleansing involves text similarity testing, entity recognition, and outlier removal via N-fold cross-validation to ensure consistency.

In model establishment, the focus is on selecting and optimizing ML algorithms for high-precision, extrapolative predictions. Standard models (GPR, random forest, neural networks) are discussed, but the emphasis is on advanced strategies to overcome data scarcity: multifidelity learning integrates low-fidelity simulation data with high-fidelity experiments via Gaussian process regression (GPR), where the high-fidelity surrogate Y_H(X) = Y_L(X) + Y_D(X) (Y_L from simulations, Y_D the correction term). Transfer learning and multitask learning leverage knowledge across related tasks or domains. For interpretability and physical grounding, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) embed physical constraints, while SHAP analysis reveals feature importance. Deep learning models like graph neural networks (GNNs) and transformers (e.g., TransPolymer) are highlighted for scalability.

Virtual design begins with 'gene' definition—modular structural or compositional units (e.g., epoxides/amines for resins)—which are combinatorially assembled into virtual candidates. High-throughput screening uses ML models to predict properties and identify top performers via multiobjective optimization: comprehensive scoring, Pareto frontier analysis, or Bayesian optimization (BO) for formulation design. BO converts multiobjective problems into single-objective via scalarizing functions and uses acquisition functions (e.g., expected improvement) to guide iterative exploration. Reverse design via generative models (VAEs, GANs) enables mutation and crossover of polymer genes to evolve structures toward target properties.
content.experiment:
The paper synthesizes multiple case studies from the authors’ recent work and literature to illustrate the ML-assisted design pipeline. Key datasets include: (1) polycyanurate resins with properties like hygroscopicity, coefficient of linear thermal expansion (CLTE), and tensile modulus; (2) poly(silane arylacetylene) (PSA) candidates for heat resistance and processability; (3) epoxy resin formulations combining 746 epoxides and 327 amines (~244k candidates); and (4) virtual polyimides (PIs) from PoLyInfo and combinatorial libraries (8 million candidates). Public databases referenced include PolyInfo, Khazana, and AI plus Polymers.

Experimental configurations vary by task. For polycyanurates, graph-based monomer representations feed into GPR models trained via multifidelity learning: low-fidelity data from molecular dynamics simulations are mapped to high-fidelity experimental data through a deviation-correction framework. Model performance is evaluated using R² and RMSE. In copolymer design, Ramprasad et al.’s multitask deep neural network uses Morgan fingerprints as input, with five-fold cross-validation and a meta-learner ensemble; performance is assessed on T_g, T_m, and T_d prediction.

Screening strategies are demonstrated through specific workflows. For PSAs, 368 candidates generated from silane/dyne genes are screened via ML-predicted thermal decomposition temperature and viscosity, with top candidates validated experimentally (e.g., PSNP-MV resin). Epoxy resins undergo multiobjective screening based on standardized mechanical property scores (modulus, strength, elongation), followed by synthesis of top candidates. Pareto frontier analysis for PIs identifies candidates exceeding existing performance boundaries in T_g–E–σ_y space. Bayesian optimization guides cocured polycyanurate formulation by iteratively maximizing a composite score of hygroscopicity, T_g, and modulus, with expected improvement (EI) as the acquisition metric.

Baseline comparisons are implicit: multifidelity GPR outperforms direct modeling on sparse data; multitask DNNs show superior transferability over single-task models; BO reduces experimental iterations versus grid search. Ablation studies include feature engineering impact (e.g., dimensionality reduction from 1081 to 8 descriptors improves epoxy model accuracy) and representation efficacy (polymer fingerprints vs. SMILES). Synthetic accessibility (SAscore < 3.8) is used as a post-screening filter for PIs, though noted as limited to monomer-level feasibility.
content.result:
The ML-assisted design framework demonstrates significant success in accelerating the discovery of high-performance polymers. In polycyanurate design, multifidelity GPR models achieved high precision by bridging simulation and experimental data, enabling identification of resins with simultaneously low hygroscopicity, low CLTE, and high modulus. For PSAs, ML screening led to PSNP-MV resin with T_d5 = 689°C and T_g = 608°C, surpassing existing analogs in both heat resistance and processability (processing window: 110–152°C). Epoxy resin screening yielded a candidate with tensile strength (89.25 MPa), modulus (3.85 GPa), and elongation (6.71%) closely matching predictions and outperforming known resins. Pareto-optimal PIs discovered via high-throughput screening exhibited properties beyond the frontier of existing materials. Bayesian optimization efficiently navigated compositional space, identifying cocured polycyanurates with balanced multiobjective properties in few iterations.

Key advantages include: (1) enhanced data efficiency via multifidelity/transfer learning; (2) improved representation fidelity through polymer-specific descriptors; (3) robust multiobjective optimization via BO and Pareto analysis; and (4) accelerated validation cycles. Limitations persist: data scarcity, especially for thermosets and processing parameters; inadequate synthetic accessibility metrics that ignore polymerization feasibility; and black-box model opacity, though mitigated by interpretable ML (SHAP, SISSO). Future directions emphasize polymer large models (e.g., PolyBERT, TransPolymer) trained on chemical language, high-throughput experimental platforms for data generation, and integration of processing descriptors (temperature, shear rate) into multiscale representations. The framework’s success underscores its potential to revolutionize polymer design for aerospace, energy, and electronics applications.

memory.abstract: The authors present RadonPy, an open-source Python library that automates all-atom classical molecular dynamics simulations to compute 15 thermophysical properties for over 1000 amorphous polymers, validates results against experiments, uses transfer learning to correct systematic biases, and identifies eight polymers with high thermal conductivity (>0.4 W/m·K) along with their underlying mechanisms.

content.background: Materials informatics (MI) has significantly advanced through the availability of large-scale, systematically curated computational property databases, particularly for inorganic crystals and small organic molecules (e.g., Materials Project, AFLOW, QM9). However, polymer informatics lags behind due to several key challenges: the high cost and computational complexity of generating polymer property data, the structural and processing diversity of polymers that complicates standardization, and industrial concerns about data sharing. Existing polymer databases like PoLyInfo rely on manually curated experimental data, which are sparse and lack multi-property records per polymer, while Polymer Genome provides limited first-principles data for only a few electronic/optical properties in crystalline or single-chain states. Crucially, no open-source platform existed to automate high-throughput all-atom classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—a powerful method for computing equilibrium and non-equilibrium properties of condensed-phase polymeric systems—due to the technical complexity of integrating molecular modeling, force field assignment, equilibration protocols, property calculations, and error handling into a unified, scalable workflow. This gap impedes data-driven polymer discovery, especially for thermophysical properties critical in modern applications like thermal management in miniaturized electronics. The authors thus developed RadonPy to address this bottleneck by enabling fully automated, large-scale MD-based property prediction for amorphous polymers, thereby creating a foundational resource for polymer informatics analogous to those that accelerated inorganic MI.
content.method: RadonPy is an open-source Python library that fully automates the end-to-end workflow of all-atom classical MD simulations for polymers, from chemical structure input to physical property output. The core input is a SMILES string representing a polymer repeating unit (with asterisks denoting connection points), along with parameters like polymerization degree, number of chains, and temperature. The workflow begins with conformational search of the repeating unit using RDKit’s ETKDG method, followed by geometry optimization and electronic property calculation (atomic charges via RESP/HF/6-31G(d), HOMO/LUMO, dipole moment, and polarizability via ωB97M-D3BJ DFT with appropriate basis sets) using Psi4. Polymer chains are then constructed via a self-avoiding random walk algorithm that preserves stereochemistry by aligning bonds coaxially during chain growth, ensuring atactic tacticity and controlling molecular weight (~1000 atoms per chain). Force field parameters are assigned using GAFF2, with modified parameters for fluorocarbons. An amorphous simulation cell (~10,000 atoms) is generated by random placement of 10 chains at low initial density (0.05 g/cm³), followed by a packing simulation (NVT, 300→700 K, Coulomb off, LJ cutoff 3.0 Å) to entangle chains without globule formation. Equilibration uses a 21-step compression/decompression protocol (NVT/NpT, 600↔300 K, 50,000↔1 atm) followed by extended NpT simulation until equilibrium criteria are met (e.g., RSD < 0.1% for density, <1% for Rg). Equilibrated cells are triplicated for reverse non-equilibrium MD (NEMD) to compute thermal conductivity via Müller-Plathe’s velocity-swap method (20 slabs, 200 fs swap frequency, NVE ensemble), with validation requiring linear temperature gradients (R² ≥ 0.95). Property calculations leverage equilibrium trajectories: density (mass/volume), Rg (chain conformation), Cp (enthalpy fluctuations), compressibility/bulk modulus (volume fluctuations), expansion coefficients (covariance of V and H), diffusion (Einstein relation), refractive index (Lorentz-Lorenz equation using DFT polarizability), dielectric constant (dipole fluctuations + n²), and nematic order (inertia tensor eigenvalues). Thermal conductivity decomposition uses the Irving-Kirkwood formalism to partition energy flux into convection, bond, angle, dihedral, improper, and nonbonded (including K-space) contributions. The entire pipeline is designed for supercomputing, with parallel execution across polymers, automatic restart on failure, and storage of trajectories (LAMMPS dump), properties (CSV), and final states (pickle).
content.experiment: The study computed 15 properties for 1138 homopolymers selected from PoLyInfo (15,335 polymers containing only H, C, N, O, F, P, S, Cl, Br, I), prioritizing those with available experimental data. Polymers spanned 20 backbone classes (e.g., polystyrenes, polyamides, polyimides). Automated MD succeeded for 1070 polymers (≥1 trial), 1001 (≥3 trials), and 759 (all 5 trials). Validation used 1001 polymers with ≥3 successful trials, comparing MD results against PoLyInfo experimental data meeting strict criteria: homopolymers, neat resin (no additives), 273–323 K, amorphous/unidentified state, linear/unidentified topology. Six properties were validated: density (N=382), thermal conductivity (N=34), refractive index (N=107), Cp (N=66), linear (N=165) and volume (N=144) expansion coefficients. Box size effects were tested on 28 polymers with 10–50 chains (1000–2000 atoms/chain), showing negligible impact. Transfer learning used shotgun fine-tuning: 100 neural networks pretrained on MD data (source task) were fine-tuned on 80%/10%/10% splits of experimental data (target task) for Cp, linear, and volume expansion coefficients. Model selection used validation RMSE, with performance reported on test sets. High-thermal-conductivity polymers (>0.4 W/m·K) were identified from 1070 polymers, requiring low SD (<0.05 W/m·K) across trials. Chemical space coverage was assessed via UMAP on ECFP6 fingerprints of 10-mer macrocycles. Decomposition analysis quantified thermal conductivity contributions for the eight high-conductivity polymers.
content.result: RadonPy successfully computed 15 properties for >1000 amorphous polymers, with strong validation against experiments: density (R²=0.890, slight underestimation due to lower polymerization degree), refractive index (R²=0.809, underestimation linked to density), and thermal conductivity (R²=0.490, limited by experimental variability and model-system gaps). Cp showed high correlation (R²=0.602) but systematic overestimation from missing quantum effects. Expansion coefficients had weak correlations (R²=0.178–0.217) due to high experimental/computational variability. Transfer learning dramatically reduced MD biases: Cp MAE dropped from 1916 to 196 J/kg·K, and expansion coefficient MAEs improved by 69–87%. Eight polymers with high thermal conductivity (>0.4 W/m·K) were identified, including six with unreported values. Mechanisms revealed via decomposition: hydrogen-bonding polymers (PI241, PI305) relied on nonbonded interactions (H-bonds, dipole-dipole), while rigid aromatic polyamides/imides (PI626, PI687, etc.) leveraged covalent bond contributions (stretching/bending). Joint property analysis showed Cp inversely proportional to density (Dulong-Petit law), thermal conductivity proportional to scaled Rg, and refractive index dominated by polarizability over density. UMAP confirmed broad chemical coverage without selection bias. Limitations include challenges in predicting properties sensitive to chain entanglement (e.g., viscoelasticity) and the need for experimental benchmark datasets with higher reliability. Future work will extend RadonPy to copolymers, blends, and oriented systems, adopt advanced notations like BigSMILES, and optimize storage by discarding intermediate trajectories.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces Joint Multi-domain Pre-training (JMP), a supervised pre-training strategy that trains a single model on 120M atomic systems from diverse chemical domains, enabling state-of-the-art performance on 34 of 40 downstream tasks and demonstrating that large-scale, multi-domain pre-training significantly improves generalization and scaling in atomic property prediction.

content.background: Machine learning (ML) for atomic property prediction has made significant strides, particularly through the development of ML potentials that approximate expensive quantum chemistry methods like Density Functional Theory (DFT). While large DFT-generated datasets such as OC20 have enabled progress, they are extremely costly to produce—e.g., OC20 required ~400 million CPU hours—making it impractical to generate bespoke datasets for every chemistry problem. Consequently, the common practice of training models from scratch for each downstream task is inefficient and limits generalization, especially in low-data regimes. Despite the success of foundation models (FMs) in natural language processing and computer vision, their adoption in atomic modeling has been limited. Most state-of-the-art results on key benchmarks like rMD17, MD22, SPICE, and MatBench still come from models trained from scratch, highlighting a gap in effective pre-training strategies. A core challenge lies in the heterogeneity of chemical space: applications span small molecules to periodic materials, data ranges from equilibrium to non-equilibrium structures (over 99.7% of OC20 is non-equilibrium), and properties vary from energies and forces to phonon peaks. Existing pre-training methods, often based on self-supervised denoising of equilibrium structures, are ill-suited for this diversity. This work addresses these limitations by proposing a supervised, multi-domain pre-training strategy that leverages diverse, large-scale datasets to learn generalizable representations, enabling strong transfer to both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.
content.method: The paper introduces Joint Multi-domain Pre-training (JMP), a supervised pre-training framework that treats each source dataset as a distinct task within a multi-task learning setup. JMP simultaneously trains a single backbone model on four large datasets—OC20, OC22, ANI-1x, and Transition-1x—comprising ~120 million atomic systems with energy and force labels, spanning catalysis and small molecules, and including both equilibrium and non-equilibrium configurations. The backbone architecture is GemNet-OC, a message-passing graph neural network chosen for its proven scalability and performance across chemical domains. During pre-training, each dataset is assigned its own energy and force prediction heads to accommodate differences in DFT functionals and software. Key technical innovations address imbalances inherent in multi-dataset training. First, temperature-based sampling with T=2 balances dataset contributions, preventing high-resource datasets from dominating. Second, a structure-wise loss reduction strategy replaces the default atom-wise averaging for force loss: instead of averaging over all atoms in a batch, the force loss is first averaged per system, then across systems. This ensures datasets with larger molecules do not disproportionately influence training. Third, loss coefficients are heuristically set per dataset: λ_E^(i)=1 and λ_F^(i)=⟨N⟩_D_i, the average number of atoms in dataset i, balancing energy and force contributions within each task without exhaustive hyperparameter tuning. For fine-tuning, pre-training heads are discarded, and new task-specific heads are initialized randomly; the entire model is then fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Forces are typically computed as the negative gradient of predicted energy (conservative forces), though direct force prediction is used when memory constraints prohibit gradient computation. The method is model-agnostic in principle but implemented with GemNet-OC. Regularization techniques—including elevated weight decay (0.1), edge dropout (p=0.1), and exponential moving average (EMA) weights—are integrated to mitigate overfitting and improve multi-task optimization, drawing on insights that strong regularization can obviate complex task-weighting schemes.
content.experiment: The evaluation spans six downstream datasets across three domains: small molecules (QM9, rMD17), large molecules (MD22, SPICE), and materials (MatBench, QMOF), totaling 40 tasks. Pre-training uses OC20 (100M), OC22 (8M), ANI-1x (2M), and Transition-1x (10M). Fine-tuning compares JMP against models trained from scratch (GN-OC-S/L, ~30M/235M parameters) and prior state-of-the-art (SOTA). Both small and large JMP variants are evaluated to probe scaling behavior. Training uses AdamW optimizer; pre-training employs linear warmup and cosine decay, while fine-tuning uses a sophisticated schedule combining warmup, cosine decay, layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD), and ReduceLROnPlateau. Ablation studies use a scaled-down pre-training set (~2.5M samples) and one task per downstream dataset. Key ablations test: temperature sampling (T=2 vs. T=∞ vs. T=1), structure-wise loss (SWL), weight decay (WD), dropout (DO), edge dropout (ED), EMA, and single-dataset (OC20-only) pre-training. Computational cost is analyzed via GPU hours and CO₂ emissions, with pre-training on 128×V100 GPUs. Dataset overlap between pre-training (ANI-1x, Transition-1x) and QM9 is assessed by excluding compositionally overlapping molecules. Additional experiments include few-shot rMD17 (50 samples), PDBBind binding affinity prediction, and comparisons to Zaidi et al. (2022)'s denoising-pretrained model.
content.result: JMP demonstrates substantial improvements over training from scratch: JMP-L achieves a 59% average relative improvement over GN-OC-L and matches or sets SOTA on 34 of 40 tasks. Critically, JMP enables effective scaling—while GN-OC-L underperforms GN-OC-S by 8% (indicating overfitting), JMP-L outperforms JMP-S by 21%, showing pre-training acts as a strong regularizer. Performance gains are consistent across domains: SOTA on 11/12 QM9 targets (except R²), 5/10 rMD17 molecules, all MD22/SPICE tasks, and all MatBench/QMOF materials tasks. Ablations confirm SWL (+7.7% over base) and regularization (WD/DO/ED, +11–13%) are crucial; OC20-only pre-training underperforms multi-domain JMP by 9.9%, highlighting the value of domain diversity. Computationally, JMP-L pre-training costs 34,400 GPU hours but reduces fine-tuning compute by 12× versus training from scratch (275 vs. 3,300 GPU hours to match performance). Dataset overlap analysis shows negligible impact on QM9 results, suggesting JMP learns generalizable representations rather than memorizing. Limitations include exclusive use of GemNet-OC backbone and discarding pre-training heads during fine-tuning. Future work could explore alternative architectures, head reuse, and larger models leveraging data/model parallelism.

memory.abstract: This paper presents DMPNN-MoE, a novel deep learning model integrating directed message passing neural networks with mixture-of-experts to accurately predict temperature-dependent small-molecule solubility across diverse solute-solvent systems, achieving state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization on a large curated dataset of 56,945 experimental measurements.

content.background: Solubility prediction is a cornerstone in drug development, materials science, and chemical engineering, as it directly influences absorption, formulation, and process design. Traditional approaches—such as the Abraham equation, Hildebrand and Hansen solubility parameters, and thermodynamic models like NRTL, UNIQUAC, and UNIFAC—rely heavily on extensive experimental data for parameter fitting, limiting their applicability to novel molecules. First-principles methods like COSMO-RS avoid parameter fitting but suffer from lower predictive accuracy. Recent machine learning (ML) advances, especially graph neural networks (GNNs), offer data-driven alternatives that require only molecular structure, enabling high-throughput predictions without quantum calculations or binary interaction parameters. However, most existing ML models are constrained to fixed solvents and constant temperatures, trained on narrow datasets that hinder generalization across diverse solute-solvent-temperature combinations. Some recent efforts have attempted generalized prediction: Ye et al. used LightGBM with extended connectivity fingerprints but employed random splits that allowed identical solute-solvent pairs at different temperatures to appear in both training and test sets, inflating performance. Yao et al. combined quantum descriptors with ML but required computationally expensive B3LYP/def2-TZVP calculations, limiting scalability. Vermeire et al. used transfer learning from water solubility to predict temperature-dependent solubility in organic solvents but struggled with absolute accuracy in multisystem or high-temperature regimes. These limitations underscore a critical need for a robust, generalizable, and computationally efficient model capable of accurate solubility prediction across diverse solvents and broad temperature ranges without reliance on costly descriptors or data leakage in evaluation.
content.method:
The paper introduces DMPNN-MoE, a novel deep learning architecture that synergistically combines Directed Message Passing Neural Networks (DMPNN) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to predict temperature-dependent small-molecule solubility. The core innovation lies in integrating directional graph message passing with dynamic expert specialization to capture complex solute-solvent interactions across heterogeneous chemical systems and temperatures.

Molecular inputs (solute and solvent) are represented as graphs where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Each atom is encoded as a 111-dimensional feature vector (including atom type, valence, formal charge, hybridization, etc.), and each bond as a 13-dimensional vector (bond order, conjugation, ring membership, stereochemistry). These graphs are constructed using RDKit and processed via DGL. Additionally, 29 molecular-level descriptors (e.g., TPSA, SlogP_VSA2) are computed via RDKit to enrich chemical context.

The DMPNN component enhances feature extraction by performing message passing over directed edges rather than undirected nodes. It initializes edge hidden states by concatenating source node and edge features: $h_{vw}^0 = \tau(W_i \cdot \text{cat}(x_v, e_{vw}))$. Messages are then propagated directionally: $m_{vw}^{t+1} = \sum_{k \in N(v) \setminus w} h_{kv}^t$, ensuring information flows along bond directionality and avoids redundant cycles. The edge state is updated as $h_{vw}^{t+1} = \tau(h_{vw}^0 + W_m \cdot m_{vw}^{t+1})$. After T iterations, node representations are aggregated from incoming edge states ($m_w = \sum_{v \in N(w)} h_{vw}^T$) and combined with initial node features to yield final node embeddings ($h_w = \tau(W_a \cdot \text{cat}(x_w, m_w))$). A global molecular vector is obtained by summing all node embeddings. For solute-solvent pairs, two independent DMPNNs generate separate feature vectors, which are concatenated with temperature and molecular descriptors to form a unified system representation: $h = \text{cat}(h_{\text{solute}}, h_{\text{solvent}}, T, x_m)$.

This system vector is fed into the MoE module, which comprises N expert networks and a gating network. Each expert $f_{\text{expert}_i}$ processes the same input to produce a prediction $y_i$. The gating network computes normalized weights via softmax: $g(h) = \text{softmax}(W_g \cdot h)$. The final output is a weighted sum: $y = \sum_i g_i(h) \cdot y_i$. This design allows the model to dynamically allocate computational focus—different solute-solvent-temperature combinations activate different expert subsets, enhancing adaptability across chemical diversity. The synergy arises because DMPNN captures fine-grained structural and interaction features, while MoE leverages this rich representation to specialize predictions contextually, improving robustness in heterogeneous data regimes.
content.experiment:
The study uses a curated dataset of 56,945 experimental solubility values (logS in mol/mol) spanning 791 solutes, 140 solvents, and temperatures from 243.15 to 403.15 K. Data were sourced from BigSolDB, CombiSolu-Exp, and literature, then rigorously cleaned: non-mole-fraction units, non-SMILES solvents, ionized solutes (SMILES with '.'), inconsistent duplicates, and solute-solvent pairs with <3 data points were removed. Remaining pairs were filtered by Van’t Hoff fit ($R^2 \geq 0.95$), ensuring thermodynamic consistency.

Model evaluation employed 10-fold cross-validation with a strict splitting strategy: all data for a given solute-solvent pair were assigned exclusively to either training or validation sets, preventing data leakage across temperatures. Performance was measured via MAE, MSE, RMSE, and $R^2$.

Baselines included graph-based models (DMPNN, MPNN, GINE, GAT, and their MoE variants) and descriptor-based models using RDKit (213 descriptors) or Mol2vec (300-dim fragment embeddings) paired with ANN, RF, or SVR. All models used identical training protocols and hyperparameters where applicable.

Ablation studies compared DMPNN vs. MPNN/GINE/GAT to isolate directional message passing benefits, and MoE-augmented vs. base models to assess expert specialization impact. Additional tests evaluated generalization: (1) rare solvents—2380 samples from solvents with <100 data points, tested against models trained on 54,565 samples (solvents ≥100 samples); (2) unseen solutes—1221 data points from 12 novel solutes absent from training, predicted by averaging 10 cross-validated models.

Comparisons with prior work used original datasets: Ramani et al.’s 5493-point dataset (273 K, 4:1 random split, 5-fold CV) and Vassileiou et al.’s 714-point dataset (298 K, 10-fold CV). DMPNN-MoE was retrained under identical splits and settings.

Feature importance was analyzed via random assignment (for one-hot/binary node/edge features) and permutation (for molecular descriptors), measuring $R^2$/RMSE changes over multiple trials.
content.result:
DMPNN-MoE achieved state-of-the-art performance with MAE = 0.256 ± 0.010 and $R^2$ = 0.863 ± 0.016 in 10-fold CV, outperforming all baselines by up to 35%. Ablation confirmed that both DMPNN’s directional message passing and MoE’s adaptive weighting contributed significantly: DMPNN alone outperformed MPNN/GINE/GAT, and MoE variants consistently surpassed their base models. Violin plots of error distributions showed DMPNN-MoE had the tightest, most symmetric spread, indicating superior robustness.

On rare solvents (2380 samples), the model retained strong performance (MAE = 0.341), with most predictions clustering near the diagonal in scatter plots. For 12 unseen solutes (1221 points), it achieved MAE = 0.413, with high accuracy for compounds like sulfentrazone (MAE = 0.155) and moderate errors for structurally complex cases like 5-hydroxy-1-methylpyrazole (MAE = 0.551). t-SNE visualization revealed MoE’s dynamic weighting: most samples engaged multiple experts (no single expert weight >0.7), demonstrating collaborative specialization.

Against prior methods, DMPNN-MoE surpassed MolMerger (MAE 0.51 vs. 0.78) and COSMO-RS/RF-pure (MAE 0.34 vs. 0.72/0.43), confirming its generalizability even on external datasets.

Feature analysis identified key solubility drivers: three-membered ring atoms, formal charge, iodine/sulfur presence (node); E/Z configuration, triple/double bonds (edge); and solute TPSA, SlogP_VSA2 (molecular descriptors). Solvent descriptors had minimal impact.

Limitations include reduced accuracy on rare solvents/unseen solutes due to training data gaps, and inapplicability to ionic liquids/polymers absent from the dataset. Future work will expand data coverage and incorporate system-specific descriptors to address these gaps.

memory.abstract: Uni-Mol is the first universal 3D molecular representation learning framework that pretrains SE(3)-equivariant Transformer models on 209M molecular conformations and 3M protein pockets, enabling state-of-the-art performance in both molecular property prediction and 3D spatial tasks like binding pose prediction and conformation generation.

content.background: Molecular representation learning (MRL) has emerged as a critical paradigm in drug design, where labeled data is scarce but the chemical space is vast. Traditional MRL methods predominantly represent molecules as 1D sequences (e.g., SMILES, InChI) or 2D topological graphs, which inherently lack explicit 3D structural information. However, from a life science perspective, molecular properties and drug effects are fundamentally governed by 3D geometry—such as conformation, binding pose, and spatial interactions. This limitation severely restricts the applicability of existing MRL models to 3D spatial tasks like protein-ligand binding pose prediction or molecular conformation generation, which are essential in structure-based drug discovery. Although recent attempts have incorporated 3D information via contrastive learning between 2D and 3D representations or by using geometric graph neural networks, their performance remains suboptimal, often due to small 3D datasets and the inability to directly use 3D coordinates as inputs and outputs during fine-tuning. These models typically treat 3D positions as auxiliary features rather than core modalities, preventing end-to-end 3D prediction. This bottleneck motivates the need for a universal, pure 3D MRL framework that can learn rich spatial representations from large-scale unlabeled 3D data and directly generate or refine 3D structures in downstream applications.
content.method:
Uni-Mol proposes a universal 3D molecular representation learning framework built on three core components: an SE(3)-aware Transformer backbone, large-scale pretraining on molecular and protein pocket conformations, and task-specific fine-tuning strategies.

The backbone is a modified Transformer architecture designed to process 3D atomic coordinates directly. Unlike standard Transformers that rely on discrete positional encodings, Uni-Mol uses continuous, SE(3)-invariant spatial encodings derived from pairwise Euclidean distances between atoms. These distances are passed through a pair-type-aware Gaussian kernel to generate initial pair representations. Crucially, Uni-Mol maintains both atom-level and pair-level representations throughout the network. The pair representation is updated via atom-to-pair communication using the Query-Key products from self-attention (Equation 1), while the atom representation is enhanced through pair-to-atom communication by injecting the pair representation as a bias in the attention mechanism (Equation 2). This bidirectional interaction efficiently captures 3D spatial relationships without significant computational overhead.

To enable direct 3D coordinate prediction—an essential capability for spatial tasks—Uni-Mol introduces an SE(3)-equivariant output head. This head computes delta positions based on the difference between final and initial pair representations (Equation 3), ensuring equivariance under rotation and translation. Unlike prior work such as EGNN, which uses absolute pair representations, Uni-Mol’s use of delta representations proves more effective, as validated in ablation studies.

Pretraining leverages two massive unlabeled datasets: 209 million molecular conformations (from 19 million molecules, each with 11 RDKit-generated conformers) and 3.2 million candidate protein pockets (extracted from RCSB PDB using Fpocket). The pretraining task is a 3D position recovery objective: input coordinates are corrupted by adding uniform noise (±1 Å), and the model is trained to recover the original positions. This is complemented by masked atom prediction (15% of atoms are masked). Notably, unlike BERT-style masking, continuous coordinates cannot be masked with a special token; instead, noise corruption with optional reassignment is used. Ablation shows that a noise range of 1 Å without reassignment yields optimal performance. The loss combines coordinate recovery (Smooth L1), pairwise distance prediction (Smooth L1), and atom type prediction (cross-entropy).

Fine-tuning strategies are tailored to task categories: (1) Non-3D tasks (e.g., property prediction) use the [CLS] token or mean atom representation with a linear head; (2) 3D molecule/pocket generation (e.g., conformation optimization) uses the SE(3) head to refine input conformers; (3) Protein-ligand binding pose prediction combines pretrained molecular and pocket encoders with a 4-layer decoder to predict inter-atomic distance matrices, which serve as a differentiable scoring function for gradient-based pose optimization—bypassing the instability of end-to-end coordinate prediction.
content.experiment:
Experiments evaluate Uni-Mol across four downstream domains using standardized benchmarks and rigorous protocols.

For molecular property prediction, Uni-Mol is tested on 15 MoleculeNet datasets using scaffold splitting (8:1:1) and 3 random seeds. Baselines include supervised models (D-MPNN, AttentiveFP) and pretrained models (GROVER, GraphMVP, MolCLR, GEM). Hyperparameters are tuned via grid search (Table 7), with smaller search spaces for large datasets. Performance is measured by ROC-AUC (classification) and RMSE/MAE (regression).

Molecular conformation generation uses GEOM-QM9 and GEOM-Drugs, following prior work. Uni-Mol optimizes RDKit-generated input conformers toward reference structures. Evaluation uses Coverage (COV) and Matching (MAT) metrics with RMSD thresholds of 0.5 Å (QM9) and 1.25 Å (Drugs). Baselines include traditional (RDKit) and deep learning methods (ConfGF, GeoMol, GeoDiff, DMCG). Uni-Mol uses recycling (4 iterations) and reports mean/median COV/MAT.

Pocket property prediction includes two settings: (1) NRDLD (113 samples) for druggability classification, compared against six prior methods; (2) a new regression benchmark with 164,586 pockets labeled by Fpocket-derived scores (Druggability, SASA, etc.), where Uni-Mol is compared against a non-pretrained variant (Uni-Molno_pretrained).

Protein-ligand binding pose prediction uses CASF-2016 as the test set and a filtered PDBbind General set (18,404 complexes) for training, excluding complexes with >40% protein sequence similarity (MMseqs2) or >80% ligand fingerprint similarity to test cases. Two evaluations are performed: (1) docking power (top-1 success rate in distinguishing native poses from decoys); (2) pose accuracy (% of predictions with RMSD ≤ threshold). Baselines include docking tools (AutoDock Vina, Smina) and DeepDock. Uni-Mol’s pose is optimized via backpropagation through the predicted distance matrix using LBFGS.

Ablation studies (Appendix D) systematically validate design choices: 3D positional encodings (GKPT best), pair representation (essential), SE(3) head (delta-based superior), pretraining strategy (MAP+3D optimal), and corruption scheme (1 Å noise best). Efficiency is benchmarked against vanilla Transformer and SE(3)-Transformer.
content.result:
Uni-Mol achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks. In molecular property prediction, it outperforms all baselines on 14 of 15 MoleculeNet datasets, with particularly large gains on 3D-sensitive tasks like QM7 (41.8 vs. 58.9 MAE for GEM) and FreeSolv (1.48 vs. 1.88 RMSE), demonstrating superior 3D representation learning. The only exception is SIDER, where Uni-Mol fails to generate valid 3D conformers for complex molecules (e.g., peptides), highlighting a limitation in conformation generation robustness.

In conformation generation, Uni-Mol sets new records on both GEOM-QM9 (97.95% COV, 0.1831 Å MAT) and GEOM-Drugs (91.91% COV, 0.7863 Å MAT), surpassing even non-pretrained deep models, and significantly outperforming RDKit. This confirms the effectiveness of its conformation optimization approach.

For pocket druggability, Uni-Mol achieves 97.3% accuracy on NRDLD (vs. 94.6% for TRAPP-CNN) and substantially outperforms its non-pretrained variant on the new regression benchmark, validating the value of pocket pretraining.

In binding pose prediction, Uni-Mol ranks 1st in CASF-2016 docking power (91.2% top-1 success) and achieves 80.35% of poses with RMSD ≤ 2 Å—22.58% relatively better than AutoDock Vina. It is also ~250× faster than traditional docking tools. However, its ligand-only conformation accuracy lags below 1 Å RMSD, suggesting room for improvement in end-to-end 3D refinement.

Ablations confirm that 3D pretraining, pair representation, and the SE(3) head are critical. The framework is highly efficient: only 6% slower than vanilla Transformer but >200× faster than SE(3)-Transformer.

Future work includes improving interaction modeling between pocket and ligand encoders, scaling model size, and developing higher-quality benchmarks.

memory.abstract: The paper introduces M3GNet, a universal graph deep learning interatomic potential trained on 187,000+ DFT relaxation trajectories from the Materials Project, which accurately predicts energies, forces, and stresses across 89 elements and enables high-throughput discovery of stable materials.

content.background: Interatomic potentials (IAPs) are essential for atomistic simulations, which underpin in silico materials design by enabling structural relaxation, dynamic simulations, and property prediction. While density functional theory (DFT) provides high accuracy in describing the potential energy surface (PES), its computational cost limits applicability to large systems or high-throughput studies. Classical IAPs, such as the embedded atom method (EAM) or universal force field (UFF), offer efficiency but suffer from narrow chemical applicability—often limited to single elements or small subsets—and poor transferability across diverse materials, especially crystalline solids. Recent advances in machine learning interatomic potentials (ML-IAPs), including neural network potentials (NNPs) and moment tensor potentials (MTPs), have improved accuracy by learning from DFT data using local environment descriptors. However, these models typically face combinatorial explosion in parameter count when extended to multi-element systems, limiting their universality. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown promise in modeling molecular and limited crystalline systems but lack the physical continuity required for IAPs—specifically, smooth energy, force, and stress responses to changes in bond topology. The emergence of large-scale DFT databases like the Materials Project, which contain not only final relaxed structures but also intermediate PES data (energies, forces, stresses from ionic steps), presents an unprecedented opportunity to train universal, accurate, and physically consistent IAPs. This work addresses the critical gap: the absence of a truly universal IAP applicable across the periodic table and all crystal types, which is necessary for accelerated discovery of novel functional materials.
content.method: The authors introduce M3GNet (Materials Graph Network with 3-body interactions), a universal graph deep learning interatomic potential that integrates the flexibility of GNNs with the physical rigor of traditional many-body potentials. The core innovation lies in a materials graph representation $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E}, \mathcal{X}, [\mathbf{M}, \mathbf{u}])$, where nodes ($\mathcal{V}$) represent atoms with embedded atomic numbers, edges ($\mathcal{E}$) represent bonds, $\mathcal{X}$ contains atomic coordinates, and $\mathbf{M}$ is the optional lattice matrix for crystals—enabling direct computation of forces and stresses via auto-differentiation. Unlike prior GNNs for materials property prediction, M3GNet explicitly incorporates three-body interactions inspired by potentials like Tersoff. The architecture comprises three stages: (1) **Featurization**: atomic numbers are embedded into a 64-dimensional learnable space; pairwise distances within a 5 Å cutoff are expanded into a smooth, differentiable basis (Kocer et al.) ensuring vanishing first and second derivatives at the cutoff. (2) **Many-body interaction module**: for each bond $ij$, three-body angles $\theta_{jik}$ are computed from neighbors $k \in \mathcal{N}_i \setminus j$. These angular interactions are expanded using spherical Bessel functions and spherical harmonics (Klicpera et al.), producing a vector $\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{ij}$ that encodes the local bonding environment. This is combined with atom embeddings via gated updates to form enriched bond features. (3) **Graph convolution blocks**: standard message-passing updates iteratively refine bond, atom, and optional state features using gated multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). The model uses three such blocks. Finally, a **readout module** sums atom-wise energies (computed via a gated MLP on updated node features) to yield total energy $E$; forces $\mathbf{f} = -\partial E / \partial \mathbf{x}$ and stresses $\sigma = V^{-1}\partial E / \partial \epsilon$ are obtained through automatic differentiation. This design ensures physical continuity—energy, force, and stress vary smoothly even as bonds form or break—while the graph structure naturally captures long-range interactions without increasing the cutoff radius. The elemental reference energies are pre-fitted via linear regression to stabilize training. The model is trained end-to-end on energies, forces, and stresses using a weighted Huber loss, with stress inclusion critical for accurate lattice relaxation.
content.experiment: The M3GNet IAP was trained on the MPF.2021.2.8 dataset derived from the Materials Project, containing 187,687 ionic steps from 62,783 compounds, with 187,687 energies, 16.9 million force components, and 1.7 million stress components across 89 elements. Data were split by material (90% train, 5% validation, 5% test), with three independent splits. Initial benchmarks used a single-element DFT dataset (Zuo et al.) for Ni, Cu, Li, Mo, Si, and Ge, comparing M3GNet against EAM, MEAM, NNP, and MTP. Two M3GNet variants were tested: element-specific models and a single 'M3GNet-all' model trained on all six elements. For universal training, three model variants were compared: M3GNet-E (energy-only), M3GNet-EF (energy+forces), and M3GNet-EFS (energy+forces+stresses). The final M3GNet-EFS model used a 5 Å radial cutoff (4 Å for three-body terms), three basis functions for distance expansion, three main blocks, and 64-dimensional embeddings, totaling 227,549 parameters. Training employed the Adam optimizer with cosine-decayed learning rate, Huber loss ($\delta=0.01$), and loss weights $w_f=1$, $w_\sigma=0.1$. Model performance was evaluated on structural relaxation accuracy (volume and energy errors vs. DFT), phonon and elasticity predictions (vs. DFT and DFPT data from Petretto et al. and de Jong et al.), and large-scale materials discovery. In discovery, 31.7 million hypothetical structures were generated via combinatorial isovalent substitution on ICSD prototypes, relaxed with M3GNet, and filtered by energy above the convex hull ($E_{\mathrm{hull-m}}$). Top candidates were validated with DFT. Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of including forces and stresses in training and demonstrated the model’s transferability to molecular systems (MD17 datasets) and general property prediction (Matbench).
content.result: M3GNet demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks. On single-element benchmarks, it outperformed classical potentials (EAM/MEAM) and matched or approached ML-IAPs (NNP/MTP), while the multi-element M3GNet-all model maintained comparable accuracy—highlighting its scalability. On the universal MPF dataset, M3GNet-EFS achieved test MAEs of 0.035 eV/atom (energy), 0.072 eV/Å (force), and 0.41 GPa (stress). Crucially, including stresses in training halved stress MAE versus M3GNet-EF, proving essential for lattice-sensitive applications. In structural relaxation, M3GNet reduced volume errors from >22% (initial structures) to <7% (vs. DFT), and energy MAE dropped from 0.169 to 0.035 eV/atom—sufficient for reliable stability assessment (as 90% of ICSD crystals lie within 0.067 eV/atom of the hull). Phonon DOS centers showed excellent agreement with DFPT (MAE 44.2 cm⁻¹, reducible to 28.8 cm⁻¹ after systematic shift correction), outperforming prior models. In large-scale discovery, M3GNet identified 1.85 million potentially stable materials from 31.7 million candidates. DFT validation of the top 2,000 candidates confirmed 1,578 as stable ($E_{\mathrm{hull-dft}} < 0.001$ eV/atom), including 574 new oxides. M3GNet-relaxed structures required ~3× less DFT time than unrelaxed inputs. The model also enabled rapid phonon screening, identifying 328 dynamically stable materials. Limitations include reliance on PBE-level training data (less accurate than well-converged DFT) and systematic phonon underestimation due to pseudopotential differences. Future improvements will leverage active learning and higher-quality data. M3GNet’s universality enables applications beyond crystals, including molecular force fields and general property prediction, as demonstrated on Matbench.
